scored.name: Natural Pearls in Estate Jewellery (Nacre / NaturalPearl / Nacre Lab)
scored.one_line: Buys antique pearl strands and jewels sold as 'cultured', 'costume' or generic 'pearls' at US, European, Indian and Gulf provincial estate auctions, uses ML over catalogue photos and text (pre-1930 dating, clasp hallmarks, drilling, lustre, size gradation, provenance words) to pick likely natural saltwater pearls, gets GIA/SSEF/Gübelin/LFG X-ray reports, and resells at Christie's and Sotheby's Geneva/Hong Kong.
scored.unproven_right: Title to an untested pearl lot bought for $50-5,000 from heirs and small houses that do not X-ray and assume cultured
scored.proving_step: Lab X-radiography/micro-CT natural-pearl report ($100-1,000); 'natural, saltwater' from GIA/SSEF is the accepted standard, functioning like NI 43-101; most fail (base rate ~1-3%)
scored.proven_buyer: Christie's/Sotheby's Magnificent Jewels buyers, Gulf and Indian natural-pearl dealers, Geneva and London dealers
scored.public_data: LiveAuctioneers, Invaluable, HiBid, Drouot, Lot-tissimo and Indian auction catalogues (millions of scattered photos and free text); historic Christie's/Sotheby's natural-pearl results as labels; probate inventories; GIA pearl research
scored.rough_step_up: $200-3,000 'cultured' strand to $20k-$5M natural, about 100-5,000x on a hit. Ladder: own pearl lab, estate-jewellery auction house, natural-gem inventory fund, branded high jewellery
scored.frame: The rung is: buy an untested lot, X-ray it, resell it with a report. Picking the lot is about 90% of the work and the physical steps (buying, shipping, the lab test) are trivial. Capitalised buyers exist: Christie's, Sotheby's, Bonhams and Woolley & Wallis buyers, plus Gulf and Indian dealers. Two things hold the score at 3. The output per hit is small. And photos cannot see a pearl's internal structure, so the ML only ranks priors (age, clasp, drilling, size spread); the X-ray does the real discovery.
scored.step_up: A typical hit is a small antique natural strand worth $2.5k-30k, not millions. Examples: a Skinner rope of 559 natural pearls (3.5-4.6mm, GIA report) estimated $2,500-3,500; a Bonhams three-row natural strand (4.1-6.3mm) sold for £7,680 in September 2025; a Woolley & Wallis strand (4.75-9.21mm, GIA report) made £31,500 in April 2025. Untested lots at provincial sales go for perhaps $200-1,000 (my estimate), so a typical hit is about 10-50x. The $1-5M results (Cowdray Pearls $3.35M at Christie's in June 2024; the $5M four-strand record at Christie's in 2016) are rare tail cases, and they almost always had known provenance before the sale. Most strands that test natural turn out mixed (for example 80 natural and 1 cultured), which cuts the value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap, not expensive. GIA's USD pearl schedule (April 2025) lists $50 for a single strand up to 25 inches and $60 over 25 inches. SSEF and Gübelin reports cost a few hundred dollars (my estimate). So the cost of a shot is mostly the lot price, about $200-1,000 plus buyer's premium, not the test. I found no published base rate. My estimate: 1-3% across all lots described as 'pearls', and 10-20% among obviously pre-1930 strands with period clasps, which simple rules already filter for. Because the test is so cheap, a buyer can X-ray everything plausible, so ML's capex lever is about 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The catalogue data is public and scattered (LiveAuctioneers, Invaluable, HiBid, Drouot) and not well summarised. Lots say 'pearl necklace' or 'untested', so the outcome is not sitting in a legible field, which is a plus. But the signal that matters is internal growth structure, and only X-ray shows it. Photos and text give weak priors (age, clasp, gradation, drill holes), and an experienced dealer reads those at a glance. Sotheby's says it assumes treatment unless a stone is stated natural, so the big houses default to cultured, but the trade knows the old-strand option is there.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought at auction from heirs and small houses. But it goes through competitive online bidding where specialist pearl dealers and pickers already bid up period 'untested' strands. The discount exists only on lots with poor descriptions or poor photos, and the 20-28% buyer's premium on each side eats into it.
scored.buyer: The final buyers are capitalised: Christie's and Sotheby's Magnificent Jewels clients, Gulf and Indian natural-pearl dealers, and London and Geneva dealers. They pay the proven price immediately once a GIA or SSEF 'natural, saltwater' report exists.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are a pearl lab, an estate-jewellery auction house, an inventory fund and a branded high-jewellery house. The whole natural-pearl auction market is probably $100-300M a year (my estimate), so there is no trillion-dollar chain. The rungs above are luxury retail and brand-building, where discovery gives no edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: The market is too small, and the value of a typical hit ($3-30k) does not scale. The signal that decides a hit (internal structure) is not in the public data at all. Only a $50 X-ray reveals it, and expert dealers already apply the visible priors. So ML adds little over a dealer's eye plus cheap blanket testing, and the 10^3x hits are rare cases with known provenance that big houses already catch.
scored.one_line_reason: A real arbitrage, but small: typical hits are 10-50x on $200-1,000 lots, the $50 GIA test makes blanket testing cheap, photos can't see the deciding signal, and the ladder tops out in a market of about $100-300M a year (my estimate).

scored.name: Old Master Sleeper Attribution (Sleeper / Sleeper Atelier / Sleeper Masters / Provenance Capital)
scored.one_line: Buys 'circle of', 'follower of', 'school of', 'entourage de' and unattributed old master and 19th-century paintings and drawings at US and European regional sales for $500-50k, uses ML over catalogue images, provenance chains (Getty Provenance Index, Lugt), RKD/Witt archives and digitised catalogues raisonnés to flag likely autograph or lost ex-collection works, then gets technical analysis (IRR, dendro, pigment) plus catalogue raisonné or committee acceptance and consigns to Christie's or Sotheby's evening sales.
scored.unproven_right: Title to an under-attributed work bought from regional houses and estates lacking specialist eyes or archive access
scored.proving_step: Technical analysis ($2-30k) plus inclusion in the catalogue raisonné or written acceptance by the recognised authority; a credentialed social consensus, softer than a slab or NI 43-101, with gatekeeping and refusal risk; most candidates fail
scored.proven_buyer: Christie's/Sotheby's Old Masters (guarantees, private sales), TEFAF-tier dealers (Agnews, Colnaghi, Weiss), museums
scored.public_data: Tens of millions of scattered multilingual regional auction images (Invaluable, LiveAuctioneers, Drouot, Lempertz); Getty Provenance Index; RKD; Frick and Witt photoarchives; Heidelberg/HathiTrust/Gallica digitised sale catalogues; museum open-access and technical imaging
scored.rough_step_up: 100-10,000x on a hit (Salvator Mundi ~$1.2k to $450M; many $5k to $0.5-5M); lumpy, slow and subjective proving weakens C1/C3. Ladder: dealer, restoration, art-backed lending, fund
scored.frame: The rung is "buy an under-attributed picture, get it re-attributed, consign it". Discovery and proving are about 80-90% of the work; the physical steps (cleaning, IRR, pigment tests) are cheap and can be outsourced. Capitalised buyers exist: Christie's and Sotheby's (which give guarantees), TEFAF dealers and museums. The weakness is the proving step. It is not an objective measurement like a drill core. It is the consent of a single named authority (the catalogue raisonné author or a committee) who can refuse, delay for years or later reverse the decision (the Salvator Mundi doubts, the Sotheby's Frans Hals fake). So the frame exists, but its gate is subjective.
scored.step_up: Real cases: Salvator Mundi sold for about $1,175 at a New Orleans regional sale in 2005 and for $450M at Christie's in 2017 (about 400,000x, but with 12 years of restoration and scholarship in between). An Artemisia Gentileschi was bought at a Danish auction for £30k and sold at Christie's for £1.9M less than a year later (about 63x). A Gerrit Dou attribution made €70k against a €4-6k estimate (France, 2024). The Thomaston "After Rembrandt" made $1.175M against a $10-15k estimate (Maine, 2024). That last case shows the step-up is often captured at the regional hammer itself by competing dealers, not by the buyer afterwards. My estimate of the typical realised step-up for a buyer who pays the contested hammer price is 3-50x. The 10^4 cases exist but are rare outliers.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published base rate. My estimate is that well under 10% of "circle of" or "follower of" lots that a specialist is willing to bid on get upgraded to autograph status. Cost per attempt is the purchase price ($500 to $50k, and contested lots get bid far above estimate) plus technical analysis ($2-30k, the candidate's figure) plus restoration ($5-50k, my estimate) plus 1-5 years of carry. ML can only improve which lots to bid on. It cannot lower the cost of the authority's consent, and the purchase price, which is most of the capex, rises exactly when a lot looks good. My estimate is a 2-3x capex lever, not 10x.
scored.data: The data really is public, illegible and scattered: millions of regional lot images on Invaluable, LiveAuctioneers and Drouot, the Getty Provenance Index, RKD, the Witt and Frick photoarchives, and digitised sale catalogues on Heidelberg and Gallica. The outcome is NOT written into a legible field: attribution labels like "circle of" are the mispricing itself, which is good for the thesis. But incumbents already read this data by eye. Hundreds of specialist dealers and sleeper hunters scan every online catalogue, and online bidding has widened the buyer pool for sleepers (Antiques Trade Gazette; The Art Newspaper's 2024 piece on "predatory sleeper hunters"). Art Recognition (Swiss, founded 2019) already offers AI attribution, though its track record is disputed.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought, not claimed for free, and the seller (the regional house or estate) often cannot read the data. That is good. But the purchase happens at an open public auction where informed dealers compete, so price discovery takes place at the hammer: the Thomaston lot made $1.175M on a $10k estimate, and the Gentileschi went to a dealer at £30k against a low estimate. Only lots that every human specialist misses stay cheap. Private estate or attic buys avoid this competition but cannot be scaled.
scored.buyer: Christie's and Sotheby's Old Master evening sales and private sales (with guarantees), TEFAF-tier dealers (Colnaghi, Agnews, Weiss) and museums. They are capitalised, but the segment is small. My estimate is that Old Masters auction turnover is roughly $0.5-1B a year globally, and only a small share of that is newly re-attributed works.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are dealer gallery, conservation studio, art-backed lending, art fund and authentication authority. That is a real ladder, but it is capped by the size of the Old Master and 19th-century market (a few billion dollars a year). There is no path to a trillion dollars, and the higher rungs (lending, funds) are crowded by Sotheby's Financial and Athena.
scored.fatal_flaw: The purchase is an open public auction, and the specialist dealer community already does by eye what the ML would do. Any lot that looks like a sleeper gets bid up to near its proven value at the regional hammer (Thomaston: $1.175M on a $10k estimate), so most of the step-up goes to the consignor, not the buyer. On top of that, proving depends on a single gatekeeper's subjective consent, which can be refused or reversed, and the end market is small.
scored.one_line_reason: The frame and the illegible data are real, but rights are bought at contested public auctions where human sleeper hunters already set the price, the proof is a subjective gatekeeper's consent, and the market is capped in the low billions, so the score is 12/25.

scored.name: Unrecognised Signed and Association Copies / Manuscripts (InkProof / Hand of History)
scored.one_line: Buys bulk old books, letters, ledgers and ephemera (estate lots, library deaccessions) at $1-5 per item, uses OCR plus handwriting and provenance ML to match inscriptions and hands against digitised exemplars (presidents, scientists, authors), gets PSA/DNA, JSA or scholarly-edition authentication, and sells through RR Auction, Heritage and Christie's books departments.
scored.unproven_right: Title to paper bought by the box or lot ($20-500) with no signature or correspondent recognised
scored.proving_step: PSA/DNA, JSA, Beckett or documentary-edition authentication ($50-500), with ink/paper dating where needed; the accepted market standard
scored.proven_buyer: RR Auction, Heritage, University Archives, Christie's/Sotheby's books and manuscripts, research libraries
scored.public_data: Founders Online, Library of Congress and national archive digitised manuscripts, documentary-edition correspondence calendars, library deaccession lists, estate and eBay lot photos, auction comps
scored.rough_step_up: $2 item to $500-500,000, 10^2-10^4x on a hit; hit rate well below 1%. Modest ladder (authentication service, manuscript auction house), low-$bn market
scored.frame: Rung: buy an unattributed paper lot, recognise the hand or inscription, get it authenticated, and consign it to a capitalised auction house. Inside that rung, recognition is perhaps 60-70% of the work (my estimate). Authentication is trivial and cheap. But physically sourcing the boxes, handling them and imaging them page by page is a large, unglamorous labour cost per item, so the physical step is not abstracted the way drilling is for Terranox. The buyers (RR Auction, Heritage, Christie's, Sotheby's, University Archives) are real and capitalised, but they take consignments on commission rather than paying a developer-style premium for a proven right.
scored.step_up: Unproven: an item costs $1-5 (estate or deaccession lots of $20-500). Proven: most authenticated hits are minor signed books or letters worth $50-500, a 10-100x step-up. An estate lot of 15 author-signed books was estimated at only $50-150 in total (estatesales.org). The tail reaches 10^4-10^5x, for example a $2.48 thrift-store 1823 Stone Declaration that sold for $477,650 (NBC News). That example is a printed document, not a hand-matched one, and such cases are extremely rare. Net proceeds lose roughly 15-25% to seller commission (industry norm, my estimate). The typical hit is about 100x, and 10^4x hits are anecdotal.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: well below 1% of items carry an unrecognised valuable hand (my estimate; no published figure exists). Cost per proving attempt: PSA/DNA charges $10-150+ by signer, plus $40-150 premium surcharges for items declared at $1,000-9,999 (psacard.com/pricing/autographs). JSA and Beckett are similar, and scholarly opinion runs $50-500. Authentication is not the expensive, mostly-failing step, because nobody authenticates blind. The real cost is acquisition, handling and imaging labour, which I estimate at $0.5-2 per item. ML triage helps select which items to send for authentication, but the capex being cut is cheap scanning labour, not costly proving attempts. So the lever exists but is small in dollars.
scored.data: This criterion mostly fails. The signal sits in the physical item the company must first buy and image; it is private, not public illegible data sitting unread. The public exemplar corpora (Founders Online, Library of Congress, documentary-edition calendars) are reference data for matching, not a map of where unrecognised items are. eBay and estate photos offer some public signal, but at low resolution and partial. Obvious signatures and inscriptions are already legible to the many scouts and dealers who check every book for signatures, which estate-sale guides explicitly tell sellers to do. The real edge is only in unsigned or unrecognised hands (letters, ledgers, marginalia), where authenticators and auction houses demand provenance, and handwriting ML without provenance is weak against forgery risk.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Title to physical lots is bought cheaply at estate sales, library deaccessions and bulk eBay lots, from sellers who do not recognise the hands. The rights are bought, not free.
scored.buyer: RR Auction, Heritage, University Archives, Christie's and Sotheby's books and manuscripts departments, and research libraries. They are well capitalised, but they mostly sell on consignment for a commission and are not principals paying for proven assets. The end buyers are collectors.
scored.ladder: The ladder is modest: lot sourcing, then attribution and authentication, then dealer or auction house, then possibly a digitisation or provenance-database business. The rare book and manuscript auction market is low-$bn per year (my estimate, roughly $1-2bn). No credible trillion-dollar path exists.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not a read of public data. Every candidate must be bought, handled and imaged physically, item by item, so this is labour-bound scouting with ML triage. The high-value hits (unrecognised hands without signatures) are exactly the ones authenticators and auction houses will not certify without provenance. Meanwhile, the obvious signatures are already picked over by a crowded field of scouts and dealers. Hits are mostly 10-100x on $2 items, with a tiny total addressable market.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real frame with cheap rights and a cheap proving step. But the signal sits in private physical items rather than public illegible data, typical hits are about 100x on a few dollars, ML lowers cheap labour cost rather than proving capex, and the ladder tops out in a low-$bn auction niche.

scored.name: SoleSource (orphan tech-data packages to DLA source approval)
scored.one_line: Buys drawing packages, design rights and tooling from bankrupt or retiring aerospace/defense OEMs and machine shops, uses ML to find NSNs where that data unlocks sole or limited approved-source status, passes DLA Source Approval Requests and first article tests, and builds a TransDigm-style aftermarket franchise.
scored.unproven_right: Tech-data rights and tooling bought for $5-100k at bankruptcy or retirement sales from sellers who cannot map drawings to live NSN demand
scored.proving_step: SAR approval or FAT per NSN family (~$10-50k); most SARs rejected today; ML over DIBBS, FLIS/PUB LOG, cFolders and award histories picks high-demand, few-source NSNs with passable data
scored.proven_buyer: DLA and service depots buy parts; TransDigm, Heico, Arcline/Kaman and PE aftermarket roll-ups buy approved portfolios at 10-20x EBITDA
scored.public_data: DLA DIBBS solicitations and awards, FLIS/PUB LOG AMSC/AMC codes, cFolders tech data, FPDS, PACER asset schedules
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-1000x ($10k package to sole-source NSN family earning $0.5-5M/yr valued 10-20x). Ladder: approved source, manufacturing, aftermarket roll-up, platform sustainment prime
scored.frame: The rung would be 'own a tech-data package and win DLA approved-source status for an NSN family'. Discovery is maybe 20-35% of the work inside that rung (my estimate): knowing which NSN to target and whether the data is good enough. The rest is physical and procedural. You need an AS9100/QPL-capable shop, have to rebuild or requalify the tooling, and must pass first article tests. The SAR takes 90-120 days and can run past 180 days (DLA Aviation 2019 briefing), and full approval takes 12-18 months (DLA RPPOB briefing). Then you have to keep making the part at a profit. Unlike a drill hit, manufacturing is not trivial or abstracted. Capitalised buyers do exist for the proven output: DLA buys the parts, and Ontic, Extant, TransDigm and Heico buy portfolios. But what they buy is a running, profitable product line, not a SAR approval letter.
scored.step_up: Unproven: orphan packages from bankruptcy sales at $5-100k (the candidate's number, not verified). A full licensed legacy line from a willing OEM costs far more: Extant paid about $27M for the Astronautics electromechanical indicator line in 2022 (BizTimes/AIN). Proven: say an NSN family earns $0.5-5M/yr in revenue. At an estimated 25-35% EBITDA margin that is $0.15-1.75M EBITDA. TransDigm trades near 20x EV/EBITDA, while deal multiples for small lines are more like 8-12x (TransDigm used 8x as its illustrative multiple in 2008). That puts a proven family at roughly $1.5-20M against $50-150k all-in (package plus SAR, FAT and tooling requalification), so about 10-130x. That is not 10^3-10^4. The $5k package that becomes a $5M/yr sole-source family is a tail outcome, not the base case (my estimate).
scored.hit_rate_capex: SAR base approval rate: DLA Land and Maritime FY17 had 111 approved vs 114 rejected, about 49% of decided packages. The DLA Casting and Forging program had 40 approved vs 4 rejected since 2014, about 91%. So the claim that 'most SARs are rejected' overstates it. The lever is capped at 1/base rate, roughly 1.1-2x, not 10x. DLA also declines SARs it judges not cost-effective (low demand, years of stock on hand, multiple sources already cited), so a high-demand, few-source filter is partly applied by DLA itself. Cost per attempt: $10-50k per SAR/FAT (the candidate's figure, an estimate). DLA briefings give no SAR fees. The bigger costs are tooling requalification and FAT hardware, which I estimate at $20-200k per family.
scored.data: The outcome is already summarised in legible fields. Each NSN's Acquisition Method Suffix Code (AMSC) and Acquisition Method Code (AMC) in FLIS/PUB LOG say whether it is sole source and why (for example, the government lacks the data). DIBBS/FPDS award histories show annual spend, unit price and number of awardees per NSN. Ranking NSNs by demand times few sources is a SQL query, not an ML problem, and existing commercial tools (GovSignals, BidLab-style aggregators) already scrape DIBBS. The only illegible part is mapping scanned bankruptcy drawing sets to NSNs and CAGE/part numbers. That is real OCR and ML work, but small in value. The tech data is also often already in cFolders/JEDMICS when the government holds the rights.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought rather than claimed first-come: tech-data licences, drawings and tooling from OEMs, bankruptcy estates and auctions. Example: the Schweizer 269 type certificate plus tooling went to auction. But valuable lines are sold by sophisticated OEMs into a competitive market of specialist buyers. Ontic (licenses legacy lines from OEMs; took the M7 Aerospace type certificates in 2022), Extant Aerospace (Astronautics line, $27M), TransDigm, Heico and DART all run organised processes, so there is no illiteracy discount. What is left at $5-100k bankruptcy sales is mostly the scraps those buyers passed on. Also, if the government already holds unlimited rights, competitors can win the same NSN without buying your package.
scored.buyer: For parts: DLA and service depots. For portfolios: TransDigm (about 80% of sales from sole-source products, about 90% proprietary, per its FY2015-2021 10-Ks), Heico, Ontic, Extant, Arcline/Kaman and PE roll-ups. They pay on EBITDA, so you only realise value after running manufacturing profitably for years. DoD IG and Congress scrutiny of TransDigm-style sole-source pricing also caps the economics of selling to DLA.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong and proven. It runs from approved source to licensed manufacturer to aftermarket roll-up to platform sustainment prime or type-certificate holder (Ontic, TransDigm). TransDigm is worth more than $70B on exactly this model. But the ladder starts at a rung where incumbents are already strong and the first rung is not discovery-dominated.
scored.fatal_flaw: The first rung is not discovery-dominated, and the discovery that does exist is already legible. Public AMSC/AMC codes and DIBBS award histories already state which NSNs are sole source and how much DLA spends on them. ML therefore has little edge, and a SAR approval rate of about 50-90% leaves at most a 1.1-2x hit-rate lever. Proving and realising value means manufacturing, qualifying and selling physical parts for years. Well-capitalised specialists (Ontic, Extant, TransDigm, Heico) already buy legacy tech-data lines at full price. A SAR also usually makes you an added source rather than the sole one, so it erodes the very pricing it is supposed to capture.
scored.one_line_reason: A real, large ladder (TransDigm/Ontic), but the outcome is in legible AMSC/DIBBS fields, SAR approval is about 50-90% so the lever is at most 2x, the proving step is manufacturing rather than a cheap test, and specialist buyers already compete for the rights.

scored.name: LoadStudy Land (greenfield large-load study options, ERCOT/SPP)
scored.one_line: Buys cheap 2-3 year options on farmland next to 345 kV lines with hidden headroom, files a large-load interconnection request, and sells the studied power-ready site to hyperscalers and data center developers.
scored.unproven_right: Options on 200-1,000 acres at ~$3-10k/acre (premiums ~$50-200/acre) from owners who cannot read transmission planning cases
scored.proving_step: Utility/ERCOT Large Load Interconnection Study and will-serve letter confirming MW at a named substation and date (~$50-250k deposits); most return large upgrades or delays; ML ranks headroom from RPG/ITP PDFs, Form 715, IRPs, constraints and retirements
scored.proven_buyer: Hyperscalers, data center developers/REITs (Stack, QTS, Aligned), infra funds (Blackstone, KKR, DigitalBridge)
scored.public_data: ERCOT RPG submissions and Large Load status reports, SPP ITP and Form 715, utility IRP PDFs, ERCOT CDR, EIA-860 retirements, county parcel rolls
scored.rough_step_up: ~80-300x (~$2.5-10k/acre unstudied to ~$800k/acre power-ready per Claros). Caveat: killed 'powered brownfields' and 'queue positions'; edge must be greenfield headroom, and sellers near substations are wising up
scored.frame: The rung is a land option plus a completed large-load study, sold as a site with a will-serve letter. It is discrete and sellable: a 'powered land' market exists. Finding the site is maybe 60-70% of the work by my estimate, not 80%+. The rest is non-trivial: the study queue, utility politics, zoning and water, plus the upgrade cost and energization date the study returns. Those come from the utility's own schedule, not from the company. Texas SB6 (2025) adds further work for loads of 75 MW and up: a study fee (about $100k minimum, from memory), proof of site control, disclosure of duplicate requests, and curtailment terms. The buyer's real purchase criterion is the energization date, which the company cannot speed up.
scored.step_up: Unproven: ag land next to 345 kV lines in ERCOT/SPP at roughly $3-10k/acre, with option premiums of about $50-200/acre (the candidate's figures; I could not verify them). Proven: the candidate cites about $800k/acre for power-ready land (Claros). From memory, trade reports put Texas power-ready land at roughly $100-500k/acre and the very top N. Virginia sites at $1-2M+/acre. Those are estimates, not verified this session. A realistic step-up for a studied site with a will-serve letter but an energization date 3-5 years out is about 20-80x on land value. It reaches about 100x+ only when there is near-term MW. Measured against the option premium alone it is larger, but the buyer prices land value. So this sits at ~10-100x, a 3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs about $50-250k in study deposits and fees, plus option premiums of about $10-200k. The candidate gives the deposit range. SB6's minimum study fee is about $100k from memory. Per-site all-in, including engineering and legal, is my estimate of $0.2-0.5M. Base hit rate is my estimate: maybe 15-35% of studies return usable MW at an acceptable upgrade cost and date. ERCOT's large-load queue grew past ~200 GW by late 2025 (from memory of ERCOT reports), against a ~85 GW peak, so most requests are speculative and will not be served on time. The lever is capped at 1/base rate, about 3-6x, not 10x. Headroom is also already computed by power-flow engineers using CEII-cleared PSS/E base cases, so ML over PDFs adds little over a standard contingency analysis.
scored.data: The data is public-ish but not truly illegible. ERCOT publishes monthly large-load interconnection status reports with MW by zone and status. RPG project submissions, SPP ITP and Form 715 are partially behind CEII access, which any developer can obtain. The proper tool is a power-flow model, which consultants such as Grid Strategies, E3 and the utilities' own engineering firms already run. The outcome (available MW at a substation and its date) is close to being summarised in legible fields: queue and status reports, plus utility hosting and capacity maps where they exist. This repeats the 'queue positions: lookup table matches ML' failure. The right can be bought cheaply from farmers. But sellers near 345 kV substations in Texas are increasingly aware (data center brokers cold-call landowners), and SB6 site-control rules plus duplicate-request disclosure reduce option-stacking.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Options on private farmland are bought, not free first-come. Option premiums are cheap, but prices near substations are rising and many options are already tied up by powered-land developers.
scored.buyer: Capitalised and real: hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon, Oracle/OpenAI Stargate at Abilene), developers and REITs (Stack, QTS, Aligned, Vantage, CyrusOne) and infrastructure funds (Blackstone, KKR, DigitalBridge). They pay a premium for MW plus a date, not for a study alone.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder: land plus a study, then permitted and powered shell, then on-site generation or a behind-the-meter gas plant, then campus development, then owner-operator. Incumbents already climbing it include Tract, Lancium, Crusoe, Hut 8 (River Bend), Prometheus Hyperscale and Skybox. The path is real but crowded and capital-intensive. Each higher rung is construction and power procurement, where ML gives no edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value comes from the utility's energization date and upgrade cost, not from discovering hidden headroom. Headroom is computable with standard power-flow models from CEII base cases. ERCOT's large-load status reports and SB6 rules already make the outcome mostly legible. Meanwhile 200+ GW of competing speculative requests and established powered-land developers (Tract, Lancium and others) erode both the hit rate and the land discount. The ML edge over a power-systems engineer is small, the same failure mode as the killed powered-brownfields and queue-position ideas.
scored.one_line_reason: The buyer and the step-up are real (about 20-100x), but discovery is not 80% of the rung, the lever is capped at about 3-6x, and the headroom signal is computable and increasingly legible to well-funded powered-land incumbents. Effectively this is a greenfield rerun of powered brownfields and queue positions.

From memory (unverified): ERCOT Large Load Interconnection Status reports showing 200+ GW of large-load requests by late 2025
From memory (unverified): Texas SB6 (2025) large-load provisions: study fee minimum ~$100k, site-control proof, duplicate-request disclosure, curtailment
From memory (unverified): powered-land developers Tract, Lancium, Crusoe, Prometheus Hyperscale, Skybox

scored.name: Entitled Acre (data center rezoning arbitrage)
scored.one_line: Options agricultural parcels in counties whose planning records imply data center approval, obtains rezoning or special exception, and sells entitled parcels to data center developers.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase options on farmland at ~$10-50k/acre near fibre and power
scored.proving_step: Approved rezoning/SUP/CUP (~$50-300k filing); increasingly contested; ML over minutes, transcripts, comp plans and opposition filings predicts approval
scored.proven_buyer: Data center developers and hyperscalers (entitled NoVA land ~$4M/acre per Avison Young)
scored.public_data: County planning commission and board minutes and transcripts, comprehensive plans, zoning GIS, local news and opposition dockets
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x, up to ~200x in NoVA; approval odds not low, so lever ~3x; brokers already do some of this
scored.frame: The rung is "option a parcel, get it entitled, sell it." It is discrete and sellable: entitled data center land trades as its own product, and Tract-style land entitlers sell exactly this to hyperscalers. But discovery (picking the parcel) is not 80%+ of the work. My estimate is 30-50%. The rest is 12-24 months of hearings, traffic and noise studies, buffer negotiation, community opposition, litigation risk and, above all, a utility will-serve or load letter. None of that is trivial or abstracted, so the physical/political step is much heavier than drilling. Without power the entitlement is worth far less, so the real proving step is zoning plus power, and power is not predictable from planning minutes.
scored.step_up: Estimates, not verified this session (search budget exhausted). In Northern Virginia, agricultural or rural land is roughly $20-100k/acre. Entitled, powered data center land in Loudoun or Prince William is about $1-4M/acre (the candidate cites Avison Young at ~$4M/acre). Prince William Digital Gateway owners reportedly sold at about $700k-1M+/acre. That is about 10-50x, and up to ~200x at the extreme with power included. Outside NoVA (GA, TX, OH, IN), farmland at ~$5-15k/acre goes to ~$50-300k/acre once entitled, about 10-30x. Much of that premium is power and fibre, not zoning, and farmland near power and fibre already prices in speculation. That puts it at about 10-100x: C2 = 3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates. My recollection of Data Center Watch (10a Labs) reports is roughly $64B of projects blocked or delayed through early 2025 and about $98B more in Q2 2025. Contested cases are rising, but most data center rezonings and special-use permits I am aware of are still approved. My estimate of the base approval rate is ~60-80%, which caps the lever at 1/0.7, about 1.3-1.7x, and nowhere near 10x. Cost per attempt is about $50-300k in filing, legal, engineering and consultant fees (candidate's figure), plus option premiums of maybe 1-5% of price on $10-50k/acre parcels and 1-2 years of carry. ML predicting approval mostly helps avoid the minority of fights that end in denial. That is a small saving, not a 10x cut in capex.
scored.data: Partly illegible: minutes, hearing transcripts, comprehensive plan text and opposition filings are scattered, unstructured PDFs and videos across about 3,000 counties. But the outcome is written into legible fields. Approved rezonings show up in zoning GIS, ordinance records and news immediately. Comprehensive plan designations (such as 'technology overlay' or 'data center opportunity zone') already flag where approval is likely, and brokers and hyperscaler site selectors track them. So the ML edge is predicting approval before filing, in a domain where approval is already the common case. That repeats the earlier "lookup table matches ML" problem (interconnection queues, powered brownfields).
scored.right_bought: Yes. The right is bought through purchase options from farmers, not claimed free. But since 2023 the data center premium has been widely publicised (Prince William farmers' consortium sales, letters offering farmers millions of dollars), so landowners near power and fibre increasingly ask speculative prices or band together to sell. The information asymmetry is weaker than in mineral claims. Owners do not need to read the minutes to know data centers are coming.
scored.buyer: The buyers are well capitalised and paying now: hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta), colocation developers (QTS, Vantage, Stack, Aligned, CyrusOne) and powered-land funds. Incumbents already doing this exact rung include Tract (Grant van Rooyen's master-planned data center land developer), land speculators and assemblers in NoVA, Ohio and Georgia, and brokerage land teams (JLL, CBRE, Cushman), along with hyperscalers' own in-house site-selection and optioning teams.
scored.ladder: There are real rungs above: entitlement, then a power and utility agreement (or on-site generation), then a powered shell, then building and leasing the campus or co-developing with a hyperscaler. Tract shows the path from entitled land into infrastructure. It is a large market (hundreds of billions in data center capex a year), but every rung above land has deep-pocketed, established competitors, and the ladder ends at being a data center REIT, not a new category.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step mostly succeeds already (an estimated ~60-80% of rezonings and special-use permits are approved), so ML can raise the hit rate by at most ~1.5x, not 10x. The value step-up is driven mainly by power availability, which planning records cannot prove, rather than by zoning. Incumbents such as Tract and brokers already run this playbook on land owners who know the premium exists.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real, sellable rung with a capitalised buyer and a 10-50x step-up. But approval is the base case, so the ML lever is under 2x. The political step plus power, not discovery, dominates the work. The outcome becomes legible in zoning records and comprehensive plans, and established players (Tract, brokers, hyperscaler site teams) already do it.
sources: Candidate brief: Avison Young figure of ~$4M/acre for entitled Northern Virginia data center land (not re-verified; my web search budget for this turn was exhausted, so no new searches ran)
Data Center Watch / 10a Labs reports on data center projects blocked or delayed by local opposition, 2024-2025 (from memory; ~$64B and ~$98B figures not re-verified this session)
Prince William Digital Gateway rezoning and landowner sale prices, press coverage 2022-2025 (from memory, estimate)
Tract (data center land developer) public descriptions of its master-planned land model (from memory)
Every hit rate, cost and price above that has no named source is my own estimate

scored.name: Rare Stamp Varieties in Bulk Mixtures (Philatelix)
scored.one_line: Buys bulk stamp accumulations, albums and mixture lots for cents per stamp, scans them at high resolution, uses ML to spot rare varieties (perforation, watermark, plate flaws, inverts, shades, listed errors), gets PF/PSE/RPSL/BPA certificates, and sells at Siegel, Spink and Feldman.
scored.unproven_right: Uncertified stamps inside albums and lots priced at a few dollars per kilogram
scored.proving_step: Expert certificate from PF/PSE/RPSL/BPA ($25-150); certificate is the accepted proof and its absence caps price
scored.proven_buyer: Siegel, Spink, Feldman and Cherrystone bidders; specialised collectors
scored.public_data: eBay/Delcampe/HipStamp lot scans (millions, unstructured); Scott/SG specialised variety descriptions; Siegel Power Search census of certified rarities as labels
scored.rough_step_up: $0.05 stamp to $500-50,000 certified variety, 10^3-10^5x on a hit; hit rate ~1 in 10^4. Ladder: auction house, expertising service, philatelic fund
scored.frame: Rung: buy an uncertified lot, find the variety, certify it, consign it to auction. Inside this rung, finding the stamp is roughly 85-90% of the work (my estimate). Buying the lot, scanning it, mailing it for a certificate and consigning it are cheap, standard steps. The physical step really is trivial, so the frame holds structurally. The problem is the buyer. Buyers are fragmented, ageing hobbyists bidding at Siegel, Spink, Feldman and Cherrystone. There is no capitalised developer paying a premium because the proven asset feeds its own pipeline. Demand is thin, so prices fall if you supply more.
scored.step_up: Unproven: kiloware sells for about AU$36-212/kg at charity auction and about US$97-231/kg on eBay off paper (listed prices; Glen Stephens and eBay). That is cents per stamp. Proven: a certified listed variety realises $50-50,000 at auction (my estimate of the range). Most varieties found in mixtures are tens of dollars. Jackpots like the unissued Audrey Hepburn stamp (EUR 169,000 including commission, from a EUR 55 box bought on eBay) are anecdotes. For the one stamp that hits, the step-up is 10^3-10^5x. Per lot purchased, the realistic expected step-up is about 2-10x (my estimate), because dealers price lots by what they might contain.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate of about 1 in 10^4 stamps is the candidate's estimate. I found no published figure. Wikipedia says kiloware normally carries high duplication of common definitives. The proving step itself (the certificate) is not mostly failing. Submitters screen first, and the PF fee is 5.5% of value with a $27 minimum for US items and $35 for foreign items, rising to $50 for used examples or overprints, capped at $1,000. The real cost of discovery is human sorting labour, not failed proofs. ML can cut that sorting labour. But every ML false positive sent for a certificate costs $27-50 on items mostly worth less than that. So the lever is narrower than 10x on certificate spend, and it is really a cost cut on labour.
scored.data: Partly illegible. eBay, Delcampe and HipStamp scans are unstructured and number in the millions. But the outcome taxonomy is already fully legible: Scott and SG specialised catalogues list every variety with its value, and the Siegel census labels known rarities. The deciding attributes are watermark, exact perforation gauge, paper, shade under standard lighting, and whether gum or regumming is genuine. Many of these are not visible in seller photos; they need watermark fluid, a perforation gauge, UV light and handling. Consumer AI identifier apps already exist and claim perforation and watermark checks (StampID, StampLens, Stamp Value AI Identifier), but they have unverified accuracy and no bulk mode.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought, not claimed for free: lots and albums are purchased at auction or on eBay. But the sellers are mostly professional dealers who are the best readers of this data. They pick lots before selling them, and 'unpicked' is a marketing claim. The cheapest lots are the most picked over. Estate albums sold by heirs are the genuinely blind-owner channel, but they come at low volume and are sought by every dealer.
scored.buyer: Specialised collectors bidding through Robert A. Siegel (about $36M in sales in 2018, about $44M in 2009), Spink, Feldman and Cherrystone (one Cherrystone sale realised $7M). These are individuals, not capitalised buyers that need supply. Bill Gross, the largest recent buyer and seller, publicly predicted a market correction and exited.
scored.ladder: The possible rungs are dealer, then auction house, then expertising service, then philatelic investment fund. But the whole addressable market is small. The top US auction house does about $36M a year, and I estimate the global rare-stamp auction market at low single-digit billions of dollars a year at most. The collector base is ageing. This is a nice niche business, but it gives no trillion-dollar or even multi-billion path, and the stamp-investment fund rung has a poor history (Stanley Gibbons' investment arm and its troubles).
scored.fatal_flaw: The ceiling is tiny and the right is not mispriced. Bulk lots are sold by expert dealers who have already picked them. The attributes that decide value (watermark, perforation gauge, shade, gum) are mostly invisible in public scans. And the end market is a few hundred million dollars a year of thin, ageing hobbyist demand with no capitalised buyer, so neither the rung nor the ladder scales.
scored.one_line_reason: The one-stamp step-up is real at 10^3x and up, but the lots are pre-picked by expert dealers, many key attributes cannot be seen in scans, certificates cost $27-50 a try, and the hobbyist market caps the whole ladder at a few hundred million dollars a year.

scored.name: Aircraft LLP Back-to-Birth Trace Reconstruction (Back-to-Birth / Unbroken Chain)
scored.one_line: Buys engine life-limited parts, landing gear and teardown engines trading as scrap or 'no-trace' because back-to-birth paperwork is broken, uses ML to read and reconcile the scanned logbooks, work orders, 8130/Form 1 tags, FAA registry files and auction documents, and sells parts with restored traceability to MROs, lessors and USM traders.
scored.unproven_right: Title to no-trace LLPs, gear or retired aircraft bought at scrap/salvage value
scored.proving_step: Complete back-to-birth trace accepted by a Part 145 station, CAMO or OEM records review, with 8130-3 / EASA Form 1; physical inspection cheap; most messy packs are written off today
scored.proven_buyer: Engine lessors (AerCap, Willis Lease), USM traders (AAR, GA Telesis), MROs pricing off LLP remaining-cycle tables
scored.public_data: FAA registry document images, SDR and AD databases, NTSB, lessor ABS disclosures; most signal is the acquired record pack rather than public data (weaker C4)
scored.rough_step_up: ~5-50x (scrap ~$5-20k to $0.3-1.5M serviceable LLP); high fraud risk requires unimpeachable provenance; large ladder to part-out, MRO, leasing
scored.frame: The rung: buy LLPs or gear with gaps in their records, rebuild the back-to-birth trace and resell them as serviceable USM. Discovery (records forensics) is my estimate of ~50-70% of the work, not 80%+. The physical step is not trivial. A part with no trace usually also needs a shop visit, non-destructive testing and re-certification under an 8130-3 or Form 1. The deciding step is acceptance by an OEM, CAMO or lessor records auditor, such as GE/CFM's TRUEngine back-to-birth review, and that is a gatekeeper's judgement, not a discovery result. Capitalised buyers exist: AerCap, Willis Lease, AAR, GA Telesis, CFM Materials.
scored.step_up: A trade publication (ISTAT Jetrader, Autumn 2020) says incomplete records can cut engine LLP market value by up to 40%. On that basis most 'gappy' parts trade at roughly 0.6x of a fully traced part, so fixing the trace gives about 1.5-2.5x. For a truly no-trace part, one vendor (oxmaint) says it may be treated as having zero remaining life, and a GE-commissioned mba study says 42% of respondents value non-OEM or alternative material at scrap at teardown. That scrap-to-serviceable case is the candidate's 5-50x (my estimate, e.g. ~$10-20k scrap vs $0.3-1.5M serviceable). Safe Fly puts a full CFM56-5B/7B LLP stack at $2.5-6.0M (unaudited vendor figure). The 5-50x case is the rare tail, and the typical uplift is under 3x. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published base hit rate. My estimate: for parts with genuine trace gaps (a missing operator period, a missing removal/install record), success is low, around 10-30%, because the documents usually do not exist anywhere, not merely unread. Cost per attempt is a records review plus outreach to past operators and MROs, roughly $2-20k per part (my estimate; ProvenAir and Bluetail do this as a service). Attempts are already cheap, so ML cutting review cost does little. ML cannot raise the hit rate when the paper is missing. The lever is a few times at most, not ~10x.
scored.data: Weak. The signal sits in the private record pack that comes with the part, not in public data. The FAA registry, SDR, AD and NTSB data do not hold per-part LLP cycle histories. The outcome is already legible: the part is sold as 'no trace' or 'incomplete BtB', which is exactly the status-field problem. Incumbents already extract this data: ProvenAir (BtB trace timelines and exception reports for engines, gear and APUs), Bluetail (a scanning network of 120+ locations), GE/CFM TRUEngine (an OEM back-to-birth audit), and CFM Materials and AAR's in-house records teams.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Title to no-trace parts or teardown engines is bought cheaply at scrap or salvage prices from lessors, part-out shops and auctions. The sellers are records-sophisticated, though (lessors employ records auditors), so there is little information asymmetry to exploit.
scored.buyer: Engine lessors (AerCap, Willis Lease), USM traders and part-out houses (AAR, GA Telesis, CFM Materials), and MROs that price parts off LLP remaining-cycle tables. They have the capital but are very averse to fraud risk.
scored.ladder: Real ladder: trace restoration, then engine teardown and part-out, then a Part 145 MRO, then engine leasing and green-time engines, then aircraft leasing. These markets are worth billions, and the AerCap and Willis Lease path shows the top of the ladder.
scored.fatal_flaw: The missing value is absent paperwork, not illegible paperwork. A no-trace LLP is no-trace because records of an operator period or a removal no longer exist, and ML cannot create them. Acceptance is decided by OEM, CAMO and lessor auditors who, after the AOG Technics forged-paperwork scandal (2023, known before this conversation), treat reconstructed provenance with more suspicion. Incumbents (ProvenAir, Bluetail, TRUEngine) already read the legible part, and the typical uplift is under 3x (records gaps cost up to ~40% of value), not 10^4.
scored.one_line_reason: The capitalised buyers and the ladder are real, but the step-up is usually 1.5-3x. The data is private and already parsed by ProvenAir, Bluetail and GE TRUEngine, and ML cannot recover records that never existed. So it fails C2, C3 and C4.

scored.name: California Lot Legality (Certificates of Compliance: Lot Legality Co. / Lotline)
scored.one_line: Buys rural California parcels assessed as one lot whose scanned deed, GLO patent and plat history shows multiple lawfully created lots (patents, pre-1972 conveyances, qualifying maps), uses ML to apply Gardner v. Sonoma / Witt / Gov. Code 66499.35 rules across the scans, obtains county Certificates of Compliance, and sells separately saleable lots to builders.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to a parcel priced as one lot (or paper-subdivision lots at $1-3k) from long-tenure owners who cannot read century-old title chains
scored.proving_step: Deed chain reconstruction plus Certificate of Compliance application (~$2-20k); a recorded, insurable county determination; case law has narrowed easy cases so base hit rate is low
scored.proven_buyer: Homebuilders, estate-lot developers, custom-home buyers and land funds
scored.public_data: County recorder scanned deeds and pre-1972 maps back to the 1800s, BLM GLO patents, surveyor record maps, assessor map books, historical ordinances
scored.rough_step_up: ~2-10x on capital deployed for whole parcels; 10^2-10^3x on each marginal lot (~$0 to $100k-1M in coastal counties); paper-subdivision lots 30-100x
scored.frame: Rung: buy a rural parcel priced as one lot, then get recorded Certificates of Compliance (CoC) for each embedded legal lot and sell those lots one at a time. The deed-chain research is real discovery work, but by my estimate it is only about 40-60% of what it takes to produce a lot a builder will pay for. A CoC certifies legality only. SLO County says it 'neither ensures that it is a buildable parcel, nor entitles the parcel owner a construction permit', and Mendocino says it does not guarantee legal access. Several things outside discovery gate the value: zoning minimum lot size, septic and water standards, access, a Coastal Development Permit in the coastal zone, conditional CoCs that require road dedications (LA County), and the county's discretion. So the physical and entitlement step is not trivial. The capitalised buyer (builders, land funds) exists, but it buys buildable lots, not legal-but-unbuildable ones.
scored.step_up: Whole parcel bought at acreage comps and resold as N certified lots: about 2-10x on capital deployed (the candidate's own figure, which I think is plausible but not sourced). The 10^2-10^3x 'marginal lot' figure is notional, because the marginal lot is already partly priced into rural acreage and its value depends on buildability. Paper-subdivision lots are not a legality play. California City lots run about $1-3.5k without utilities and about $10k with all utilities on the street (listings found in search). The roughly 3-10x spread there comes from utilities, not lot legality, because those lots are already on recorded maps. No source shows a 10^3x step on a CoC alone.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: county CoC fees are $1,400 per parcel in Sacramento County and $2,179 + $110 per lot in Tehama County. A title chain, survey and land-use attorney review probably add $5-15k (my estimate), for about $5-20k all in. Base hit rate: I found no published figure. Gardner v. Sonoma (2003), Witt Home Ranch (2008) and the Solano 1909-map case all rejected pre-1929 antiquated maps without separate conveyance. The surviving routes are separate patents, pre-1972 conveyances under the 66412.6 presumption, and qualifying maps. I estimate about 10-30% of screened candidates yield an extra unconditional, buildable lot. The lever is capped at about 3-10x, and much of the screening is already cheap desk work, so ML mostly cuts the cost of triage rather than the cost of proving.
scored.data: Strong on illegibility. The signal sits in scanned county recorder deeds going back to the 1850s, BLM GLO patents, pre-1972 maps and old ordinances, and assessor parcels (APNs) do not map to legal lots. The outcome is NOT already in a legible field until someone files a CoC. Recorded CoCs are legible afterwards, but that is downstream of the work. Nevada County notes that title companies 'do not make a binding determination' on lot legality, which confirms the gap. Weaknesses: the final determination is discretionary and made by the county, not read off the data. Merger ordinances (Gov. Code 66451.11) let counties merge contiguous substandard lots held by the same owner. And land-use attorneys and surveyors already do this reconstruction by hand for sophisticated sellers.
scored.right_bought: Yes. It is fee title bought from long-tenure rural owners who price on acreage comps. This is a real purchased right, not a free first-come filing. Two discounts erode it: high-value coastal parcels, where the upside is largest, usually have sophisticated owners and brokers who already order lot-legality reviews, and the buyer must buy the whole parcel, so capital at risk is large relative to the upside.
scored.buyer: Homebuilders, estate-lot developers, custom-home buyers and land funds. They are capitalised, but they pay for buildable, serviced, permitted lots, and they discount lots that are legal but unbuildable or lack access.
scored.ladder: Lot legality, then entitlement (CDP, septic, access), then horizontal development, then homebuilding. These rungs are real, but homebuilding is a fragmented, low-margin commodity business with no obvious path to a dominant very large company. The rural-California lot pool is also limited, and coastal counties are hostile to added density.
scored.fatal_flaw: A legal lot is not a buildable lot. The CoC (the proving step) does not deliver the step-up. Value depends on zoning minimums, septic and water, access, coastal permits and county discretion, including conditional CoCs and lot-merger ordinances. So discovery is not 80%+ of the rung, and buying the whole parcel at acreage price caps the real return on capital at about 2-10x, not 10^3-10^4x.
scored.one_line_reason: The data is genuinely illegible and the asset can be bought, but a CoC proves legality, not buildability, so the step-up is about 2-10x on capital and entitlement work dominates. This is a decent land-arbitrage niche, not a Terranox-shaped rung.

scored.name: Percolate (septic-feasibility lots in failing-perc counties)
scored.one_line: Buys 'unperked / perc failed' rural lots near zero, uses ML over scanned neighbouring septic permits, soil logs and well records to pick those likely to pass under today's mound/alternative-system rules, gets county septic approval, and sells buildable lots.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title or options on as-is untested rural lots (~$1-5k in PA, NJ, VT, NY, VA, NC)
scored.proving_step: Soil pits plus sanitarian-witnessed perc test (~$500-2,500); approved permit is a recorded determination lenders accept
scored.proven_buyer: Small and regional homebuilders, modular buyers with construction loans, lot aggregators
scored.public_data: County health department scanned septic permits and soil logs, state well-log databases, SSURGO, failed-perc notes in deed files, tax-sale lists
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-40x ($2k to $40-80k); base pass rate for failed lots may be 20-40%, so moderate lever
scored.frame: The rung is turning an unbuildable rural lot into one with a septic permit. Inside it, finding the lot is about 60-70% of the work (my estimate). The physical proving step is cheap: soil pits plus a perc test with a sanitarian present, $500-1,500 per retest per BuildingAdvisor. But the system that makes the lot buildable is not trivial. A sand mound runs ~$15-20k (Maryland DNR minutes) and alternative systems $10-25k+. The buyer pays for that, and it comes straight out of what they will pay for the lot. Buyers are small builders and individual buyers with construction loans. They have some capital but are scattered and price lots against local comparables, not against a big payoff the way a mine developer does.
scored.step_up: Kent Island, MD appraisal study (Tidewater Property Appraisers, 2003-2012): non-buildable lots (failed perc or never tested), 117 sales, mean $16,098, range $500-$47,000. Buildable lots, 197 sales, mean $137,382, range $47k-$255k. Ratio of means is ~8.5x. Island County, WA values septic-denied lots at ~$5-7k as recreational land. The candidate's $2k to $40-80k (20-40x) assumes buying at the very bottom of the range. After the $15-25k alternative-system premium the buyer must absorb, the net step-up is more like 5-15x (my estimate). That is about 10^1, not 10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt is $500-1,500 per retest (BuildingAdvisor) and up to ~$2,500 with soil pits and a design. Base pass rate on previously failed lots under mound/alternative rules is the candidate's estimate of 20-40%. I found no published rate, and BuildingAdvisor calls a retest 'possible but not likely' to change the result. If the base rate is 20-40%, the ML lever is capped at 2.5-5x, not 10x. Proving is also already cheap compared with the purchase price, so even a better hit rate saves little money.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible: scanned county septic permits and soil logs. But the key outcome is already written down in legible form. The county health file records the perc failure and the limiting condition (depth to seasonal high water table or bedrock, perc rate in minutes per inch), and SSURGO gives soil depth and drainage class in a structured database. Whether a lot qualifies for a mound depends on fixed numeric limits (e.g. PA steep-slope elevated sand mound: 12-15% slope, 3-30 min/in, at least 20 in of suitable soil) applied to that recorded log. A sanitarian can make that call by reading one page, so ML adds little over a rule lookup. Rights can be bought cheaply ($500-16k), and some owners do not know that newer alternative-system rules apply to them. That gap is real but thin, and local septic designers and land flippers already exploit it.
scored.right_bought: Fee title or an option on the untested or failed-perc rural lot, bought from owners or at tax sales for roughly $500-16k (Kent Island non-buildable range; the candidate assumes $1-5k).
scored.buyer: Small and regional homebuilders, modular-home buyers with construction loans, and lot aggregators. They are scattered and price-sensitive, and their pricing already subtracts the $15-25k alternative-septic cost.
scored.ladder: Lot to finished spec home or small subdivision, then a homebuilder. Homebuilding is a huge market, but it is low-margin and local, and owning failed-perc lots gives no moat for climbing. Septic installation and maintenance is another small rung. There is no clear path to a very large company built on an information edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already written down in legible form: the failed-perc log and SSURGO list the limiting soil condition, and mound eligibility follows fixed numeric limits. ML therefore has almost no edge over a sanitarian's lookup. Meanwhile the step-up is only ~10x, and the $15-25k alternative system the buyer must install eats much of it.
scored.one_line_reason: Real arbitrage, but small: ~8.5x mean step-up (Kent Island), proving that is cheap and passes 20-40% of the time (capping the lever at 2.5-5x), and outcomes already recorded in soil logs and SSURGO. It is a lot-flipping business, not a 10^4 discovery rung.

scored.name: Sportfinder (chance mutations to patented cultivars)
scored.one_line: Options discovery and propagation rights on limb sports and chance seedlings in commercial orchards flagged by ML over imagery and harvest reports, takes them through DUS trials to plant patents/PVP, and licenses to club-variety managers.
scored.unproven_right: Discovery and propagation right on a specific tree or limb, bought for a small fee from growers who let sports go unregistered
scored.proving_step: USPTO plant patent or UPOV/PVP grant after DUS trial plus genotyping (~$20-50k, 2-4 years); most sports unstable or not distinct
scored.proven_buyer: Club-variety managers and nurseries (Zespri, Prevar, Stemilt, Mission Produce, Driscoll's)
scored.public_data: USPTO plant-patent texts, UPOV PLUTO, USDA NASS orchard surveys, NAIP and Planet imagery, nursery registries (really needs drones)
scored.rough_step_up: >10^3x per hit (~$0 tree to $1-50M license) but rare hits, slow proving and weak public data
scored.frame: The rung is: get the propagation right to a sport, prove it is stable and distinct, then patent or PVP it and license it to a nursery. Finding the sport is maybe 30-40% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The rest is physical and slow. Budwood has to be grafted onto rootstock and grown out for several years to see whether the mutation holds; Penn State extension describes collecting budwood from the limb and growing the trees out for exactly this reason. Then come DUS trials, genotyping and patent prosecution, about 2-4 years and roughly $20-50k (the candidate's own figure, not verified). Unlike a drill hole, that is not trivial or abstracted. Buyers do exist: nurseries such as Willow Drive, Van Well and Brookfield, and club managers such as Kiku and Prevar.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a limb on a grower's tree, worth about $0 on its own, plus a finder or option fee of roughly $1-5k (my estimate; I found no published figures). Proven: apple royalties run about $1-1.35 per tree, e.g. Honeycrisp at $1-1.30 per tree and WA 64 at $1.35 per tree plus $0.03/lb of fruit. A typical colour-strain sport might sell 100k-1M trees over its life, so about $0.1-1M of license value (my estimate). The $1-50M range in the pitch only applies to rare blockbusters like Royal Gala. Historical anchor: the 1923 Starking Delicious limb reportedly sold for $6,000. A realistic step-up on cash invested is about 10-100x, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published base rate. Most sports either revert (they are often chimeras; a Ceres grower in South Africa reported Gala reversions) or are not distinct from the 20+ already-patented Gala sports. My estimate is that well under 10% of flagged sports are commercially worth patenting. Each attempt costs about $20-50k and takes 2-4 years (candidate's figure). The ML lever is weak because whether a sport is stable is a chimera or genetic property that only shows up when you propagate it, and imagery cannot see it. ML at best finds candidates, and growers already spot those by eye at harvest. So ML improves the cheap step (spotting) and not the expensive one (proving stability and distinctness).
scored.data: USPTO plant-patent texts are already legible and searchable. A patent is the written outcome itself, which is the failure mode where the regulator already records the answer. NAIP (60cm) and Planet (3m) imagery cannot resolve a single mutated limb; doing so needs private drone or harvest-line imaging, so the signal is not in public data. NASS orchard surveys are aggregates. Growers and packers are the people who notice sports today, and nurseries actively look for sports and buy their rights (Willow Drive owns Royal Red Honeycrisp; Gala alone has more than 20 patented sports, including Royal, Waliser, Gala 0502 and GalaMic). There is no illegible-data edge.
scored.right_bought: In principle the right can be bought cheaply from a grower. In practice, a sport of a protected variety (any club or patented cultivar, i.e. Cosmic Crisp, SweeTango, Pink Lady, Zespri kiwifruit) is an Essentially Derived Variety under UPOV 1991. Commercialising it needs the parent breeder's consent, and club grower contracts typically assign mutation rights to the variety owner. Sports of off-patent varieties (Gala, Fuji, Honeycrisp) are free to patent, but they are low-value colour strains competing in a crowded field.
scored.buyer: Licensing nurseries (Willow Drive, Van Well, C&O, Brookfield) and variety managers (Kiku, Prevar, Zespri). These are the same parties that already scout and buy sports, so the buyer is also the competitor.
scored.ladder: Sport rights, then a nursery or variety-licensing business, then club-variety management, then owned orchards and packing, then fresh-produce marketing (Zespri model, about NZ$4-5B in revenue). A real ladder exists, but it is low-margin agriculture, with no path to a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The valuable sports cannot be owned and the ownable sports are not valuable. Sports of protected or club varieties belong in practice to the parent breeder (Essentially Derived Variety rules plus club contracts). Sports of off-patent varieties are colour strains earning about $1 per tree in a field that already has 20+ patented Gala sports and nurseries scouting by eye. Beyond that, public imagery cannot see a limb, and stability, the expensive unknown, only shows up through years of propagation, so ML does not reduce the proving cost.
scored.one_line_reason: Rights to valuable sports belong to parent breeders under Essentially Derived Variety rules and club contracts; the free ones are about $1-per-tree colour strains that nurseries already scout for. Public imagery cannot resolve a limb, and proving takes years of propagation, which ML does not shorten.

scored.name: Positive Bank (rare-biomarker clinical remnant specimens)
scored.one_line: Buys consented, de-identified FFPE and plasma archives from closing labs and failed biobanks near zero, uses ML over scanned pathology reports to pick likely rare-marker positives (NTRK, RET, ROS1, MET ex14), confirms by CLIA assay, and sells validated positives to CDx teams.
scored.unproven_right: Title to archived residual specimens under IRB-compliant consent/waiver at <$5 per block
scored.proving_step: CLIA/CAP-validated NGS or IHC with orthogonal confirmation, the standard FDA CDx studies require
scored.proven_buyer: Diagnostics and pharma CDx teams (Roche, Foundation Medicine, Illumina, Thermo, Qiagen) and brokers paying ~$500-5,000 per positive
scored.public_data: Scanned pathology reports in the acquired archive (not public), SEER/TCGA/GENIE priors; key data is acquired, weakening C4
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^3x per positive ($3 to $1-5k); positives 0.5-2% so triage cuts assay spend ~10x; consent/HIPAA binding. Ladder: bank, validation CRO, owned CDx
scored.frame: Rung: buy residual FFPE/plasma archives, triage, confirm the marker, sell confirmed positives to CDx teams. My estimate is that discovery (triage) is about 40-60% of the work, not 80%+. The physical and regulatory steps are real costs: confirmatory NGS runs about $300-1,500 per sample and orthogonal confirmation is extra (estimate); pathologist review, sectioning, chain of custody, IRB waiver or consent checks, and HIPAA de-identification all scale per specimen. The assay is outsourced to CLIA labs, so it is abstractable but not trivial. A capitalised buyer does exist (Roche/FMI, Illumina, Thermo, Qiagen CDx teams and the CROs serving them).
scored.step_up: Claimed: under $5 per block unproven, $500-5,000 per validated positive, so about 100-1000x gross. Estimates from domain knowledge (no live search, see data): commercial vendors such as Discovery Life Sciences, BioIVT and Precision for Medicine sell uncharacterised FFPE blocks at roughly $100-500 each and molecularly characterised rare-fusion positives at roughly $1,000-5,000. Archives from closing labs can be close to free, but the realistic all-in cost of an unproven block (acquisition, IRB, retrieval, pathologist QC) is more like $20-50 (estimate). Net of the confirmatory assay (~$500) the real uplift per positive is about 10-100x, and it caps out because CDx demand is a few hundred positives per marker per study.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rates (literature, from memory): NTRK fusions about 0.3% of solid tumors (Westphalen et al. 2021, npj Precis Oncol); in NSCLC, ROS1 about 1-2%, RET about 1-2%, MET ex14 about 3-4%. The lever is capped at 1/p, which is about 30-300x. The cost per proving attempt is about $300-1,500 for NGS (estimate). Cheap pre-screens already exist (pan-TRK IHC at about $50-150, ALK/ROS1 IHC, and enriching by tumor type such as secretory breast carcinoma or MASC for NTRK), so the extra value of ML over standard enrichment is small. The roughly 10x triage cut mostly comes from known clinical priors, not from proprietary ML.
scored.data: The data fails both parts of C4. (1) It is not public: the key signal is the pathology reports inside the acquired archive. SEER/TCGA/GENIE are only priors, and anyone can read them. (2) The outcome is often already written in a legible field. NTRK, RET, ROS1 and MET ex14 are guideline-mandated (NCCN) for advanced NSCLC and pan-tumor NTRK testing. Since about 2017-2018, many of these specimens carry an NGS or IHC result in the pathology or molecular report itself, so finding positives is a text lookup, not ML. Older archives from before testing was routine have lower prevalence and older, degraded FFPE (lower DNA/RNA quality), which hurts how well the assay works. Rights: the archives can be bought cheaply from closing labs and failed biobanks, but CAP/CLIA retention rules (blocks kept 10 years), institutional ownership, state law and Common Rule/HIPAA limits on secondary commercial use make clean title uncertain and slow to get, block by block.
scored.right_bought: Bought, not claimed first-come: archives from closing labs, bankrupt biobanks and hospital pathology departments. The purchase price can be close to zero, but the cost of clean title is not (IRB waiver, de-identification, proof of consent scope, CAP/state retention rules), and owners often keep custody duties. Sellers do not 'fail to read the data': the pathology reports in their archives often already state the biomarker result.
scored.buyer: CDx and assay-validation teams at Roche/Foundation Medicine, Illumina, Thermo Fisher, Qiagen, Labcorp/Invitae and Tempus, plus specimen brokers. They are well capitalised, but each CDx validation or bridging study needs about 50-300 positives per marker (estimate), so the total market is perhaps tens of millions of dollars a year. Incumbents already serving it include Discovery Life Sciences (millions of characterised specimens), BioIVT, Precision for Medicine/ProteoGenex, iSpecimen (marketplace), Cureline, Tissue Solutions, Geneticist Inc, and the large reference labs (Tempus, Caris, FMI), which hold their own consented positive cohorts and data.
scored.ladder: Proposed path: biobank, then validation CRO, then owned CDx. Each rung is a services or diagnostics business with modest margins. An owned CDx needs a pharma drug partner and PMA approval, and the market is held by FMI, Tempus, Caris and Guardant. The chain tops out at a mid-size diagnostics company (billions of dollars), not a trillion-dollar vertical integration. There is also tension with the rubric: selling specimens to CDx teams sits close to 'selling to incumbents'. It does own the asset, but the upside is bounded by those incumbents' study budgets.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already summarised in a legible field, and the market is tiny. These rare markers are standard-of-care tested, so modern pathology and molecular reports already state NTRK/RET/ROS1/MET ex14 status. Finding positives is a text lookup that incumbents such as Discovery Life Sciences and the large reference labs already run over far bigger consented archives. Older, untested archives that could hide unknown positives have lower DNA/RNA quality and messier consent. On top of that, total CDx demand is a few hundred positives per marker per study, so even a perfect hit rate cannot make this a large, step-up-driven business.
scored.one_line_reason: The step-up is real (about $5 to $1-5k) and hit rates are low (0.3-4%), but the signal sits in private reports that often already state the answer. Cheap IHC and tumor-type pre-screens already supply most of the triage gain, incumbent biobanks already sell characterised positives, and demand is capped at a few hundred specimens per study.
sources: NOTE: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was exhausted (200-call limit), so no live searches ran. Every figure is from domain knowledge and should be checked.
Westphalen CB et al., 'Genomic context of NTRK1/2/3 fusion-positive tumours from a large real-world population', npj Precision Oncology 2021 (NTRK about 0.3% of solid tumors)
NCCN NSCLC Guidelines: broad molecular testing including ROS1, RET, MET ex14 and NTRK recommended for advanced NSCLC
Published NSCLC prevalence: ROS1 1-2%, RET 1-2%, MET ex14 3-4% (e.g. Bergethon 2012 JCO; Lipson 2012 Nat Med; Frampton 2015 Cancer Discov)

Vendor landscape (estimate, from memory): Discovery Life Sciences, BioIVT, Precision for Medicine/ProteoGenex, iSpecimen, Cureline, Tissue Solutions, which sell FFPE blocks and characterised positives at about $100-5,000
CAP Laboratory Accreditation retention requirements: paraffin blocks kept at least 10 years
HIPAA de-identification (45 CFR 164.514) and Common Rule (45 CFR 46) limits on secondary research use of residual specimens

scored.name: PoolProof (standard-essential patent rescue)
scored.one_line: Buys bankruptcy-estate, lapsed-revivable and auction telecom/video patents for ~$5-20k, uses ML to map claims onto 3GPP, IEEE 802.11 and HEVC/VVC specs, pays for pool essentiality evaluation, and places certified patents in pools (Avanci, Via LA, Access Advance) or sells to aggregators.
scored.unproven_right: Issued or revivable patents, declared or undeclared, held by bankrupt or exiting firms who cannot tell which claims read on the spec
scored.proving_step: Pool-appointed evaluator essentiality determination (~$10-15k); only ~20-40% of declared SEPs are truly essential, far fewer undeclared
scored.proven_buyer: Patent pools paying royalty shares; aggregators and licensors (Sisvel, Acacia, InterDigital-type, RPX)
scored.public_data: ETSI IPR declarations (400k+), 3GPP/IEEE spec archives, USPTO file wrappers, PTAB, assignment and maintenance-fee records, EPO Register
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x ($10k patent to $0.3-1M+ NPV once certified essential)
scored.frame: Rung = owning a patent and getting it certified essential by a pool evaluator. Inside that rung, finding the claim-to-spec read is most of the work (est. 70-85%). The physical step is a paid evaluation (~$10-15k per patent per standard, Via LA/Access Advance-style fees, my estimate) and costs little. Real buyers exist: pools pay royalty shares, and aggregators (Sisvel, Acacia, InterDigital, RPX) buy. The catch is that the payout is a royalty stream for the patent's remaining life, split by patent count. It is not a lump sum on a hit, and buying patents takes legal diligence (chain of title, FRAND encumbrances, revival risk).
scored.step_up: Unproven: telecom/video patents out of bankruptcy or lapsed are an estimated ~$5-50k each in bulk. Known anchor (my recollection, not checked this run): Richardson Oliver Insights put the average brokered asking price at roughly $150-300k per patent in the 2020s. Proven: an essential 4G/5G/HEVC patent might be worth ~$0.2-1M NPV (my estimate). Pool income per patent is diluted across thousands of listed families (Avanci charges ~$15-32 per vehicle across 100+ licensors; Access Advance lists 20k+ patents). Realistic step-up is ~5-30x, not 10^3-10^4. Many bankruptcy SEPs also have under 8 years of life left, which cuts the NPV further.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: studies of declared SEPs put true essentiality at ~20-50%. My recollection is Goodman & Myers ~50% for 3G, Stitzing/Fairfield and Cyber Creative ~25-35% for 4G/5G; I could not re-check these because the search budget was used up. The rate for undeclared patents is much lower, maybe 1-5% (my estimate). Cost per attempt: ~$10-15k evaluation plus ~$5-20k acquisition. For declared patents, the lever is capped at 1/0.3 ≈ 3x, not 10x. For undeclared patents the lever is bigger, but ML has to beat cheap keyword screening first.
scored.data: ETSI IPR declarations, 3GPP/IEEE/ITU specs, USPTO/EPO file wrappers and maintenance-fee records are all public. They are big but mostly machine-readable text, not scanned images. In part, the outcome is already written down in public: pools publish lists of certified essential patents, and ETSI declarations flag candidates. Incumbents already run ML essentiality screening, including LexisNexis IPlytics, Unified Patents, Amplified, PA Consulting, Sisvel, InterDigital in-house and Chinese CATR studies. So the data is not illegible to incumbents. That makes the edge thin.
scored.right_bought: Patents are bought, not claimed first-come. Rights are acquired from bankruptcy trustees, sellers exiting the business, or by paying the fees to revive lapsed patents (revival within 2 years needs an 'unintentional' delay statement, so it carries legal risk). Valuable telecom estates are sold through competitive brokered auctions (Nortel $4.5B, Kodak ~$525M, BlackBerry/Malikie ~$900M). That kills the cheap-buy thesis for good assets. The cheap ones are the dregs the brokers already screened.
scored.buyer: Patent pools (Avanci, Via LA, Access Advance, Sisvel) pay royalty shares. Aggregators and licensors (Acacia, InterDigital, Sisvel, Dominion Harbor, RPX for defensive purchases) buy patents outright. These buyers have money but price shrewdly and have their own essentiality tools.
scored.ladder: Climbing the chain means: aggregator, then licensing company, then FRAND litigation and contributing to standards (an InterDigital/Nokia Technologies model). The ceiling is roughly InterDigital at ~$5-10B market cap, or Nokia Technologies at ~EUR1.4B a year in revenue. This is a rent-extraction ladder that ends at licensing. It does not lead to a production chain with a trillion-dollar end state.
scored.fatal_flaw: Two things together. First, the base essentiality rate for declared SEPs is high (~25-50%), so ML can lift the hit rate by at most ~3x. Second, the outcome is already semi-legible (ETSI declarations, published pool lists) and is screened by funded incumbents with their own ML essentiality tools (IPlytics, Sisvel, InterDigital).
