Any valuable bankruptcy SEP is sold in a competitive brokered auction, so there is no ~1,000x discount on undiscovered value. What is left is a ~5-30x arbitrage on royalty streams with limited remaining life.
scored.one_line_reason: A real but small patent arbitrage: the step-up is ~10x not 10^4, ML can raise the hit rate only ~3x because 25-50% of declared SEPs are already essential, the data is screened by incumbents, and the ladder tops out as a licensing company.
sources: No live web sources this run: the shared WebSearch budget (200 calls per turn) was used up before any query ran. All figures below are from memory or my own estimates, not re-verified.
Goodman & Myers (2005), 3G Patents essentiality study (~50% essential), from memory
Fairfield Resources / Stitzing, Saeaeskilahti, Royer, Audenrode (2017) 'Over-declaration of SEPs' (~25-35% essential), from memory
Richardson Oliver Insights patent market reports (average asking price ~$150-300k per patent), from memory
Nortel patent auction $4.5B (2011); Kodak patents ~$525M (2012); BlackBerry patents to Malikie ~$900M (2023), from memory
Avanci 4G/5G vehicle program rates ~$15-32 per vehicle, from memory
Incumbent essentiality tools: LexisNexis IPlytics, Unified Patents, Sisvel, InterDigital, from memory

scored.name: Die-Variety Coin Cherrypicking (VarietyHunt / GradeHunt / Dieline / VarietyVault / Die Hard / Variety Mint)
scored.one_line: Buys raw, unattributed coins in bulk (estate hoards, rolls, eBay/HiBid/Catawiki/Numisbids lots, and European/Indian/LatAm markets with no slab culture) at melt or face, uses vision ML over listing photos and own scans to flag rare die varieties, doubled dies, overdates, VAMs and mint errors, submits only hits to PCGS/NGC, and sells slabs through Heritage, Stack's Bowers and GreatCollections.
scored.unproven_right: Title to an unattributed raw coin bought at melt/face or a $1-50 raw lot price from sellers who cannot read die markers
scored.proving_step: PCGS/NGC variety attribution plus grade ($20-150 per coin); the slab label and population report are the accepted proof standard and price is read off CoinFacts, Greysheet and Heritage comps
scored.proven_buyer: Heritage, Stack's Bowers, GreatCollections bidders, registry-set collectors, wholesale dealers on CDN/Greysheet bid sheets
scored.public_data: Millions of eBay/HiBid/Proxibid/Catawiki/estate raw listing photos; PCGS CoinFacts/VarietyPlus, VAMworld, Cherrypickers' Guide, CONECA files as labels; Heritage archive of slabbed images and prices; PCGS/NGC population reports
scored.rough_step_up: 10^2-10^4x per hit ($1-30 raw to $500-50,000 attributed; off-metal errors at 10^4); base hit rate 1 in 10^3 to 10^6 so ML triage is the lever. Weak: small TAM, supply-limited, thin ladder (grading prep, auction house, vault/fractional)
scored.frame: The rung is: own a raw coin, prove its variety, sell the slab. Inside that rung, discovery (spotting die markers) is about 85-90% of the work. The physical step, PCGS or NGC attribution, is a mail-in service that is fully outsourced. A buyer exists and Heritage, Stack's Bowers and GreatCollections have deep liquidity. But the buyers are fragmented hobby collectors and dealers paying retail. There is no capitalised developer who pays a multiple because the proven asset feeds a bigger project. The frame is real but small: each asset is one coin worth tens to hundreds of dollars.
scored.step_up: The variety hits you can realistically find, meaning ones the seller did not recognise, are mostly about 2-20x. Greysheet lists the Top-100 1878 8TF VAM-5 'Doubled Rib' at $95 low-MS, against about $55 for the base 1878 8TF low-MS (roughly 1.7x at the low end, with wide grade spread). A widely repeated anecdote is a $500 coin bought for $20 (25x). Guides say RPMs and doubled dies bring 10-100x over the common coin. The 10^4-10^5x hits (1955 DDO cent, off-metal errors) are famous and every seller and app already checks for them, so they rarely trade at face. My estimate of the blended realised step-up on an ML-flagged hit is about 3-10x. Raw Morgans also cost about $50+ at 2026 silver melt, not $1.
scored.hit_rate_capex: PCGS attribution is a $20 add-on to grading (Regular tier $40, so $60 per coin). NGC VAM attribution is a $10 add-on. My estimate of the base hit rate is 1-5% of Morgans for any premium VAM (PCGS attributes 317 Morgan VAMs out of 3,000+). It is far below 10^-4 for major doubled dies in circulated rolls. The proving cost is only spent on suspected hits, so it is not the expensive, mostly-failing step. The real cost is human loupe time spent searching. ML can triage that, but listing photos usually lack the resolution to show die markers: CoinAILyzer explicitly says photo scans cannot attribute VAMs. The lever is real but bounded by photo quality and by the cost of buying the coin at melt.
scored.data: Millions of eBay, HiBid and Catawiki raw-listing photos are public and unstructured, and the Cherrypickers' Guide, VAMworld, CONECA files and the Heritage archive work as labels. No regulator writes the outcome into a status field. However, sellers increasingly put 'VAM?' or 'DDO?' in titles. PCGS population reports and CoinFacts make variety value legible once someone looks. Many consumer apps (CoinKnow, CoinValueChecker, HeritCoin) already claim to detect doubled dies, and thousands of human cherrypickers work the same lots. So part of the edge is already competed away and part of the outcome is semi-legible.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Title to the coin is bought outright and cheaply from sellers who cannot read die markers, at face, melt or a raw lot price. This is a clean purchase, not a first-come claim. The catch is that the purchase price is set by melt for silver or by date/mint for keys, so the cost basis is not near zero.
scored.buyer: Heritage, Stack's Bowers and GreatCollections auction bidders, PCGS/NGC registry-set collectors, and wholesale dealers on CDN/Greysheet bid. These are liquid but fragmented retail collectors and thin dealer bids, not one capitalised buyer whose own economics justify paying the step-up.
scored.ladder: Thin. The possible next rungs are grading-prep or submission services, a dealer or auction house, and vault or fractional ownership. The US rare-coin market is roughly single-digit billions a year (my estimate), and the top of the chain (PCGS/Collectors, Heritage) is a hobby-scale business, not a trillion-dollar path. Supply is capped by the existing stock of old coins.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no 10^3-10^4 step-up on hits that can actually be found. Unrecognised varieties mostly realise 2-20x on a $20-60 coin, so each hit is worth tens to hundreds of dollars. The famous 10^4x errors are already screened by every seller and app. The whole market is a supply-capped hobby with no capitalised buyer and no ladder to a large company.
scored.one_line_reason: It is a clean buy-prove-sell loop with an outsourced proving step. But the step-up is mostly 2-20x per coin, many human pickers and apps already compete for the same lots, listing photos are too poor to show die markers, and the market is a small hobby with no ladder.

scored.name: Raw Vintage Card Pre-Grade Arbitrage (GemRate / Gradeless)
scored.one_line: Computer vision over public eBay, estate and auction listing photos predicts which raw vintage cards will grade PSA 9/10 and spots misidentified parallels/short prints; buys them as commons, submits only top predictions to PSA/BGS/SGC, and resells through Goldin, Heritage or Fanatics Collect.
scored.unproven_right: Raw ungraded card bought at raw comp from sellers who cannot see condition grade
scored.proving_step: PSA/BGS/SGC grade ($20-150); population report plus grade sets the price at once; gem-grade base rate on vintage stock is a few percent
scored.proven_buyer: Goldin, PWCC/Fanatics Collect, Heritage and eBay buyers; card funds such as Collectable
scored.public_data: eBay sold-listing image archive, PSA population reports and APR auction results, Heritage archive photos
scored.rough_step_up: Usually 3-50x, up to 100x+ (raw $20 1950s-70s star card to $2-50k PSA 9/10); crowded edge (TAG and AI pre-grading exist), so C4 is weak. Ladder: grading company, marketplace
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a raw card, grade it, sell the graded slab. Inside that rung, picking the card is roughly 80-90% of the work (my estimate). Grading is the physical step and it is cheap and outsourced: $20-150 per card at PSA, BGS or SGC. TAG Priority is $149 and Walkthrough $299. The buyers who take the output are real and have money: Goldin, Fanatics Collect, Heritage, SCP, Memory Lane, eBay. This is the strongest part of the candidate. It is held back by the time it takes to get a grade back and by the capital tied up in raw cards. Most of the capex is buying the raw card, not proving it.
scored.step_up: Best case is about 100x or more. The 1969 Topps #260 Reggie Jackson rookie in PSA 9 sold for $84,000 (Spring 2022) and $67,500 (2025), against an estimated $3,250 for PSA 8. No source gave a raw comp. My estimate is $300-1,500 for a decent raw copy, so a PSA 9 hit is roughly 50-200x and PSA 8 is roughly 2-10x. That top-end step-up exists only for a handful of star rookies. A typical raw $20 vintage star card that grades PSA 7-8 returns 1-5x, often below cost once fees and slab costs are paid. The value of a single hit is about 10^2 at best, not 10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: For random vintage stock the base rate is far below 1%. The 1964 Topps set has 1,133 PSA 10s out of 208,893 graded (0.5%). The 1964 Hank Aaron #300 has 8 PSA 10s out of 3,248 graded. The 1960 Topps Jim Brown has 0 PSA 10s out of 2,709 graded (GemRate via SI). The 1969 Reggie had about 37 PSA 9s with 1 higher out of a few thousand graded in 2018, and 12,120 have been graded in total. These rates are already selection-biased upward, because people submit cards they think will grade well. A proving attempt costs $20-150 to grade plus the raw purchase (my estimate is $50-1,500 for a star card). Since 1/base rate is large, the theoretical ceiling on the ML lever is high. In practice the raw purchase dominates capex, and pre-screening rejects candidates before you buy them, so the realistic saving is maybe 2-3x. That is in line with vendor claims of 40-60% grading-cost savings from AI pre-screening, which are unverified.
scored.data: The data is public: eBay sold-listing photos, Heritage and Goldin archive images, PSA population reports and auction results. It is legible to anyone with eyes. Condition shows up in the listing photo itself, so every bidder, dealer and pre-grading app sees the same signal. The outcome distribution is already summarised in a legible field: PSA pop reports and GemRate give per-card grade counts and gem rates. Many tools already score raw-card photos for predicted grade: CardGrade ($4.99/mo), PreGradeCards (claims 89% within ±1 grade), Gemix, Ximilar's grading API, and TAG's photometric imaging. Only blurry, low-resolution listing photos keep the signal partly hidden. That is the only real edge left, and it is noisy, because surface defects and print lines often cannot be seen in seller photos.
scored.right_bought: Yes, raw cards are bought outright and can be cheap. But sellers of nice-looking raw vintage are mostly dealers and collectors who know grading economics. Sharp-looking star cards get bid up toward their expected graded value. The real discount is limited to estates, sellers who don't know the hobby, and bulk lots, which are small, high-touch supply. Vintage high-grade stock has been sifted through grading since 1991. Misidentified parallels and short prints are a better niche, but they are mostly a modern-card phenomenon and are covered by card-ID apps.
scored.buyer: Goldin (owned by eBay), Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC), Heritage, SCP, Memory Lane, eBay, and fractional funds such as Collectable. The market is liquid and the grade plus pop report set the price at once.
scored.ladder: The ladder above the rung is the grading company (PSA, now owned by Collectors, is about a $4B+ business), then a marketplace or auction house (Goldin, Fanatics Collect), then vaulting and fractionalisation. The total addressable market is the trading-card market, about $10-15B a year by my estimate. A company could become a decent mid-size collectibles platform. There is no trillion-dollar path, and the grading and marketplace incumbents (Collectors/PSA, Fanatics, eBay) are entrenched and well-capitalised.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving signal, card condition, is visible in the same public photo every buyer, dealer and pre-grading app already looks at, and PSA pop reports publish the outcome distribution. There is no hidden information to arbitrage. Sharp raw vintage is already priced near its expected grade, and the 10^2 jumps are limited to a few star rookies.
scored.one_line_reason: The rung is clean: grading is cheap and outsourced and buyers have money. But the step-up is about 10^2 at best and rare, the edge is crowded and visible to anyone (photos, pop reports, AI pre-graders, TAG), and the ladder tops out at a market of roughly $10-15B.

scored.name: Unheated / Premium-Origin Coloured Stones (Origin Lab / Unheated / Origin Report Co)
scored.one_line: Buys cut sapphires, rubies and emeralds in estate jewellery and old dealer stock (European, Indian, Bangkok/Jaipur lots) priced as generic or 'assumed heated', uses ML over photos (colour zoning, silk), mount era, cut style and provenance text to predict no-heat Kashmir/Burma/Colombian origin (and natural fancy-colour diamonds), gets SSEF/Gübelin/GRS/AGL/GIA origin reports, and resells at Geneva and Hong Kong. Trading cut stones, not mining.
scored.unproven_right: Title to an uncertified stone or estate ring bought at melt or commodity gem prices
scored.proving_step: Origin plus treatment report ($300-2,000); accepted standard major houses price from; most stones are heated or common origin
scored.proven_buyer: Christie's, Sotheby's, Phillips Geneva/Hong Kong jewellery sales; top jewellers (Graff, Harry Winston); trade houses
scored.public_data: Estate auction photo and description archives (LiveAuctioneers, Invaluable, Drouot, Dorotheum, Indian houses); published lab inclusion atlases; historic certified-stone results
scored.rough_step_up: About 5-300x per stone ($1-5k to $50k-1M for unheated Kashmir/Burma of size); below 10^3, low hit rate, weak ladder (own lab, recutting, branded jewellery)
scored.frame: Rung: buy an uncertified cut stone or estate ring, get an SSEF/Gubelin/GRS origin and treatment report, and resell at auction. Discovery is maybe 60-80% of the work, and the physical step (shipping the stone to a lab) is cheap. The catch is that every 'shot' means buying the stone outright before you can test it, so the right costs about as much as the asset. There are capitalised buyers (Christie's, Sotheby's, Bonhams, Graff, trade houses), but they also run in-house specialists who scout the same estates.
scored.step_up: Typical no-heat premium over a comparable heated stone is 30-100% (Spectra: 20% to over 100%) and up to 3-10x (SkyJems: 300-1000%). That is a 1.3-10x step, not 10^3. Heated sapphire runs about $1-4k/ct against $5-25k+/ct unheated (Spectra). For Kashmir, heated is about $5-30k/ct against $20-200k+/ct unheated (Angara). The best sleeper case I found: Bonhams HK, a 12.92ct ring appraised under $10k (other houses estimated $3.8-6.3k), re-estimated at $120-510k after SSEF/Gubelin confirmed no-heat Kashmir. That is about 20-80x, and it is a rare outlier. Record: Regent Kashmir 35.09ct at $9.5M, $271,515/ct, Christie's HK 2025. The starting asset is never near zero, because estate stones already sell at melt plus commodity gem value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rate: 90-99% of sapphires on the market are heated, per dealer claims with no cited survey. Kashmir/Burma no-heat stones are a far smaller share, my estimate well under 1% of estate coloured stones. Cost per attempt: stone purchase ($1-5k, which is mostly recoverable on resale at a haircut) plus a report. Gubelin was about GBP 220 and SSEF about GBP 400 (old PriceScope forum figures), AGL about $200. Current SSEF/Gubelin fees for large stones run $500-2,000+ (my estimate). The real per-shot capex is the purchase spread plus report plus transaction friction, about $500-3k, not the stone price. The lever exists, but the ML prior comes from photos. Heat detection needs microscopy and FTIR/LA-ICP-MS, so ML raising precision from 1% to 10% is unproven. My estimate is a 2-3x lift, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public but weak. The signal that settles heat and origin (silk integrity, discoid fractures, trace elements, FTIR spectra) is physical and microscopic. It is not visible in auction photos of mounted stones. Where a stone already has a lab report, the auction description writes the outcome into a legible field ('Kashmir origin, no indications of heating', standard Sotheby's/Christie's lot text), which kills the edge for certified stock. The remaining edge is only in uncertified regional lots (Drouot, Dorotheum, Indian houses), where mount era, cut style and provenance text are weak priors that specialists already use by eye.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought outright from estates and regional auctions at commodity or 'assumed heated' prices. But you buy the whole asset at a non-trivial price, not a cheap option on it. The sellers often consign to Bonhams, Christie's and Sotheby's, whose specialists catch sleepers before sale (Bonhams found and certified the 12.92ct Kashmir itself). Competition: Bangkok, Jaipur and Geneva coloured-stone dealers, plus auction-house specialists, already work this arbitrage by hand.
scored.buyer: Christie's, Sotheby's, Phillips, Bonhams (Geneva/HK); Graff, Harry Winston; Bangkok/Geneva trade houses. All are capitalised and pay up for SSEF/Gubelin no-heat Kashmir/Burma/Colombian stones.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are your own gem lab (a services business with credibility moats held by SSEF, Gubelin and GRS), recutting, and a branded high-jewellery house. Graff-scale is a few $B in revenue. Coloured-stone mining is excluded and politically constrained (Kashmir has been mined out since the 1880s; Burma is sanctioned). There is no path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving signal is physical, not informational. Whether a stone was heated, and where it came from, can only be read with a microscope and spectroscopy on the stone itself. Photos and mount style carry only a weak prior, and certified outcomes are already written into the auction lot text. That leaves no illegible public dataset where ML beats auction-house specialists, and each shot means buying the whole stone, with a 1.3-10x typical step-up, not 10^3.
scored.one_line_reason: A real but small arbitrage. The usual step-up is 1.3-10x (sleepers hit 20-80x at most), the signal sits in the physical stone rather than in public data, certified outcomes are already legible in lot text, specialists already hunt sleepers, and the ladder tops out at a jewellery brand.

scored.name: Issue Points (first-state book and print attribution)
scored.one_line: Buys bulk lots of old books, maps and prints by the box, uses vision ML over listing and estate photos to detect first-edition first-state issue points, inscriptions and association copies, and has them collated and catalogued to bibliographer standard for sale through Heritage, Christie's, Swann and ABAA dealers.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of books and prints bought at $1-20 per item from estate clearances and thrift wholesalers who cannot check issue points
scored.proving_step: Collation against the standard descriptive bibliography plus acceptance by an ABAA/ILAB dealer or major auction cataloguer; cheap
scored.proven_buyer: Heritage, Christie's, Sotheby's, Swann, ABAA dealers, institutional libraries
scored.public_data: Descriptive bibliographies and issue-point references, ABE/Biblio listing photos, WorldCat and HathiTrust page images, estate-sale photo dumps
scored.rough_step_up: $5 book to $1k-100k+, 10-1000x on a hit; low hit rate, small market, weak ladder
scored.frame: Rung: buy mixed lots and resell the attributed items to a dealer or auction house. Spotting the valuable item is maybe 50-60% of the work (my estimate). The physical side is real and has to be done for every item: buying whole boxes, shipping and storing them, examining each book by hand, collating it page by page, grading condition and writing up the listing. That handling does not shrink as volume grows, unlike a drill program that is abstracted per hectare. A capitalised buyer does exist (Heritage, Christie's, Swann, ABAA dealers). So the frame partly exists, but discovery is well short of 80%.
scored.step_up: Unproven: $1-20 per item. Proven: the trade's own vendor numbers put typical rare finds at $50-$500+ profit per book (underpriced.app). Anecdote: a scout bought a book at an estate sale for $3; it was valued at $150 and the dealer offered half (WPLN). $10k+ hits do exist but are very rare. Average auction lot is about $2,000 (568,593 lots sold in 2024 for $1.137B, Rare Book Monthly), and those lots have already been attributed. Typical step-up on a hit is 10-100x; occasionally above 1000x. Per box bought, the step-up is much lower.
scored.hit_rate_capex: No reliable published hit rate (search found only anecdotes). My estimate: under 1% of bulk-lot items are worth $100 or more, and about 0.01% are worth $5k or more. Each proving attempt is cheap: $1-20 to buy the item plus roughly $1-5 of labour to examine it. Formal collation and auction consignment cost more, but only for the hits. The work is not costly or mostly failing per attempt in the way a drill hole is. The binding cost is labour and the supply of lots to look through, not failed proving. ML photo triage could raise the share of items worth buying, but it saves dollars per box, not $100k drill holes.
scored.data: Public but semi-legible. Issue points are written up in descriptive bibliographies, and dealers and specialist scouts know them well. ABE and eBay listings often already say "first edition/first printing", so the outcome is frequently written in a legible field, at least as the seller's claim. Estate-sale and lot photos are illegible and scattered, which is the real edge. The edge is strongest on pre-ISBN books, where barcode-scanning apps (BookScouter and others) do not work. Competitors: thousands of human scouts, sale-flipper apps, and dealers who already pick through estate sales.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Items are bought cheaply ($1-20, or by the box) from estate clearers, thrift wholesalers and online lots whose owners do not check issue points. Supply is fragmented and contested: scouts get to the good lots first, and estate liquidators increasingly check eBay and ABE comparables themselves.
scored.buyer: Heritage, Christie's, Sotheby's, Swann, ABAA/ILAB dealers and institutional libraries. They are capitalised but the market is small: about $1.23B of book and paper auction sales in 2025 (Rare Book Monthly).
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are becoming a dealer, then an auction house or marketplace. The whole chain is the rare book and paper market, about $1-2B a year at auction plus online sales of unknown size. There is no trillion-dollar chain; the ceiling is a niche dealer or auction business.
scored.fatal_flaw: The market is small and the work is labour-bound. Every hit needs hands-on examination and collation, and typical hits are worth $100-500. Total book auction volume is about $1.2B a year, and there is no meaningful ladder above dealer or auctioneer. ML improves box-picking at the margin rather than unlocking a 10^4 jump on an expensive proving step.
scored.one_line_reason: Rights are bought cheaply and there is a real illegible photo edge on pre-ISBN books, but proving is cheap and labour-bound, typical hits are only 10-100x on $5 items, and the whole market is about $1.2B a year with no ladder.

scored.name: Firstfile Complex Generics (ML-selected BE, sold as approved ANDAs)
scored.one_line: Targets complex generics (topicals, inhalers, LAIs, GI-local drugs) with product-specific guidance but no approved generic because BE usually fails, uses ML over scanned FDA review packages to pick passable formulations and Q1/Q2/Q3 targets, and sells approved ANDAs with CGT exclusivity to generics majors.
scored.unproven_right: Opportunity to file an ANDA on an uncontested reference drug; the asset is the formulation dossier, not a bought right (weak C4)
scored.proving_step: In-vitro BE (IVRT/IVPT, Q3) ~$0.3-1M, in-vivo where required; FDA approval confers 180-day CGT exclusivity
scored.proven_buyer: Teva, Viatris, Sandoz, Amneal, Hikma
scored.public_data: Drugs@FDA scanned chemistry and biopharm reviews, product-specific guidances, Orange Book, Paragraph IV list, FDA off-patent no-generic list
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-50x ($1-3M spend to $20-150M ANDA value); physical step non-trivial, partly fails C1
scored.frame: The rung is "approved ANDA for an uncontested complex reference drug, sold to a generics major." Inside it, picking a formulation (the discovery) is maybe 20-35% of the work. That is my estimate. Most of the effort goes into reverse-engineering Q1/Q2/Q3 sameness, building and characterising the device for inhalers, scaling up to exhibit batches at a cGMP site, running stability, the BE studies themselves, and getting through pre-approval inspection and 1-3 FDA review cycles (GDUFA goal is about 10 months per cycle). The physical step is the core of the work, not a trivial add-on, which makes this structurally closer to the geothermal counter-example than to Terranox. A capitalised buyer does exist: Teva, Viatris, Sandoz, Amneal, Hikma and Dr. Reddy's buy ANDAs.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a formulation idea or an ANDA filing opportunity is worth about $0, but it costs real money to reach a filing. Development cost by product type (my estimates, except where a source is named): roughly $3-10M all-in for an IVRT/IVPT topical once scale-up and exhibit batches are counted, not the claimed $0.3-1M; for an inhaler, more than $100M per AB-rated product (Datamonitor, cited by Nanopharm/Aptar), with a single 900+ subject clinical-endpoint BE study at about $45M. Proven: Dr. Reddy's paid $350M for 8 complex-generic ANDAs from Teva in 2016, mostly pending, one approved. That averages about $44M per ANDA (my division, not a disclosed per-ANDA price). Most single-product ANDAs sell for about $5-50M (my estimate), and the value decays quickly once the 180-day CGT exclusivity ends and a second entrant arrives. The step-up is about 5-15x on development spend for topicals and about 1-3x for inhalers. That is nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published BE failure rate for complex generics. My estimate is that 30-60% of first in-vitro or in-vivo BE attempts fail for topicals and LAIs. Clinical-endpoint studies carry a "high risk of not meeting endpoints" (FDA, acyclovir ointment example). Even a perfect predictor caps the lever at about 2-3x (1 divided by a base hit rate of roughly 0.3-0.5), not 10x. Most of the capex is also fixed cost spent whether or not BE passes (scale-up, device, stability, site), so ML only touches a fraction of the spend. Cost per proving attempt: about $0.3-1M for an IVPT/IVRT study (candidate's figure, plausible), about $45M for a clinical-endpoint BE study (Nanopharm), and more than $100M for an inhaler program (Datamonitor).
scored.data: The data is only partly public and partly illegible, and the outcome is already in legible fields. Drugs@FDA publishes chemistry and biopharm reviews only for APPROVED applications. ANDA Complete Response Letters, which hold the failure information, were not part of FDA's 2025 public CRL releases; those cover NDAs and BLAs, and ANDA CRLs exist only as monthly counts (82 in August 2025, per Lachman). So the most valuable negative data is private to whoever filed. The targets themselves are written up in legible lists: FDA's Off-Patent Off-Exclusivity No-Approved-Generic list, product-specific guidances that spell out the BE method and often the Q1/Q2 expectations, the Orange Book, the Paragraph IV list, and the CGT designation list (312 designations by July 2024). The "which drugs are uncontested" answer is already summarised by the regulator. Incumbents also have in-house formulation labs, so they extract their own data and do not need to read these files.
scored.right_bought: No. There is no right to buy. Anyone can develop and file an ANDA on an uncontested reference drug, first come first served. CGT exclusivity goes to the FIRST APPROVED applicant, lasts only 180 days, and is forfeited unless the product is marketed within 75 days of approval. The "asset" is a race position, not something bought cheaply from an owner who cannot read the data. This fails the core Terranox mechanic.
scored.buyer: Generics majors buy approved or pending ANDAs: Teva, Viatris, Sandoz, Amneal, Hikma, Dr. Reddy's (bought 8 ANDAs for $350M) and Senores (bought 14 ANDAs from Dr. Reddy's in 2025). The same firms are also the direct competitors: they run in-house complex-generic programs on the same FDA lists, alongside Lupin, Cipla, Glenmark, Teva Respiratory, Xiromed and CDMO-backed developers.
scored.ladder: There are real rungs above: own manufacturing or a CDMO, then commercial distribution, 505(b)(2) improved versions, and branded specialty. A Teva-scale generics company is worth about $20-40B (my estimate), but it is a low-margin, price-eroding business. Winning a few uncontested ANDAs does not give structural leverage up the chain, because each product is a separate race with 180 days of protection at most.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no ownable, purchasable unproven right. The opportunity is an open race that the FDA itself lists publicly (the no-approved-generic list and product-specific guidances), with only 180 days of exclusivity. The proving step is a $3-100M+ manufacturing, BE and regulatory build, not a cheap drill hit. And the failure data an ML model would need (ANDA CRLs and failed BE results) is not public.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a capital-heavy formulation and manufacturing race on targets the FDA already publishes. There is no right to buy cheaply, the step-up is about 5-15x (not 10^3-10^4), and ML can lift the hit rate by about 2-3x at most.

scored.name: Cargo Title (subrogated title to sunk cargoes proven by ROV survey)
scored.one_line: Buys title to historic lost cargoes (bullion, specie, high-value metals in cargo, not seabed minerals) from underwriters, P&I clubs or governments for a nominal sum, uses ML over Lloyd's List, logbooks and convoy records to narrow position, locates the wreck by AUV/ROV, confirms title by admiralty arrest, and sells the located claim to salvors.
scored.unproven_right: Legal title to a specific sunk cargo bought for a small fee or percentage before its location is known
scored.proving_step: Side-scan sonar plus ROV identification (~$0.5-2M) and admiralty in rem arrest or Receiver of Wreck filing
scored.proven_buyer: Deep-ocean salvors (Odyssey Marine, Ocean Infinity mold) and specialist funds
scored.public_data: Lloyd's List archive, UK National Archives Admiralty records, NOAA AWOIS/ENC, convoy and war-loss records, CLIWOC logbooks
scored.rough_step_up: 10^2-10^4x on title cost (SS Gairsoppa ~$200M+ silver); recovery is expensive, so the rung only works if the located claim is sold pre-recovery. Reviewer: cargo, not seabed geology, so kept outside mineral exclusion
scored.frame: The rung is: get the cargo right, locate and identify the wreck, then sell the located claim before recovery. Archival narrowing is the part ML could improve, and my estimate is that it is about 40-60% of the work, not 80%+. The physical step is not trivial. Deep-water sonar and ROV ID cost about $0.5-2M per campaign, and an early Odyssey SEC filing puts mobilisation alone at $100k to several hundred thousand dollars per project. Odyssey's burn was reported at about $2.4M a month. Proving a location also does not settle the asset's value. Cargo condition, sovereign-immunity claims (Odyssey lost the Mercedes case to Spain) and recovery cost all stay open until recovery. The market for 'located but unrecovered claims' is extremely thin; in practice the title holder tenders a salvage contract to a salvor who carries both search and recovery.
scored.step_up: Unproven: in practice, governments and underwriters do not sell title for a fee. They tender a salvage contract and keep about 20%, and the salvor gets about 80% of net salved value. That was the UK Department for Transport's tendered deal with Odyssey on Gairsoppa and Mantola in 2010. Proven: Gairsoppa's headline value was about $200M+, but Odyssey's total monetisation over two years was only about $80M. On SS Central America the underwriters got about 7.5% and the salvor about 92.4%. My estimate is that a located but unrecovered claim might be worth 5-20% of gross cargo value to a salvor, because of recovery and legal risk. If title could really be bought for about $10-50k, that implies roughly 100-1000x on title cost. But no observed market price for located claims exists, so this is unproven.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published base rate, so these are estimates. Searches for a well-researched single target seem to succeed often (Odyssey found both Gairsoppa and Mantola). Area surveys are mostly noise: Odyssey's Atlas project searched 5,000+ sq nmi and recorded about 300 wrecks, of which only a handful had commercial cargo. The cost per proving attempt is about $0.5-2M for deep water (my estimate, consistent with Odyssey filings and 'single-digit millions' for the Gairsoppa survey plus recovery). The main uncertainty is not where the wreck is but whether the cargo is there, is intact and is legally clear. ML over archives cannot see that. So I estimate the realistic lever on capex at about 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The sources are public and semi-illegible: Lloyd's List, Admiralty/National Archives war-loss files, convoy records and CLIWOC logbooks. But the outcome is largely already legible. The insured cargo value and the approximate sinking position are written in the war-loss and insurance records (the UK government knew Gairsoppa's 1941 claim was about £325k and roughly where she sank), and NOAA AWOIS/ENC and Wrecksite.eu list positions. Incumbents already mine these archives: Odyssey keeps an in-house research team, and Ocean Infinity and specialist historians do too. The ML edge is small, because the hard part is the last-mile sonar ID, not reading the records.
scored.right_bought: Mostly not available as described. The owners are sophisticated sovereigns such as the UK Department for Transport. They know what they own, and they award exclusive salvage contracts by competitive tender to the best rate of return, not sell title cheaply. Many underwriter interests have been ruled abandoned (Central America) or sit with Lloyd's syndicates that would insist on a share. Warship and state cargoes carry sovereign immunity (the Mercedes case), and UNESCO 2001 and heritage law limit commercial salvage. Old bills of sale are a precedent (Murphy v. Dunham, 1889), but there is no modern market for buying title in advance.
scored.buyer: Weak. Odyssey Marine is a loss-making microcap that pivoted to seabed minerals. Ocean Infinity mainly sells survey services. Specialist treasure funds are small and episodic. None has a 'developer spends $40k/ha to make $100k/ha' economics that would make it pay a large fixed price for a located claim before recovery. Salvors would prefer to contract with the title holder directly for about 80%.
scored.ladder: Short. Above the rung are recovery, then bullion refining and numismatic sales. The pool is finite and non-renewable: perhaps a few hundred commercially valuable deep cargo wrecks worldwide (my estimate), with very lumpy revenue (about $80M from the best-known modern success). It does not lead to a large adjacent industry, so there is no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no capitalised buyer that pays a large price for a located but unrecovered claim. Value is realised only after expensive recovery that carries legal risk. The title holders are sophisticated sovereigns who tender salvage contracts (about 20/80 splits) rather than sell title cheaply. And the asset pool is small and finite.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a niche treasure-salvage business. Odyssey's history shows it: archival research is already done, title comes from tendered contracts rather than cheap purchase, and value appears only at recovery.

scored.name: Unmatched Catalog (orphan music rights proven into collectable royalties)
scored.one_line: Buys obscure catalogues and orphaned writer/publisher shares from estates and defunct labels for a few times trailing royalties, uses ML to match works to MLC, PRO and Content ID unmatched pools and scanned copyright registrations, registers and claims, then sells to catalogue funds at standard multiples.
scored.unproven_right: Copyright or royalty-share assignments with near-zero reported income from heirs and defunct companies
scored.proving_step: Validated registration and claim at MLC, PROs and CMOs releasing held royalties; royalty statement history is the accepted proof
scored.proven_buyer: Concord, Primary Wave, Round Hill/Hipgnosis successors, Reservoir paying 10-20x NPS
scored.public_data: US Copyright Office Catalog of Copyright Entries (scanned pre-1978), MLC works database and unmatched portal, PRO repertories, Discogs, streaming metadata
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x on purchase price; outcome partly legible in existing databases
scored.frame: The rung is: buy an orphaned share, prove chain of title, register and claim it, then sell the resulting royalty stream. Most of the work in this rung is finding and documenting the asset (my estimate is about 60-70%: identifying the work, tracing heirs, building chain of title). The "physical step" is filing registrations at the MLC, PROs and CMOs. That step costs almost nothing, so in that sense it is abstracted, just as the rubric wants. Two things hold it back. Building legal chain of title (probate, assignments, termination-right checks) is real, slow legal work, not discovery. And the capitalised buyers (Concord, Primary Wave, Reservoir, Round Hill successors) do buy, but only aggregated catalogs, typically above about $1M NPS (estimate). They do not buy single orphan shares. So the frame exists, but it needs an aggregation layer first.
scored.step_up: None of these numbers were verified this run; the web search budget was used up, so all are from memory or estimated. Large catalogs trade at about 10-20x NPS (the candidate's figure, which matches reported Hipgnosis, Concord and Reservoir deals of 2020-23). Small catalogs on marketplaces like Royalty Exchange trade at about 5-10x (my recollection). The candidate proposes buying at "a few times trailing" income on near-zero earners. If a claim lifts annual income from about $0-50 to about $500-2,000 per work (estimate for obscure long-tail works), the value multiple on purchase price is about 3-30x. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The ceiling is the value of usage that already exists, not newly created value. The asset is never near-zero in a deep sense: the plays are already happening and the money is sitting in the black box.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is a registration or claim filing, which costs about $0-100 per work (MLC registration is free; my estimate is $50-500 per work for the legal and data-cleanup labour). It is not an expensive, mostly-failing drill. The hit rate on works chosen from the MLC unmatched list is high, because those works are already known to have usage. The real failure point is chain-of-title disputes and heirs who cannot be traced. The real cost is the acquisition price plus legal fees, and ML does not reduce either by 10x. So the lever is small: perhaps 2-3x on targeting effort. It falls far short of the about 10x capex lever Terranox gets.
scored.data: The outcome is already largely legible, and this is what kills the ML edge, as in the earlier hunts. The MLC publishes a public Unclaimed Royalties / Data Quality portal that lists unmatched recordings with usage. DSPs transferred about $424M of historical unmatched royalties to the MLC in Feb 2021 (from memory). The MLC reports match rates of about 90% or more of usage dollars. Rights holders and their admins can see which works are earning but unclaimed. The genuinely illegible part is the scanned pre-1978 Catalog of Copyright Entries, and it is partly solved already: the renewal records have been digitised and searched by NYPL, Internet Archive and Stanford. Incumbents in claiming and auditing include Songtrust, Sentric, Kobalt, Exploration.io, TuneRegistry, Royalty Exchange, Duetti and specialist black-box recovery auditors. The right can be bought from heirs and defunct labels, which fits the "bought, not free" test. But sellers can be told what they own by any admin service at no upfront cost, which squeezes the purchase discount.
scored.right_bought: Copyright or royalty-share assignments bought from heirs, estates and defunct labels and publishers. Buying is possible but slow: probate, multiple heirs, and termination rights under 17 USC 203/304 that let authors' heirs reclaim the rights later. Unclaimed MLC money is eventually distributed to existing publishers by market share, so the window to claim it is finite and contested.
scored.buyer: Catalog funds and publishers: Concord, Primary Wave, Reservoir, Round Hill/Hipgnosis successors (Recognition/Blackstone), Duetti, Sony/UMG/Warner publishing. They pay about 10-20x NPS for scale catalogs and less for small aggregated long-tail pools (estimate).
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: aggregate into a catalog fund, then publishing administration, then a label or publisher, then rights-management infrastructure. The whole music publishing industry is about $10B+ a year in revenue (estimate). That is a meaningful path but bounded, with no trillion-dollar route. Incumbents (Sony, UMG, Warner, Kobalt) already occupy every rung.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is already legible and already being claimed. The MLC's public unmatched portal and the royalty statements show which works earn, so the proving step only collects existing small usage (about 3-30x on purchase price, not 10^3). It costs almost nothing per attempt and has a high hit rate, so ML gets no 10x capex lever on a low base hit rate.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real but small arbitrage. Claiming is cheap and mostly succeeds, the unclaimed outcome is published by the MLC, and the step-up is about 10x on long-tail dollars. It is royalty recovery with a buy-in, not a 10^4 discovery jump.
