scored.name: Corridor Title (fibre easement rights from scanned utility and pipeline deeds)
scored.one_line: Reads scanned 1920s-70s transmission and pipeline easement deeds to find corridors where the utility holds no communications rights, buys telecom easements from each landowner, insures continuous title, and sells the route to long-haul fibre builders and hyperscalers.
scored.unproven_right: Communications easements at ~$500-3,000 per parcel along corridors whose recorded scope is power or pipe only
scored.proving_step: Title commitment/ALTA policy insuring a continuous communications easement; cheap paper test; most corridors fail on gaps or broad 'any purpose' language; ML OCR plus clause classification picks clean corridors
scored.proven_buyer: Zayo, Lumen, Bandwidth IG, Ziply and hyperscalers building inter-campus routes
scored.public_data: County recorder deed images, utility easement indexes in PUC dockets, PHMSA NPMS, HIFLD transmission lines
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x via contiguity; cousin of the untested-promising rail corridor title idea; risks: holdouts and pole/tower consent
scored.frame: The rung would be "assemble and insure a continuous communications easement along an existing power or pipe corridor". Inside that rung, reading the deeds is maybe 30-40% of the work (my estimate). Most of the work is buying from every landowner in sequence, because one holdout breaks the chain, and winning consent from the utility. You cannot use towers or poles without the utility's say, and you cannot bury cable inside its strip without a crossing or encroachment agreement. A title policy is cheap, but it does not make the route buildable: the utility can still block access. So discovery is well under 80% of the work, and the hard physical and political step is not abstracted away. Fibre builders do buy routes, but they buy built, lit or dark fibre (IRUs). They do not buy paper easements.
scored.step_up: My estimate, no sourced numbers (search budget ran out). Unproven: about $500-3,000 per parcel, or roughly $1-5 per linear foot. That is in line with what landowners were paid in the 2000s railroad and utility fibre-trespass class settlements (from memory, not re-verified). Proven: a route's ROW is about 10-20% of long-haul build cost, at an estimated $30-100k per mile. Builders also have cheap fallbacks: highway and county road ROW by permit, railroads, and utilities' own OPGW and leased fibre. So a corridor is worth at most a few times what its parcels cost to assemble, about 2-5x, not 10-100x. It is nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate. Each title search or commitment costs about $200-1,000 per parcel (my estimate). The real cost per attempt is the land-agent negotiation, about $2-10k per parcel including the easement price, and that spend is lost if any one parcel holds out. The paper test (is the deed scope "power only" or "any purpose") probably passes 20-50% of parcels. Contiguity across 50-200 parcels per 10-mile segment then fails on holdouts. ML improves only the cheap title screen, not the expensive holdout or consent step. The capex lever is around 2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The deeds are public but illegible: scanned county recorder images from the 1920s-70s, a real OCR and clause-classification problem. The outcome is not written into a legible field, and NPMS/HIFLD give geometry only, not easement scope. That is a genuine ML edge. Against it: state courts are split on apportionment. Some (e.g., Indiana, Mississippi, Iowa-type cases) let utilities add communications under the existing easement, and some state statutes explicitly allow it. So "power-only" wording does not guarantee the utility lacks the right. Incumbents already do this work by hand: utility land departments, telecom ROW agents, and the plaintiff firms behind the fibre-trespass class actions.
scored.right_bought: Yes. The rights are bought cheaply, parcel by parcel, from farmers who cannot read the deed scope. They are not free first-come rights. But the holdout problem is severe: every parcel must be bought. And the utility, which controls physical access, is a second counterparty with a veto.
scored.buyer: Zayo, Lumen, Bandwidth IG, Ziply and the hyperscalers are well capitalised. But they buy finished fibre or lease capacity, and they route on highway or rail ROW where permits are routine. They would want the utility's sign-off before paying a premium. A naked easement chain with no utility consent is worth little to them.
scored.ladder: A ladder exists: easements, then a dark-fibre build, then a lit network, then a long-haul carrier or IRU business. But every rung above the first is a capital-heavy construction business with entrenched competitors, the utilities themselves among them (e.g., they monetise OPGW and lease fibre). It is moderately large, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: A paper easement from the landowner does not make the corridor buildable. The utility controls the towers, poles and the occupied strip, and can block access or claim apportionment rights. Builders also have cheap substitute ROW (highways, rail, the utility's own fibre). So the proven value is only a few times the purchase price, and holdouts and utility consent, not discovery, dominate the work.
scored.one_line_reason: The deed-scope ML edge is real, but the step-up is about 2-5x because substitute ROW is cheap. Holdouts and utility consent are the real work, so discovery is not 80% of the rung.
sources: No web searches ran: the per-turn search budget shared across agents was exhausted on the first call. Every number above is the model's own estimate from background knowledge, not a sourced figure.
Background knowledge (not re-verified): the 2000s nationwide railroad/utility fibre-optic trespass class settlements (Sprint, Qwest, Level 3, WilTel) paid landowners roughly $1-6 per linear foot.
Background knowledge (not re-verified): state courts are split on whether a utility easement can be apportioned to communications use, and some state statutes allow it outright.
Background knowledge (not re-verified): utilities already monetise OPGW and lease fibre on their corridors.

scored.name: Photomatch Bins (game-used sports memorabilia)
scored.one_line: Buys 'game-issued' and team-sale jerseys, bats and helmets in bulk, uses ML to match wear, repairs and tagging against game photos and broadcast frames, and sells items with an accepted photomatch letter through Goldin or Heritage.
scored.unproven_right: Equipment sold by teams and arena sales as 'issued' or unverified at $100-1,000
scored.proving_step: Photomatch letter from Resolution, MeiGray or PSA (92% of top-25 2023 game-worn sales were photo-matched); most items fail
scored.proven_buyer: Goldin, Heritage, SCP, Lelands, memorabilia funds and collectors
scored.public_data: Getty, AP and newspaper photo archives, team galleries, broadcast footage, Baseball-Reference logs, past lot photos
scored.rough_step_up: ~2-10x for already game-used items, up to ~100x for unverified star items; below target
scored.frame: The rung is: buy an unverified jersey, bat or helmet, then get a photomatch letter for it. Inside that rung, discovery is roughly 85-90% of the work (my estimate): pulling photos and frames, matching wear, repairs, tagging and numbering, then submitting to a photomatcher. The physical work is trivial: buy the item, ship it, consign it. Buyers do exist and pay a premium for matched items (the candidate cites 92% of the top-25 game-worn sales in 2023 being photo-matched). But the buyers are collectors and funds paying for rarity. They are not a developer whose model already makes the price step-up work. The frame is real but small and mostly about taste.
scored.step_up: I could not verify numbers: the shared web search budget was used up before my first query ran, so every figure here is my own estimate from prior knowledge. An item that is already sold as game-used rises roughly 2-5x once photomatched (an unmatched star game-used jersey at ~$2-5k becomes ~$5-25k). A team-issued, unworn item that turns out to be a matched game-worn star piece can rise 10-100x ($300 to $10k+). That 100x case is the rare tail. The typical step-up is 2-10x, well below the 10^3-10^4 target. The candidate's own estimate says the same.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates, not sourced. A photomatch costs roughly $100-500 per item at Resolution Photomatching or Sports Investors Authentication. Fees are tiered, sometimes a share of value, plus a few weeks of turnaround. Base hit rate on bulk team-issued or arena-sale lots is likely 5-30%. Many items were never worn in a game, and lesser players have too few photos. ML could pre-screen candidates so you submit only likely hits. The lever is capped at about 3-10x, and the cost per attempt is already small, so a 10x cut in total discovery cost saves little money. The real limit is how many star-quality inputs exist, not the cost of each match attempt.
scored.data: The images are public and hard to read by machine: Getty and AP archives (licensed, not free), team galleries, broadcast footage, past auction lot photos. But the outcome is often already written into a legible field. The MLB Authentication Program (since about 2001) puts holograms on game-used items, and its public lookup records the game, player and use. NFL, NBA and NHL team sales and MeiGray carry game and season details on their letters of authenticity. Photomatchers (Resolution, SIA, MeiGray) already run large private image databases, so the illegible-data edge is shared by a few specialist incumbents. The upside is that rights are bought cheaply in bulk from team and arena sales and eBay sellers who do not cross-check photos.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Equipment marked team-issued or unverified is bought at $100-1,000 at team and arena sales, at auctions and on eBay. It is a real purchase from sellers who mostly do not research it. Teams, though, increasingly authenticate and sell their star game-used items themselves at full price, which shrinks the supply of underpriced star items.
scored.buyer: Collectors and memorabilia funds paying through Goldin, Heritage, SCP/Sotheby's, Lelands and REA. This is a hobby demand pool of perhaps low single-digit billions a year. It is not a capitalised industrial buyer that has to buy the output.
scored.ladder: Weak. Possible rungs above are an auction house, an authenticator, or fractional ownership. Those are adjacent services in a niche hobby, not a vertical chain toward a trillion-dollar end market. The ceiling is roughly a few-hundred-million-dollar dealer or auction business.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is only about 2-10x, and the market is a finite hobby pool. Leagues (MLB holograms) and team letters already put the game-used outcome in a legible field, and photomatchers already hold the image databases. So the ML edge is narrow, and the upside is capped well below 10^3.
scored.one_line_reason: The discovery-heavy rung is real and the right is bought cheaply, but the step-up is 2-10x, not 10^4. League authentication already writes the outcome into a public field, photomatchers do this already, and there is no ladder of rungs above.
sources: No live sources: the shared web search budget was used up before any query in this task ran, so all numbers are estimates from prior knowledge
MLB Authentication Program hologram lookup (mlb.com/authentication), cited from prior knowledge
Resolution Photomatching and Sports Investors Authentication fee schedules, cited from prior knowledge
Candidate brief: 92% of top-25 2023 game-worn sales were photo-matched

scored.name: VoucherWorks (FDA tropical-disease PRV from foreign-approved drugs)
scored.one_line: Licenses US rights to tropical-disease drugs approved only abroad (India, Brazil, China, WHO PQ), files a US NDA on foreign data plus bridging work, and sells the priority review voucher earned on approval to big pharma (~$100-160M).
scored.unproven_right: US development and marketing rights to FDA-listed tropical-disease drugs never filed with FDA, valued near zero by generic makers and state institutes
scored.proving_step: FDA approval resting mostly on foreign data plus bridging PK/BE and CMC (~$5-20M); ML ranks dossier completeness
scored.proven_buyer: Large pharma buying vouchers (Gilead, AbbVie, Novartis); Bavarian Nordic sold one for $160M in 2025, Knight's for $125M
scored.public_data: FDA tropical disease list (21 USC 360n), CDSCO and ANVISA approval PDFs, WHO PQ assessment reports, CTRI/ReBEC/ChiCTR, multilingual regional journals, DNDi/MMV documents
scored.rough_step_up: ~$0.1-1M right to ~$100-160M voucher, ~100-1000x; proving costs millions (weaker C1) and is near the killed stranded-drug-rescue idea
scored.frame: The rung is a US NDA plus a tropical-disease PRV for a drug that is already approved abroad. Discovery is maybe 10-20% of the work, my estimate. You can find the whole set of eligible molecules in an afternoon from the 21 USC 360n disease list, the WHO EML and the WHO PQ list. Most of the work is regulatory, clinical and CMC: bridging PK/BE, bringing a foreign API maker up to US GMP with a pre-approval inspection, labeling, and the post-2016/2017 statutory requirements. From memory and unverified: the application must contain new clinical investigations essential to approval that the sponsor conducted or sponsored, and the product must be marketed in the US within a year. The physical step is the hard part, so this has the same shape as the geothermal counter-example.
scored.step_up: Unproven US rights to an off-patent foreign-approved drug: my estimate is $0.1-2M upfront plus a share of the voucher, since owners now ask for a split. The proven asset, the voucher, sells for about $100-160M (task brief: Bavarian Nordic $160M in 2025; Knight/Paladin's miltefosine voucher $125M in 2014). Gross that is about 100-1000x. Net of $5-20M+ in proving cost and the owner's share, it is about 5-15x on capital deployed. The step-up applies to the voucher, which is a regulatory bounty. The drug's US sales are near zero.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is high, not low. These drugs already have foreign approval and large real-world use. FDA approval of tropical-disease PRV applications built on foreign data has been frequent: Coartem 2009, Impavido 2014, benznidazole 2017, moxidectin 2018, Egaten 2019, Lampit 2020, artesunate (Amivas) 2020, fexinidazole 2021, and others, all recalled from memory. My estimate is a 50-80% approval probability once a sponsor files. Cost per attempt is $5-20M (task brief; my estimate puts some at $20-40M if a new trial is required). With a base rate of about 0.6, ML can raise it by at most about 1.7x (cap = 1/base rate). That is nowhere near the needed 10x capex cut. Risk sits in execution, not in finding the asset.
scored.data: The outcome is already in legible fields. Drugs@FDA and the Orange Book show whether a moiety has US approval. FDA publishes every PRV awarded. The disease list is statutory. WHO PQ and the WHO EML list every quality-assured tropical-disease drug and who makes it. Few candidates remain: pyronaridine-artesunate (Shin Poong), DHA-piperaquine, arterolane-piperaquine (Sun), antimonials, paromomycin for leishmaniasis, tribendimidine (China), arpraziquantel (Merck KGaA consortium), recalled from memory. Each is known to its owner. CDSCO, ANVISA and CTRI documents add little beyond what WHO PQ public assessment reports already summarise. ML ranking of dossier completeness is a consultant's spreadsheet task across about 20-50 molecules, not a large illegible corpus.
scored.right_bought: Rights can be licensed, but owners are not naive. Since Coartem and Impavido (2009-2014), every holder (Sun, Shin Poong, Sanofi, Merck KGaA, DNDi, MMV) knows a voucher is worth about $100M+. DNDi and MMV push access terms and voucher-sharing. There is no information asymmetry to buy against: owners can read their own dossiers.
scored.buyer: Large pharma voucher buyers (Gilead, AbbVie, Novartis, Sanofi and others) form a real, liquid, capitalised market of about 5-10 sales a year (my estimate). Prices fall as the supply of vouchers grows.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Above the voucher the next rung is US commercialisation of low-revenue tropical drugs (travel medicine, small markets) or becoming a specialty pharma, as Knight Therapeutics and 60 Degrees Pharma did. Neither path leads anywhere near a trillion dollars. The candidate pool runs out after a handful of molecules, which caps the company at about 5-15 vouchers in total.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no discovery problem to solve. The eligible molecules are a small, fully legible, already-arbitraged list (drug lists plus Drugs@FDA tell you everything), and owners know what a voucher is worth. The proving step is a high-probability but costly regulatory and CMC effort. ML therefore cannot cut capex 10x, and the rung's work is dominated by the physical and regulatory step, the same failure shape as geothermal and the killed stranded-drug-rescue idea.
scored.one_line_reason: The voucher payoff is real (about $100-160M), but the candidate list is short and public, owners know what vouchers are worth, approval is the likely outcome rather than a rare hit, and the cost sits in regulatory work rather than discovery. ML has almost nothing to find.
sources: Task brief figures: Bavarian Nordic PRV sale $160M (2025), Knight/Paladin PRV sale $125M
21 USC 360n tropical disease PRV statute and FDA list (recalled from memory; requirement for new clinical investigations and US marketing added 2016/2017, not verified in this session)
Drugs@FDA / Orange Book and FDA's published list of PRVs awarded (legible outcome fields; from memory)
WHO Prequalification and WHO Essential Medicines List (public registries of tropical-disease drugs; from memory)
NOTE: WebSearch quota was exhausted (shared turn limit), so no live searches were run; every number other than the brief's voucher prices is my estimate or recalled from memory

scored.name: Ridgeline Wind Options (complex-terrain wind, 'ERA5-blind' sites)
scored.one_line: Buys cheap wind lease options on ridges and gaps where reanalysis maps (Global Wind Atlas, NREL WTK) underpredict wind, proves the resource with a 12-month LiDAR plus short-mast campaign to IEC 61400-12 / MEASNET, and sells the option and P50/P90 package to a utility-scale developer, who pays the step-up.
scored.unproven_right: Wind lease or easement options on ranch, forest and private ridge land at about $2-10/acre/yr, from owners told by public maps that their land is 'Class 3'
scored.proving_step: About $60-120k per site: floating/ground LiDAR or SoDAR correlated to long-term reference data, written up by an accredited consultant (DNV, UL) as a bankable P50/P90. Most sites come back at or below the map, so the base hit rate is low.
scored.proven_buyer: Utility-scale wind developers and IPPs (NextEra, Invenergy, Pattern, RWE), buying development-stage projects at about $20-100k/MW
scored.public_data: Scanned 1970s-90s DOE/NASA/BPA/state energy office candidate-site met-tower reports; FAA OE/AAA obstruction filings for old met masts; ASOS/AWOS and RAWS records; USGS 3DEP lidar; abandoned-project wind data in state PUC and county permit dockets
scored.rough_step_up: About $250/MW/yr option to $20-100k/MW proven site, roughly 100-400x per acre nominally; realistically 30-100x because interconnection and permitting remain
scored.frame: Proposed rung: a land option plus a bankable P50/P90 met package. Inside that rung, wind discovery is maybe 50-60% of the work (my estimate). The rest is landowner contracting across many parcels (a utility-scale project needs roughly 50-85 acres/MW of lease area, which means dozens of owners), the 12-month physical measurement campaign, and the consultant write-up. The bigger problem is that a project with resource data alone is not a rung buyers purchase separately at a premium. Developers buy projects that hold interconnection queue positions, permits and community acceptance. Measured wind is one diligence item among about six. Zoomed out, resource confirmation is a small share of what makes a project valuable, and no frame exists where it is 80%+ and has a buyer.
scored.step_up: Unproven: option payments of $1.25-$40/acre/yr in sample contracts and guides (SD development agreement $1.25/acre/yr; ND Crownbutte $100 per 160-acre quarter section/yr, about $0.63/acre; AES form $12-20/acre; Landgate $5-40/acre). At roughly 60 acres/MW (my estimate), that is about $40-2,400 per MW per year. Proven but still early-stage: real pipeline deals price very low. ERG paid up to EUR 4M (about $4.5M) for 224 MW of German pipeline, about EUR 18k/MW, and partly as deferred success fees. Western Wind's 2012 term sheet was $20M for 4,000 MW, about $5k/MW. Higher prices ($105k/MW Ontario 2011, paid at construction milestones; C$290k/MW for construction-ready Halkirk) only appear once permits, PPA and interconnection exist. So a site with land plus measured wind and nothing else plausibly sells for about $5-20k/MW, against about $0.5-2.5k/MW of option cost: roughly 5-30x, mostly from aggregating land rather than from the wind measurement. A higher-than-map wind reading lifts value maybe 1.2-2x over the same site with a mapped resource. Most of the claimed 30-100x needs work the candidate does not do (interconnection, permitting).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: the candidate's $60-120k per site is plausible but my estimate. The search found no published onshore $/site figure; a lidar unit is a reusable capital asset, and a 12-month campaign plus a DNV/UL report sits in that range. Base hit rate (site measures materially above the map): no source found. A WindEurope 2024 poster validating the Global Wind Atlas (GWA) against 50 masts found bias ranging from -28.7% to +20.2% with an average of +8.5%. On average the atlas overpredicts, and the scatter cuts both ways. So perhaps 20-30% of complex-terrain sites come in meaningfully above the map (my estimate). The lever is capped at 1/hit rate, about 3-5x, not 10x. ML on old met-tower reports will also find that developers already run mesoscale and CFD resource maps (Vaisala/3TIER, UL Windnavigator, AWS Truepower legacy) that beat reanalysis in complex terrain, which shrinks the real edge further.
scored.data: The data really is illegible and scattered. Scanned 1970s-90s DOE/BPA/state candidate-site met reports, FAA obstruction filings for old masts, and old project dockets are not in a structured field. No regulator status field writes down the answer. But the outcome is partly summarised already: commercial wind-resource maps and mesoscale models, which developers subscribe to, produce site-level speed estimates. Ridge flow is where models disagree, but measured mast data from the 1980s at 30-50 m heights says little about 120-150 m hub height in today's terrain and forest cover. Lidar on ridges also needs CFD flow-curvature correction (Vaisala/WindSim study of 20 sites). So the public data narrows the search but does not stand in for the measurement.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought cheaply, at $1-40/acre/yr option payments, so that part of the thesis holds. But ridge and forest land in good wind areas is heavily canvassed by developer land agents, and landowners compare offers. Ridges add problems: turbine transport and roads, IEC turbulence and icing classes, visual and avian or bat permitting (ridges are raptor corridors), and forest clearing. These lower buildability exactly where the resource upside sits. Assembling contiguous multi-owner options is slow and gives no exclusivity over the data insight.
scored.buyer: Utility-scale developers and IPPs: NextEra, Invenergy, Pattern, RWE, Apex, EDF, and also landowner-aggregator developers. These buyers are capitalised, but they mostly originate their own greenfield sites with in-house meteorology teams and pay well only for projects de-risked on interconnection, permits and offtake. US onshore wind build-out has also slowed: weaker policy support after 2025 and a shift of developer pipelines toward solar plus storage reduce demand for early-stage wind sites.
scored.ladder: The rungs above exist and are large: develop (interconnection, permits, PPA), then build and own an IPP, then supply power. Climbing from land plus resource to a full developer is a well-trodden but crowded path, and many small developers do exactly this today. Winning the smallest rung gives no structural advantage, since there is no proprietary resource, and the higher rungs are dominated by interconnection-queue and capital advantages, not discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: Wind resource is not the binding constraint on value. Interconnection, transmission, permitting and offtake are, and the grid interconnection queue thesis was already killed. A site with land and a bankable P50 but no queue position is early-stage pipeline priced at about $5-20k/MW, not a 10^3x jump. Mast validation also shows public atlases overpredict on average (+8.5% mean bias), so 'ERA5-blind' upside sites are a minority. They also cluster on ridges that are the hardest to permit and build, which repeats the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: the physical and regulatory work dwarfs the discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: The land option is cheap and the old met data is illegible. But measured wind alone moves a site maybe 5-30x into an early-stage pipeline market of about $5-20k/MW, where interconnection and permitting, not discovery, set the price, and ML's hit-rate lever is capped near 3-5x.

scored.name: Dedicate (nuclear-grade spares from industrial surplus via 10 CFR 21 dedication)
scored.one_line: Buys surplus industrial and cancelled/closed-plant inventory (valves, relays, breakers, pumps) at scrap prices, uses ML to match lots to obsolete safety-related parts operating reactors cannot source, runs a cheap commercial-grade dedication under an Appendix B program, and sells to utilities at nuclear prices.
scored.unproven_right: Title to un-pedigreed surplus lots (Bellefonte, Pilgrim, Indian Point, OEM overstock) bought at $10-1,000 per lot
scored.proving_step: Commercial-grade dedication under 10 CFR 21 / EPRI 3002002982 critical-characteristic tests (~$2-20k per part type); ML over ADAMS FSARs, Part 21s, LERs and surplus listings predicts lots that match and pass
scored.proven_buyer: Nuclear utilities (Constellation, Vistra, Duke, TVA, Southern) paying $5k-500k to avoid ~$1M/day forced outages; restarts (Palisades, Crane, Duane Arnold)
scored.public_data: NRC ADAMS scanned FSARs, Part 21 reports, LERs, inspection reports; GSA/GovDeals/DLA Disposition listings; scanned OEM catalogues; decommissioning asset sale notices
scored.rough_step_up: ~50-500x per part ($100 valve to $10-50k dedicated item), up to ~1000x when it ends a forced outage. Ladder: dedication house, reverse-engineered replacements, qualified component maker, new-build supply chain
scored.frame: The rung is "own a surplus lot, dedicate it, sell it as a safety-related spare", and it is a real, sellable rung with capitalised buyers (utilities). Discovery, meaning finding which lot matches an obsolete safety-related part, is not 80%+ of the work inside it. My estimate is that matching is 20-40%. The rest is engineering and physical work: the critical-characteristics evaluation, the technical evaluation for equivalency, and for many safety-related items seismic, EQ and LOCA qualification testing (Curtiss-Wright lists seismic tables, P/T/humidity chambers and LOCA simulation as part of dedication). It also includes Appendix B program overhead and the utility's own acceptance. For un-pedigreed lots, traceability and counterfeit/fraudulent-item (CFSI) screening adds work that no amount of discovery removes. So the physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted.
scored.step_up: The unproven price is about $10-1,000 per surplus lot at scrap or GovDeals prices (the candidate's own figure, unverified). The proven price is set by the buyer's alternative, not by the scrap basis. That alternative is a new commercial-grade item plus dedication from Paragon, Curtiss-Wright or Westinghouse, or a RAPID/PIM pooled spare. Published markups for nuclear-grade over commercial are about 2-3x for N-stamp valves and up to 10x for nuclear steels (ARIES/PPPL 2011 Cadwallader slide). The dedicated-item value is therefore roughly 3-10x the commercial replacement cost. The 50-500x "step-up" is mostly a scrap-versus-retail arbitrage that any surplus dealer captures; it is not value created by proving. The ~1000x case, ending a forced outage at about $1M/day, is rare and lumpy. Utilities manage it with emergency procurement, RAPID, and sister-plant cannibalisation. Honest value created by the proving step is about 3-30x (C2 = 2).
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published pass rate for commercial-grade dedication. My estimate is that once a part is correctly identified as form-fit-function equivalent, dedication passes most of the time (>70%). The failures come mainly from missing traceability or aged elastomers and shelf-life, not from discovery error. Cost per attempt is about $2-20k per part type (the candidate's estimate; my search found no published figure). For EQ/seismic items it can be $50-200k+ (my estimate), and that is testing cost ML does not cut. A high base hit rate caps the ML lever at about 1.5x, nowhere near 10x. The scarce thing is demand, meaning knowing which obsolete part a utility needs. Utilities publish that need themselves through RAPID requests and obsolescence lists.
scored.data: The data is public but mostly legible. Part numbers, manufacturer and model are structured fields in surplus listings and in utility inventory systems. Curtiss-Wright/Scientech RAPID already pools member inventories into a "virtual warehouse containing millions of parts" and identifies replacements for obsolete parts. Utilities also run Pooled Inventory Management (PIM), which holds over $247M of shared critical components and has addressed obsolescence since 2002. The scanned ADAMS FSARs, Part 21s and LERs are illegible, but they say little about which specific spare a plant lacks, and the matching problem is largely a part-number lookup that existing tools already solve. The outcome, "is this item dedicable for application X", is effectively written into the utility's own item equivalency evaluations and RAPID catalogue, so the ML edge is weak.
scored.right_bought: Rights are bought, not free first-come: surplus lots are bought from GSA, DLA, GovDeals, OEM overstock and decommissioning owners. Two problems weaken this. First, decommissioning-plant inventory with nuclear pedigree, such as Pilgrim or Indian Point under Holtec, is already sold into RAPID and to sister utilities at near-nuclear prices, so it is not cheap. Second, industrial surplus is cheap precisely because it has no pedigree, and that makes it the hardest to dedicate. One utility reports selling $4M of inventory to other nuclear plants through RAPID, which shows sellers can already reach these buyers.
scored.buyer: US nuclear utilities: Constellation, Vistra, Duke, TVA, Southern and others. All are well capitalised and pay nuclear prices for safety-related spares, and restarts such as Palisades, Crane and Duane Arnold add demand. The buyer is real. The weakness is that they already have entrenched dedication vendors and pooled-inventory channels.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder above the rung: dedication house, then reverse engineering, then qualified component maker, then new-build supply chain. Paragon Energy Solutions is the proof point and the incumbent. It was acquired by Mirion for about $585M (Sept 2025) on roughly $150M of 2026 revenue and claims 20,000+ proprietary parts in 100% of North American reactors. Curtiss-Wright Nuclear, Westinghouse and Framatome sit above it. The ceiling is a valuable but bounded niche, likely a few-billion-dollar company, not a trillion-dollar chain. New-build supply could extend it.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck and proving does not create the step-up. Matching surplus to obsolete parts is a near-legible part-number lookup that Curtiss-Wright/Scientech RAPID and pooled utility inventories (PIM) already do. Dedication passes at a high rate and its cost is dominated by physical qualification testing, which ML cannot cut. The proven price is capped at roughly 3-10x a new commercial-plus-dedication alternative supplied by entrenched vendors (Paragon, Curtiss-Wright, Westinghouse). The claimed 50-500x is scrap-to-retail surplus arbitrage, not a 10^3-10^4 proving jump.
scored.one_line_reason: A real business with real buyers and a real ladder (Paragon sold for $585M), but it fails the Terranox shape. The work is mostly physical testing, the hit rate is already high, part matching is legible and already done by RAPID and PIM, and the step-up from proving is about 3-30x, not 10^4.

scored.name: Equipment Qualification Packages for reactor restarts and SMR builds
scored.one_line: Buys EQ and seismic qualification reports, designs and stock from defunct qualification vendors and decommissioning plants near zero, uses ML over ADAMS to match them to equipment restarts and new builds need, extends them under IEEE 323/344 and 10 CFR 50.49 by similarity plus limited testing, and sells qualified components or files. Overlaps Dedicate.
scored.unproven_right: Qualification files, EQ binders and component stock bought near zero in liquidations
scored.proving_step: Qualification by similarity plus targeted aging/seismic tests ($20-200k vs $1-5M fresh); ML over EQ master lists and SERs predicts extendable qualifications
scored.proven_buyer: Restart owners (Holtec Palisades, Constellation Crane), SMR developers (TVA/GE BWRX-300, X-energy, Kairos), EPCs (Bechtel, Westinghouse)
scored.public_data: NRC ADAMS EQ master lists, SERs, PSDARs, Part 21 notices, NUREG/CR reports, decommissioning auctions
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-1000x on a hit (near-zero file and stock to a $1-10M qualified component line)
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy surplus or obsolete safety-related stock plus its EQ file, then sell it as a qualified component. Inside that rung, finding the part is perhaps 20-30% of the work (my estimate). Most of the work is physical and regulatory: a 10 CFR 50 Appendix B QA program, commercial-grade dedication, re-establishing traceability, aging, LOCA and seismic tests, and taking on Part 21 defect-reporting liability. Paragon advertises 4 shake tables, 12 aging ovens and 6 environmental chambers, which shows that testing capacity is what the business runs on. The buyers (Palisades, Crane, EPCs) are well capitalised, but proving a part is not trivial or abstracted.
scored.step_up: Unproven: decommissioning spares go to public auction. Vermont Yankee sold about $20M of book-value spares, tools and supplies in 1,000+ lots in 2016, and the auctioneer expected many buyers to be 'local guys'. No source gave recovery rates. I estimate auction lots clear at about 5-20% of book (estimate). Proven: a dedicated or qualified part sells at roughly OEM nuclear-grade price, about 1x book and sometimes more for obsolete items (estimate). That is roughly a 5-20x step-up on stock, not 100-1000x. The candidate's '$1-10M qualified component line' assumes repeat orders, which does not happen on a single hit. Restart and fleet demand for any given obsolete part number is a handful of units.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: I estimate that qualification-by-similarity on a candidate the engineers have already matched succeeds about 30-60% of the time (estimate). Similarity is a standard IEEE 323 method; for example, Westinghouse used it for Watts Bar 2 mineral-insulated cable. Most failures come from the environment envelope not bounding the new plant, not from bad matching. Cost per attempt: the candidate gives $20-200k for similarity plus targeted tests against $1-5M for fresh qualification. I found no published per-test cost, so both figures are unverified. With a hit rate of 30-60%, ML's lever is capped at about 2-3x, not 10x. SMR environment envelopes (BWRX-300, Xe-100 helium, Kairos FLiBe salt) differ from legacy LWRs, so legacy qualifications rarely bound them, and for the non-LWR SMRs the base rate is close to zero.
scored.data: ADAMS is public but messy. The EQ master lists, SERs and Part 21 notices give the licensing envelope and component IDs. The decisive documents, the EQ test reports and qualification packages, are usually vendor-proprietary and withheld under 10 CFR 2.390, so they are not public. Whether a qualification can be extended depends on test-report details that are not in ADAMS. Incumbents already extract this. Paragon advertises '30 years' of EQ and qualification and dedication services, and Curtiss-Wright QualTech NP does EQ and seismic testing. Plant EQ engineers and EPRI's equipment databases cover component matching. There is no legible 'answer field', but the people who can read the files are the same incumbents who would bid against you.
scored.right_bought: Stock can be bought at auction or in investment-recovery deals. The EQ files are the problem. The intellectual property in a test report usually belongs to the OEM or test lab, and the licensee holds a copy under a licence. When parts leave the plant, their Appendix B pedigree and traceability chain often lapse, so the file does not transfer cleanly with the stock. The sellers can read their own data (utilities know what they hold). Paragon already runs a nuclear 'investment recovery' business that buys exactly this excess inventory and says it holds $100M+ of parts in its warehouse. So there is no information asymmetry to exploit.
scored.buyer: The buyers are restart owners (Holtec Palisades, Constellation Crane, NextEra Duane Arnold) and LWR SMR builders (TVA and OPG BWRX-300). EPCs such as Westinghouse and Bechtel sit in the middle, but they are also competitors. The buyers are capitalised, but volumes are small and they prefer established Appendix B suppliers.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: obsolete-parts dedication, then reverse-engineered equivalent parts, then nuclear-grade component OEM, then I&C and EQ testing lab, then an EPC-adjacent supply-chain integrator. The ladder is real but the ceiling is visible. Paragon (PE-owned) and Curtiss-Wright's nuclear segment are what the top looks like: valuable, but these are niche supplier businesses, not a path to a trillion-dollar company. The SMR build-out could widen it if new-build qualification is in scope, but that is fresh qualification, not discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: Incumbents already run this exact business. Paragon Energy Solutions buys excess and obsolete nuclear inventory through investment recovery (it says it holds $100M+ in stock) and runs its own EQ lab, and Curtiss-Wright QualTech NP, Westinghouse and Framatome cover the rest. Inside the rung, the work is mostly physical testing plus Appendix B QA and Part 21 liability, not discovery. The decisive EQ test reports are proprietary rather than public, so there is no illegible public signal for ML to exploit and no seller who cannot read their own inventory.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a qualified-spares and dedication business that Paragon already runs. Testing and QA, not discovery, make up most of the rung, and the step-up is about 5-20x, not 10^3. Base hit rates are high, so ML's lever is at most 2-3x, and the key data (vendor EQ reports) is proprietary, not public.

scored.name: Easement Hunter (landlocked parcel access from deed chains)
scored.one_line: Buys landlocked parcels near zero (often at tax sale), uses ML over scanned deed chains, plats and road petitions to find recorded, forgotten or implied access, proves it with a title commitment carrying an ALTA 17 access endorsement, and sells the insurable parcel to neighbours or developers.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to parcels with no recorded access (tax-delinquent, heirs' property) at ~$200-2,000
scored.proving_step: Title abstract plus ALTA survey (~$3-10k) leading an underwriter to issue an access-endorsed commitment
scored.proven_buyer: Adjacent owners, homebuilders, timber/solar aggregators, land funds requiring insurable title
scored.public_data: County recorder scanned deed books and microfilm, plats, road petitions and vacations, BLM GLO records, county GIS, tax-sale lists
scored.rough_step_up: ~20-500x ($500 to $20-150k with insured access); cousin of the rail-corridor title idea using a standard insurance product as proof
scored.frame: The rung is: own a landlocked parcel, find access, and sell it with insured title. Discovery (reading deed chains for a forgotten easement or common-ownership history) is maybe 50-60% of the work (my estimate). Proving access is not a cheap, abstracted physical step. ALTA 17 requires the land to actually abut a named, open public street, so it does not apply to landlocked land. ALTA 17.1 needs an easement that is already recorded and insurable. An implied easement or easement by necessity only becomes insurable after a court judgment, and that means litigation with a neighbour who can contest it and claim adverse possession. Clearing the tax-deed title also usually needs its own quiet title action. The buyer is usually a single adjacent owner or a small land investor, not a capitalised buyer paying a large multiple.
scored.step_up: Appraisal evidence puts the landlocked discount at 46-90% off road-access value. The Montana DNRC paired-sales study of 19 pairs found an average 46.4% discount for no legal access. A New York appraisal study supports discounts of up to 90%. Fixing access is therefore worth about 2x (typical) to 10x (best case), not the 20-500x claimed. The $200-2,000 tax-sale price already reflects small, low-value rural parcels. Their road-access value is often only $2k-20k (my estimate), not $20-150k.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate (how often a landlocked parcel has a recorded but forgotten access easement) is not published. I estimate under 10%, because most parcels are landlocked precisely because no access was ever recorded. Cost per proving attempt: title abstract plus ALTA survey at about $3-10k (the candidate's own figure). A quiet title action adds about $950 per parcel in the 2011 South Bend memo ($750 legal, $156 filing fee, $40 recording, publication extra), and a contested easement-by-necessity suit costs far more. Each attempt costs 5-20x the parcel price, so ML can only help by triaging which parcels to buy. The ceiling on the gain is 1/hit rate, but the total payoff per hit stays small.
scored.data: Partly favourable. Scanned deed books, microfilm, plats and road petitions are genuinely public, illegible and scattered, and incumbents (title plants) only index them by name and grantor, not for access logic. But the outcome is partly legible already: county GIS parcel layers show road frontage, and a title abstractor finds a recorded easement routinely in an ordinary search. That leaves the ML edge mainly in implied easements and old road dedications that were never formally vacated.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Fee title is bought cheaply at tax sales or from heirs, and the sellers cannot read the data. Caveats: redemption periods, and tax-deed title that underwriters often will not insure until a quiet title action is done.
scored.buyer: Mostly the one adjacent owner (a monopsony with leverage, since that owner is also the party who would be sued for an easement by necessity). Small land investors and occasional timber, solar or homebuilder aggregators. Competitors: existing land wholesalers and tax-deed flippers already target landlocked lots and sell them to neighbours. The buyer is not capitalised in the Terranox sense.
scored.ladder: Weak. Rungs above (assembling land for development, entitlement, homebuilding) exist, but landlocked slivers are not the scarce input for them. The road leads to a land wholesaling or assemblage business, not a trillion-dollar vertical chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is only about 2-10x, because the landlocked discount is 46-90%. On top of that, proving access usually needs a recorded easement, a court judgment or a neighbour's cooperation, not a title commitment. Each proving attempt ($3-10k plus quiet title) costs more than the parcel itself, and the realistic buyer is the single neighbour who holds all the leverage.
scored.one_line_reason: Real public-but-illegible deed data and cheap tax-sale rights, but a 2-10x step-up, proving that needs litigation, and a neighbour monopsony make this a small land-flipping business, not a 10^4 discovery rung.

scored.name: Hillside Clear (geotechnical clearance of hazard-zone lots)
scored.one_line: Buys vacant hillside lots in mapped landslide/seismic hazard zones (LA, Bay Area), uses ML over decades of scanned neighbouring geotech reports and grading permits to pick competent-bedrock lots, gets a city-approved geotech report, and sells build-ready lots.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to hazard-zone lots (~$20-80k where buildable lots are $500k-2M+)
scored.proving_step: Geotechnical borings and report (~$15-40k) plus city review approval (e.g. LADBS Grading Division); moderately expensive
scored.proven_buyer: Spec-home builders and HNW custom-home buyers
scored.public_data: LADBS and county scanned geology/soils reports and approval letters, CGS Seismic Hazard Zone reports, USGS landslide inventory, LiDAR, historical aerials
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-30x ($30k to $500k-1M); weaker frame because the proving step is not trivial
scored.frame: Rung: buy a hazard-zone hillside lot, get LADBS Grading Division approval of its geology/soils report, resell it as a lot that has passed geology review. Discovery is about 20-30% of the work here, not 80%+ (my estimate). Geology approval is only one of several gates. A cheap LA hillside lot is usually cheap because of a substandard street (the City can require a 20-28 ft paved roadway), haul-route limits, sewer or septic, Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone rules, floor-area caps tied to slope under the Baseline Hillside Ordinance, and hillside construction costs (shoring, caissons, seasonal grading limits). One engineering geologist's forum post claims roadways can cost three times the house. A geology letter clears none of these other gates, so the lot is not truly build-ready. The physical step is also not trivial: borings plus the report cost about $15-40k (the candidate's own estimate), which is about the price of the lot itself. Buyers exist (spec builders and wealthy custom-home buyers), but they are not paying for the geology answer alone.
scored.step_up: Claimed: about $30k raw to $500k-1M, or 10-30x. That compares lots that differ on far more than geology: access, utilities, fire zone, view, allowed floor area. The fair comparison is the same hazard-zone lot with and without an approved geology report. I found no sales data for that comparison. My estimate is roughly 1.5-4x, because the buyer still carries the costs of piles, caissons, street work and utilities. Sources searched: LA planning and CEQA filings; they hold no lot price comparisons.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: I found no published LADBS approval rate. The evidence points to a high rate. A 2018 LADBS approval letter (ENV-2017-5203-B) cleared a lot inside a state Seismic Hazard Zone for earthquake-induced landslides, on the condition of drilled piles socketed into bedrock. Coastal Commission reports from 1997-1999 approved Pacific Palisades hillside homes once a geologist showed the site could be built safely, adding deed restrictions. In practice the answer is usually "approved, with expensive engineering", not "rejected". My estimate is a 60-85% approval rate, which caps the ML lever at about 1.2-1.7x, not 10x. Cost per attempt: about $15-40k for borings, lab work and the geologist/engineer report, plus months of LADBS review (candidate estimate; no fee schedule found). An existing-home geologic inspection costs only $1.3-1.6k, per HSH. The real uncertainty is how much foundation remediation the lot will need, and that cost lands in construction, not in discovery.
scored.data: This is the strongest criterion. LADBS scanned geology/soils reports and approval letters, CGS Seismic Hazard Zone reports, the USGS landslide inventory, LiDAR and historical aerials are all public and hard to read at scale, and nobody structures them across the city. But the coarse answer is already in legible public fields: CGS hazard-zone polygons and LA's ZIMAS parcel flags (hillside area, landslide zone, fire zone, substandard street). On top of that, the conditions in neighbours' approval letters, which list the reference reports and required piles, are in effect the answer for adjacent lots. Local hillside geotechnical firms (one cited LADBS bulletin requires an engineer and geologist for hillside reports) and repeat hillside builders already carry this knowledge in their heads.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Fee title is bought from private owners, often absentee holders or heirs of odd old paper lots. Prices of about $20-80k are the candidate's figure, and LA hillside lots do trade in that range (my estimate; I found no sourced comps). The purchase discount is real, but mostly for the non-geology reasons listed under frame. Sellers and neighbours can usually look up the hazard flags on ZIMAS, so the information gap is thin.
scored.buyer: Spec-home builders and wealthy custom-home buyers. They have the capital, but they price lots on what the whole build will cost and what the finished home will sell for, not on geology alone.
scored.ladder: Rungs: lot clearance, then entitlement and street/utility work, then spec homebuilding, then hillside developer. The chain is real but local, fragmented and capped by the LA and Bay Area hillside lot supply plus the Baseline Hillside Ordinance floor-area caps. That makes it a good regional builder, not a path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Geology is not the binding constraint and is rarely a clean yes/no outcome. Most hazard-zone lots can get LADBS approval if someone pays for caissons or piles into bedrock, so the base hit rate is high and the ML lever is under 2x. The price gap between a $30k lot and a $1M lot comes mostly from access, streets, utilities, fire zone, the slope-based floor-area cap and construction cost, and a geology letter fixes none of these. The rung's output is therefore not build-ready, and the real step-up from geology alone is about 2-4x, not 10^3.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a minor share of what makes a hillside lot buildable, approval with engineering is the usual outcome (high base hit rate, small ML lever), and the geology-only step-up is about 2-4x, nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
sources: https://planning.lacity.gov/odocument/3d701a9c-e285-408a-b6a0-f37a37a5f200/ENV-2017-5203-B.pdf (2018 LADBS approval in a seismic landslide zone, conditioned on bedrock piles)
https://planning.lacity.gov/odocument/da1baaea-b542-4da7-af1d-940ea26b8991/DIR-2017-4229.pdf (hillside lot: grading pre-inspection waiver and grading permit)
https://documents.coastal.ca.gov/reports/1999/4/T9e-4-1999.pdf (Coastal Commission hillside approvals with deed restrictions)
https://amirjawaherian.com/blog/brentwood-hillside-lots-a-development-minded-buyer-guide (substandard street, 28 ft roadway, fire zone constraints)
https://planning.lacity.gov/pdiscaseinfo/document/ODQw0/fe3b456d-e5a5-4f0e-9fa7-879f1ff43502/pdd (denial for a lot on a substandard hillside street)
https://www.biggerpockets.com/posts/804870 (engineering geologist anecdote: roads up to 3x the house cost, septic, hillside build costs)

scored.name: Ancestor Vines (certifying old-vine age from archives)
scored.one_line: Buys neglected old vineyards (Chile Maule/Itata, South Australia, California Zinfandel, Spanish Garnacha) cheaply and uses ML over scanned titles, colonial records and old aerials to prove planting dates, registering vines under old-vine standards so grapes and blocks reprice.
scored.unproven_right: Freehold dry-farmed old vineyard valued as bulk-grape land from growers who cannot document vine age
scored.proving_step: Registration under Barossa Old Vine Charter, Historic Vineyard Society or Old Vine Conference registry plus DNA variety ID; cheap; many prove younger or replanted
scored.proven_buyer: Premium wineries and négociants (Penfolds/TWE, Torbreck, Ridge, Bedrock, Concha y Toro)
scored.public_data: Scanned SA Land Services titles, Chile SAG cadastre and Archivo Nacional, NAIP aerials, California assessor and Sanborn maps, old-vine registries
scored.rough_step_up: Grapes ~5-20x, land ~3-10x; weak C2, strong C4
scored.frame: Rung: buy an undocumented old vineyard, prove vine age, and resell the block or its fruit as certified old-vine. Discovery is probably 30-40% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Most of the value comes from physical and commercial work: rehabbing neglected dry-farmed head-trained vines, farming to premium spec (low yield, hand picking), and winning contracts with named winemakers. The buyers (Penfolds/TWE, Ridge, Bedrock, Torbreck, Concha y Toro) are capitalised, but they pay for fruit quality and the story, not for a registry certificate. Certification alone does not move an asset to a new value tier the way a drill hit does.
scored.step_up: Grapes: California Zinfandel averaged $591/ton statewide and $642/ton in Lodi in 2017. A restored Lodi old vineyard got about $1,600/ton, and top Napa/Sonoma old-vine Zinfandel goes over $4,500/ton. That is about 2.5-7x, and the top end is Napa/Sonoma location premium, not age. Chile Itata: big buyers paid about 80 CLP/kg, and Ventisquero paid 2x and then 4x the original price. So the fruit step-up is about 2-5x. Land: I found no per-hectare figure. My estimate is 2-5x, capped by low old-vine yields (2.5-5 t/acre). Overall about 3-5x, far below 10^3. Score 2.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap: a registry submission plus a DNA variety ID costs roughly $100s-$2k per block (my estimate). Lodi, HVS and the Barossa charter rely largely on grower records, testimony and the physical vines. Base hit rate, my estimate: maybe 30-60% of candidate 'old-looking' blocks qualify at the 35- or 50-year tiers. Gnarled trunks, head training and dry farming are visible proxies, so the lever is capped at about 2-3x, on a cost that is already negligible. There is no expensive, mostly failing proving step for ML to cut 10x. Score 1.
scored.data: Partly illegible: scanned SA Land Services titles, Chile's Archivo Nacional and SAG cadastre, Sanborn maps and historic aerials. But the outcome is often already legible. Lodi publishes and updates lists of its old-vine plantings (2022 revision). The Historic Vineyard Society, the Old Vine Conference registry, the Barossa Old Vine Charter (Vinehealth Australia mapped the tiers in 2017) and the South America old-vine register already list blocks with planting dates. Vine age is also physically readable from trunk girth and training system, and every serious old-vine winemaker scouts it in person. The edge is narrow: maybe a few percent of unregistered blocks where a document pushes the age over a tier line, e.g. 70 to 100 years.
scored.right_bought: Yes, freehold vineyards can be bought from growers. The Lodi grower piece notes owners pulling out old vines because they don't pencil at average prices, and Itata/Maule smallholders are distressed. But sellers know they have old vines, and buyers like Ventisquero and Concha y Toro already hunt Itata and Maule for old País and are bidding prices up 2-4x. So the purchase discount is shrinking and is not caused by an information gap ML could close.
scored.buyer: Premium wineries and négociants: Penfolds/TWE, Yalumba, Torbreck, Langmeil, Ridge, Bedrock, Turley, Concha y Toro, Ventisquero, Torres. They are capitalised but small in aggregate. Old-vine premium spend is likely in the tens of millions per year globally (my estimate). Barossa Ancestor vines total about 12.5 ha, and all old-vine tiers are about 10% of Barossa Shiraz.
scored.ladder: Rungs above: farming, then a winery/brand, then distribution. These are ordinary wine-industry rungs with low margins and brand-driven economics, and there is no path to a trillion-dollar or even multi-billion company. The total old-vine segment is tiny, and wine is a mature, fragmented market where the brand, not the asset, captures the value.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is only about 3-5x, and it comes from farming, location and winemaker brand rather than from proving age. Vine age is cheap to establish, often physically obvious, and already written into public registries (Lodi's old-vine list, the Historic Vineyard Society, the Old Vine Conference, the Barossa charter). So there is no expensive, low-hit-rate proving step for ML to improve and no 10^3 jump to capture.
scored.one_line_reason: Certifying vine age only reprices fruit about 3-5x. The proving step is already cheap and mostly visible, and registries already record the outcome, so the ML edge and the step-up both fall far short of the Terranox pattern.

scored.name: Dendro-Proven Italian Violins (Cremona Dendro / Cozio Arbitrage)
scored.one_line: Buys 'school of', unlabelled and doubted 17th-19th c. violins, violas and cellos at US and European provincial auctions and estate sales for $2-20k, uses ML over scroll, f-hole and varnish photos and the Tarisio Cozio archive to rank likely classical Cremonese, Venetian or Neapolitan makers, proves them by dendrochronology plus a recognised expert certificate, and resells through Tarisio and top dealers.
scored.unproven_right: Clear title to an unattributed or 'attributed to' instrument bought at trade prices from sellers who cannot read maker morphology
scored.proving_step: Top-plate dendrochronology against master chronologies and same-tree matches (~$500-1,500), then expert certificate (Tarisio, Beare, Vatelot lineage); most candidates fail
scored.proven_buyer: Tarisio, Bonhams, Ingles & Hayday, top dealers, instrument funds and soloist-lending foundations
scored.public_data: Tarisio Cozio archive (~30k instruments with photos and sales), published dendro chronologies, LiveAuctioneers/Invaluable/Vichy Enchères/regional catalogue photos
scored.rough_step_up: ~30-1000x on a hit ($5k trade fiddle to $150k-2M+); base rate well under 1%; small market (low $bn), weak C5
scored.frame: The rung is buying a doubted instrument, attributing it, and reselling it. Discovery and attribution are most of the work (my estimate is about 80%), and the physical steps (restoration, setup) are modest, so that part fits. The proving step itself does not fit. Dendrochronology only sets the earliest possible date for the wood. Tarisio's Cozio archive lists a Claude Chevrier violin made in Mirecourt around 1860 whose top has a youngest ring of 1716, so old wood does not prove the maker. The real proof is a certificate from a small group of experts (Beare's, Tarisio, the Vatelot lineage, Rattray and a few others) who judge by eye. That makes the proving step a subjective gatekeeper the company does not control, not an objective test like a drill hit.
scored.step_up: Price paid unproven is assumed at $2-20k (the candidate's figure, not checked). Proven prices: a Ferdinando Gagliano bought by a pawn shop for $50 was reported to be worth $250k (Fox Business). A Giuseppe Guadagnini bought for EUR 50 at a flea market was estimated at EUR 100k or more (DutchNews, 2012); that is an estimate, not a confirmed sale. A Stradivari sold at Christie's for $2.73M (NBC). Those headline sleepers were 1000-5000x, but they came from flea markets and pawn shops, not trade auctions. From the realistic entry price of a $5-20k provincial-auction 'school of' lot, a hit on a mid-tier Italian maker is worth about $100-400k, so 10-50x. Strad- or Guarneri-level finds are vanishingly rare. My realistic estimate is 10-100x, so C2=3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: my estimate is well below 1% for doubted lots turning out to be certifiable classical Italian work. Most 'school of' Italian instruments are Mirecourt, Saxon or later copies. Cost per attempt: dendrochronology about $500-1,500 (candidate's figure; reports are sold on request and no fee is published). Beare's certifies 'against payment of an agreed fee' after a free first look, with no public rate. My estimate is a few hundred dollars to a few percent of value. The main cost of each attempt is the purchase price ($2-20k), not the test. A free expert look plus a cheap dendro report already acts as a low-cost filter, so ML mostly helps choose which lots to buy. At a 1% hit rate the theoretical lever is up to 100x. The practical lever is smaller, because trade buyers already screen these lots by eye and photos rarely show what experts judge on (varnish in hand, the inside of the instrument, linings and blocks).
scored.data: The data is public but not very illegible. Auction photos on LiveAuctioneers and Invaluable are visible to every dealer, and the Cozio archive (about 30k instruments) is curated and run by Tarisio, the main buyer and certifier. In effect the outcome is already recorded in a legible place: certified instruments are listed in Cozio and dealer records, and 'school of' or 'attributed to' in a catalogue is itself the trade's verdict. Sellers are not unable to read the market. Regional auctions are watched by dealers and scouts worldwide with absentee and online bids, so real sleepers get bid up. The right is genuinely bought, not free. But the buyer pool is the same expert cartel, so there is no information asymmetry for ML to exploit. C4=1.
scored.right_bought: Clear title to the physical instrument, bought at auction or estate sale. Provenance and theft risk are real: the Gagliano in the pawn-shop case turned out to be stolen and was returned to its owner.
scored.buyer: Tarisio, Bonhams, Ingles & Hayday, top dealers (Beare's, Rare Violins of New York and others), instrument funds and lending foundations. They are well capitalised, but they are also the certifiers and the direct competitors for the same lots.
scored.ladder: Weak. Possible rungs above: becoming a dealer or auction house, running an instrument fund, lending to soloists, or setting up a certification lab. The total market for fine stringed instruments is small, roughly a low single-digit $bn of trading per year (my estimate), so there is no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proof is a subjective certificate from the same small group of expert dealers who are also the buyers and the competitors for these lots, and dendrochronology only dates the wood, not the maker. So ML cannot itself turn a hit into value, and the step-up depends on a gatekeeper that has every reason to buy the lot itself or discount it. A small market caps any upside.
scored.one_line_reason: A fun arbitrage, but proof depends on dealer-experts who are also the buyers, dendrochronology does not prove the maker, auction lots are already screened by the trade, the realistic step-up is 10-100x, and the market is tiny.

https://www.beares.com/services/certificates (certification against an agreed fee after a free initial appraisal)

scored.name: Surplus Interconnection Rights at under-used legacy generators
scored.one_line: Options unused interconnection headroom (FERC Order 845 Surplus Interconnection Service) from small old under-run generators, gets an ISO SIS study approved, and sells approved MW at the existing POI to co-located data center or battery developers skipping the queue.
scored.unproven_right: Contractual rights to surplus interconnection capacity plus site lease at muni peakers, LFG plants, small hydro and old QF cogens, at ~$1-5/kW, from owners unaware their ISA allows more MW
scored.proving_step: ISO/RTO Surplus Interconnection study and executed amended ISA, requiring no network upgrades; many fail; ML compares scanned ISA/LGIA MW to actual hourly output (EIA-923, CEMS) and constraints
scored.proven_buyer: Data center co-location developers, battery IPPs, hyperscaler energy teams
scored.public_data: FERC eLibrary scanned interconnection agreements, EIA-860/923, EPA CAMPD/CEMS, ISO SIS manuals and study reports
scored.rough_step_up: ~30-100x ($1-5/kW to plausibly $50-300/kW, unverified); distinct from killed queue positions because the signal is scanned contract vs actual output, not a legible field
scored.frame: The rung is "an approved amended ISA for surplus MW at an existing POI." On paper, discovery is a large share of the work, perhaps 60-70% (my estimate): finding headroom, getting owner consent and running the ISO study. The physical step (battery or solar build) belongs to the buyer. But the rung is not cleanly sellable. Under Order 845, Surplus Interconnection Service (SIS) is offered to the existing interconnection customer or its affiliates, or to a third party only with the customer's consent. So the asset stays tied to the incumbent's ISA and site, and you never own it outright. SIS is also an INJECTION right. A co-located data center is load, and load co-location goes through the separate PJM co-location / FERC EL25-49 framework, not SIS. So the named hyperscaler buyer mostly cannot use what this rung produces. Battery IPPs can.
scored.step_up: I could not verify any numbers because the shared web-search budget was used up before this task ran, so both figures are estimates. Option on surplus MW: ~$1-5/kW, the candidate's own unverified figure. Approved SIS MW sold to a battery IPP: plausibly $20-100/kW, my estimate based on how much queue-skipping is worth in PJM/MISO, where new-entrant timelines run 3-5+ years. That is roughly 10-50x, not 10^3. The ratio is also overstated: once the owner knows the headroom exists, the $1-5/kW option price stops being real, because the owner controls consent and can run SIS itself.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I estimate a high base hit rate, ~50%+ (unverified). SIS is designed to avoid network upgrades, and ISOs study it on an expedited track: MISO and PJM have processed many battery-at-existing-plant SIS requests. A study costs tens of thousands of dollars in deposits and engineering, plus about 6-12 months (estimate). That is cheap compared with a normal queue entry. With a high base hit rate, the cap of 1/hit rate limits ML's lever to about 2x, nowhere near 10x.
scored.data: The core signal is legible. ISA MW / Capacity Interconnection Rights figures sit in ISO queue and capacity data. Nameplate is in EIA-860, hourly or monthly output in EIA-923 and CEMS/CAMPD, and you can get capacity factor from a spreadsheet join. Scanned FERC eLibrary ISAs add some detail, such as non-standard limits, but the key outcome (unused MW-hours at the POI) is already computable from structured public data. That is the same failure as the killed queue-positions idea. Owners are munis, LFG operators, hydro and QF owners, and their RTO desks know their CIRs. Developers and brokers already canvass these sites. Data-center site-selection firms also mine EIA data for exactly "underused generator plus POI." The ML edge is near zero.
scored.right_bought: The right can be contracted, but it is not separable. You need the owner's consent, a site lease and a joint ISA amendment. The owner keeps holdup power through the whole proving step and can renegotiate once the value is visible. It is not a clean purchased title that you then realise yourself.
scored.buyer: Battery and solar IPPs (well capitalised, real buyers for the SIS injection MW). The pitch also names data-center and hyperscaler buyers, but they need load service or behind-the-meter arrangements, which fall under different rules: PJM co-location tariff proceedings and state retail law, not SIS.
scored.ladder: There is a moderate ladder. You could go from SIS rights to owning hybrid storage at existing POIs, to acquiring the under-used plants themselves (repowering or replacement interconnection), to building powered campuses for load. That is a real path to a large IPP or developer roll-up, but it is crowded with capitalised players (NextEra, Engie, Lightsource, LS Power, data-center developers).
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is not hidden in illegible data, and it does not belong to you. Unused interconnection headroom can be computed from legible public fields (ISA/CIR MW against EIA-923/CEMS output). The existing interconnection customer legally controls SIS and captures most of the step-up. And SIS is an injection right, so it cannot serve the data-center load buyer that the big step-up depends on.
scored.one_line_reason: The headroom is visible in legible fields, the incumbent owner controls and captures the SIS value, SIS is generation-only so data centers cannot use it, and the high base approval rate leaves ML little room to improve the hit rate.
sources: No live sources: the shared web-search budget was used up before this task ran, so every number here is an estimate from background knowledge and none is verified
FERC Order No. 845 (2018), Surplus Interconnection Service provisions (background knowledge)
FERC docket EL25-49 / PJM co-located load proceedings (background knowledge)
EIA-860, EIA-923, EPA CAMPD/CEMS public datasets (background knowledge)

scored.name: Mendel Herd (genomic-elite calf arbitrage)
scored.one_line: Buys ungenotyped calves cheaply from commercial dairy herds, runs a ~$40 SNP chip whose result becomes an official CDCB genomic evaluation, and sells rare elite calves to AI studs and embryo firms that pay immediately.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of an ungenotyped calf (~$100-600) from herds without genomic data
scored.proving_step: Tissue-tag SNP genotyping (Zoetis Clarifide/Neogen ~$40-50) submitted to CDCB, returning an industry-standard genomic PTA
scored.proven_buyer: AI studs and embryo/IVF companies (STgenetics, Select Sires, ABS, Semex); STgenetics paid A$251k for a record GTPI heifer
scored.public_data: CDCB/USDA AIPL sire summaries, Holstein Association registry, scanned DHIA test sheets, sale catalogues; ML ranks herds with hidden elite sire use. Caveat: Mendelian sampling is random, so edge rests on mis-recorded or unregistered elite pedigrees
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^3x on a hit ($300 to $30-250k); lever capped by calf-level randomness. Ladder: embryo/IVF, semen line, full genetics company
scored.frame: Rung: own an ungenotyped calf, genotype it, sell it if elite. Inside that rung the physical proving step really is trivial: a tissue tag and a SNP chip at about $40-50 (Zoetis Clarifide/Neogen list prices, from memory, unverified). Discovery, meaning which calf to buy, is about 90% of the work, so the shape is right. The buyers are real and have capital: AI studs and IVF firms (STgenetics, Select Sires, ABS, Semex). The weakness is that the 'discovery' is not illegible. Each calf's expected genetic value is its parent average, which CDCB already computes from recorded sire and dam PTAs. The only part left unknown is Mendelian sampling, which is random and has an SD of about half the additive genetic SD (textbook quantitative genetics). ML cannot predict that from any data. Frame scored 2.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a commercial Holstein heifer calf is worth about $300-800. That is my estimate from 2024-25 market memory, when beef-on-dairy cut heifer supply and pushed prices up. Proven elite: an ordinary 'good genomic' heifer adds little at sale; a stud contract for a top-genomic heifer or her embryos is maybe $5k-50k (estimate). Records like STgenetics' A$251k (the candidate's own figure) are one-in-a-million outliers. Realistic step-up on a hit is 10-100x, and 10^2.5 only for the extreme tail. No search verification; my web search budget was already used up (shared limit), so all numbers here are memory or estimate.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The cost per proving attempt is already tiny: about $45 to genotype plus about $500 to own the calf (estimates). AI studs only want roughly the top 0.1-0.5% on GTPI/NM$, and those animals come almost entirely from elite IVF matings of top sires on top dams. A commercial-herd calf has a parent average several Mendelian-sampling SDs below that bar. My estimate is that the base hit rate for a 'stud-grade' calf from an ungenotyped commercial herd is under 1 in 10,000, possibly far lower. ML can only re-rank by pedigree, which CDCB parent average already does. So the lever is near zero, not 10x: the expensive part (buying and raising calves) is not what ML improves, and the cheap part (the chip) is not where the waste is.
scored.data: The outcome is written into a legible public field by design. The genotype becomes an official CDCB genomic PTA, and the pre-test expectation (parent average from registered or DHIA-recorded sires) is already standardised and computable by anyone. CDCB holds over 10 million genotypes and most heifers in large US herds are already routinely genotyped (estimate from memory). That leaves an adversely selected pool: the untested herds are the ones without elite sires. The candidate's own caveat makes the point: the edge needs mis-recorded elite pedigrees, which is a thin, fraud-adjacent niche. That part of the data is illegible, but it is not where the value is.
scored.right_bought: Yes, calves can be bought cheaply at auction or from dairies (about $300-800, estimate). The sellers are not ignorant of the data, though. Genotyping costs $45 and is pushed by Zoetis/Neogen and the studs themselves, and producers who suspect an elite calf just test it themselves. There is also a practical problem: elite sale value needs a registered, parentage-verified pedigree, and unregistered commercial calves often lack one.
scored.buyer: AI studs and IVF/embryo firms (STgenetics, Select Sires, ABS/Genus, Semex, Alta/URUS) buy elite heifers and contract flushes, but they mostly source from their own elite IVF pipelines and registered breeders. In effect they are the incumbents who already do this discovery at scale with full genomic data.
scored.ladder: The ladder exists in principle: elite heifer, then embryo/IVF program, then semen sire line, then a full genetics company (Genus is about a $1-2B market cap; the global bovine genetics market is a few $B). It is not a trillion-dollar path. Each rung is held by entrenched cooperatives and incumbents with decades of proprietary genomic data.
scored.fatal_flaw: Elite genetic merit is mostly predictable from pedigree, and that prediction is already public and legible (CDCB parent average). The rest (Mendelian sampling) is random, so ML cannot predict it. Commercial ungenotyped calves start several SDs below stud-grade, so the hit rate is about 1 in 10^4 or worse and cannot be improved. The proving step costs $45, so there is no expensive proving capex for ML to cut.
scored.one_line_reason: The physical step is trivial and the buyer is real, but the outcome is already legible (genomic PTA, parent average) and the unknown part is random, so there is no ML hit-rate lever. A cheap $45 test leaves no capex to cut.
