CDCB / USDA AIPL genomic evaluation program: over 10M genotypes on file (from memory)
Standard quantitative genetics: Mendelian sampling variance = 1/2 additive variance (textbook)
Zoetis Clarifide / Neogen Igenity dairy SNP test pricing about $40-50 (from memory)
Calf price $300-800 and stud contract values $5-50k are author estimates

scored.name: Carbon Folio (radiocarbon-proven early manuscript fragments)
scored.one_line: Buys loose undated parchment and papyrus leaves at minor auctions, uses palaeographic ML over catalogue images to pick likely early fragments, proves them with accredited AMS radiocarbon dating, and sells hits to museums and collectors.
scored.unproven_right: Title to an undated or misdated leaf ($200-3,000) from sellers who cannot date the script
scored.proving_step: AMS radiocarbon at an accredited lab (Oxford, ETH, Arizona) ~$600; most dates come back late
scored.proven_buyer: Museums and institutional/Gulf collectors (Museum of the Bible, Qatar Museums, university libraries), major auction houses
scored.public_data: Invaluable/LiveAuctioneers image archives, e-codices, Qur'anic fragment databases, Dead Sea Scrolls digital library
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^3x ($1k to $100k-1M+ for 7th-9th century); provenance and UNESCO 1970 cap volume; weak ladder
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a loose undated leaf, date it, resell it. The physical step (posting a 10-20 mg sample to an AMS lab) is trivial and outsourced, so the work is mostly discovery, perhaps 60-70%. But a large share of the work is not discovery: establishing pre-1970 provenance, export and legal title, and authentication beyond the radiocarbon date. Radiocarbon dates the death of the animal or plant that became the writing surface, not the writing, so forgeries on genuinely old blank parchment pass the test. Buyers therefore demand palaeography, ink analysis and an ownership chain, and that chain is the gating work (estimate). Capitalised buyers exist (Qatar Museums, the Museum of the Bible, university libraries, Christie's and Sotheby's). Since the Dead Sea Scroll forgeries and the Obbink/Oxyrhynchus papyri thefts, they are explicitly provenance-first and date-second.
scored.step_up: Unproven: $200-3,000 per leaf at minor auctions (candidate's figure; consistent with my recollection of LiveAuctioneers/Invaluable listings for 'Kufic leaf' or 'medieval vellum leaf'). Proven: a 9th-10th century Kufic Qur'an leaf typically fetches about $10k-60k at Christie's or Sotheby's (my estimate from memory of sale results). A 7th-8th century Hijazi leaf can reach the high six figures or more; Christie's sold an early leaf for about GBP 2m in 2011 (from memory, not verified this session). So on a hit the realistic step-up is about 10-100x, and 10^3x only for the rare Hijazi or 7th-century case. Crucially, the uplift is only realised if provenance clears. A radiocarbon date on an unprovenanced leaf does not let a museum buy it.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: about $500-800 per AMS sample. This is my estimate from memory of commercial (Beta Analytic, about $600) and academic lab pricing. The candidate's figure is about $600. Adding the leaf purchase, an attempt costs about $1-4k. Base hit rate: unknown and not found (all searches failed). My estimate is that well under 1% of loose 'early' leaves at minor auctions are pre-9th century, because dealers and the Islamic-art departments at major houses already cherry-pick. The lever is real in principle (capped at 1/base rate, so potentially more than 100x). But most of the cost of an attempt is the leaf, not the test, and the hard filter is provenance, which ML over images does not address.
scored.data: Partly legible already. Auction catalogues routinely carry a dating field ('Kufic, Near East, 9th century'), so the outcome is often summarised by the seller's own attribution. Specialist dealers and palaeographers (Déroche-trained specialists at Sotheby's and Christie's, Sam Fogg, Les Enluminures) read script style as their core competence. The Corpus Coranicum / Computing Qur'anic manuscripts project has already compiled radiocarbon dates for early Qur'ans. Images are public but low-res and scattered, so there is some illegibility. The right is bought cheaply from sellers who cannot date it, and that part fits the model. But a seller who cannot date a leaf usually also cannot document its provenance, which is what kills resale.
scored.right_bought: Title to a physical leaf, bought at auction for $200-3,000. It is a real purchase, not a free first-come claim. But clean title is uncertain: UNESCO 1970, US and EU import rules (EU Regulation 2019/880) and source-country patrimony laws mean an unprovenanced leaf may be legally or ethically unsellable to institutions.
scored.buyer: Qatar Museums, the Museum of the Bible, university libraries (Birmingham, Tübingen), Gulf private collectors, and the Islamic-art departments of Christie's and Sotheby's. They have the capital but are provenance-constrained. The Museum of the Bible has repatriated thousands of items and found all 16 of its Dead Sea Scroll fragments to be forgeries (2018-2020, from memory).
scored.ladder: Weak. Rungs above (conservation, scholarly publication, dealership, an auction house) are small, reputation-driven businesses. The total market for early manuscripts is likely tens of millions of dollars a year (estimate). There is no path to a very large company and nothing comparable to mine development.
scored.fatal_flaw: Provenance, not date, is what lets a leaf be sold to the capitalised buyer. A cheap undated leaf from an unsophisticated seller almost by construction lacks the pre-1970 ownership chain museums now require. A radiocarbon hit therefore does not realise the step-up: it gives you a valuable-on-paper, institutionally unsellable object with forgery and looted-antiquity risk. Radiocarbon also cannot rule out a modern forgery on old parchment. On top of that, the market is tiny and the ladder is absent.
scored.one_line_reason: The proving step is cheap and outsourced and buyers exist, but provenance and legality gate resale, catalogues already state a date, and the market is too small to climb.

scored.name: Isoarchive (certifying legacy enriched stable-isotope lots)
scored.one_line: Buys uncertified surplus and residue lots of enriched stable isotopes (Yb-176, Mo-100, Ni-64, Zn-68) from government/university surplus and lab closures, uses ML over declassified AEC/OSTI reports and manifests to find likely high-enrichment lots, certifies by NIST-traceable mass spectrometry, and sells to radiopharma target makers.
scored.unproven_right: Title to unlabelled or uncertified lab chemical lots sold as surplus or scrap
scored.proving_step: Accredited TIMS/MC-ICP-MS isotopic certification (~$1-3k per lot), required by GMP target supply chains
scored.proven_buyer: Radioisotope producers (ITM, NorthStar, Eckert & Ziegler, SHINE)
scored.public_data: OSTI declassified scanned AEC reports, DOE Isotope Program archives, GSA/university surplus manifests, historical inventories
scored.rough_step_up: Potentially 10^3-10^4x on rare hits; small volume, untested base rate, export-control and chain-of-custody checks. Ladder: feedstock, target manufacturing, isotope production
scored.frame: The rung is turning an uncertified enriched-isotope lot into certified, GMP-qualifiable feedstock. Inside that rung, finding the lot is maybe 30-40% of the work (my estimate). The rest is physical and regulatory: chemical repurification and conversion to the oxide or metal form the target maker wants, documenting chain of custody, export-control checks (Mo-100, Ni-64, Yb-176 move under licence), and qualifying as a supplier under the buyer's GMP drug master file. Isotopic assay is cheap, but a radiopharma buyer does not accept "certified isotopics" alone: it needs chemical purity, provenance and an audited supplier. Here the physical and regulatory step is not trivial. It looks more like the geothermal counter-example than like drilling.
scored.step_up: These are estimates from prior knowledge, not verified this session. Virgin enriched Yb-176 (>97%) sells for roughly $5k-20k/g. Ni-64 is about $15-30k/g, Mo-100 about $1-3k/g, and Zn-68 about $3-10k/g (DOE NIDC and Isoflex quote on request). An unlabelled surplus vial might be bought for $10-100. On a true hit, certified recycled material might sell at 20-60% of virgin price after repurification. For gram-scale lots that is roughly 10-1000x on the purchase price, but the dollar value per lot is only $1k-$50k. The step-up depends on getting the lot for nearly nothing rather than on proving creating value, and absolute dollars per hit are small.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate of a random surplus lot being an unrecognised high-enrichment isotope is unknown. I estimate it is extremely low (<0.1%), because enriched isotopes cost thousands of dollars per gram and are tracked lot by lot. A full MC-ICP-MS or TIMS certification costs about $1-3k per lot (candidate's figure). But a quadrupole ICP-MS screen costs about $50-200 (my estimate) and already tells you whether a sample is enriched. Proving is therefore cheap and is not the bottleneck. ML cannot cut capex 10x on a step that already costs about $100. The bottleneck is finding sellable lots at all.
scored.data: The OSTI declassified AEC reports are public and illegible (scanned), which fits. But the outcome is largely already summarised legibly in two places. DOE/ORNL calutron-era material sits in the NIDC accountable inventory, which records lot, enrichment and mass. University and national-lab holders received the material with certificates of analysis and track it under sample-loan and return agreements; many ORNL isotopes were loaned and must go back. Most valuable lots are therefore labelled, or legally DOE property, rather than ownerless surplus. GSA and university surplus manifests describe items generically ('lab chemicals'). Lots can be bought, but the owners usually know the value: the same labs that paid $10k/g. Ownership of loaned DOE material is also contested.
scored.right_bought: Title to surplus or lab-closure chemical lots, bought through GSA, university surplus auctions or lab decommissioning contracts. Material on DOE loan has to be returned, so it cannot be bought.
scored.buyer: Target makers and radioisotope producers: ITM (Yb-176 for n.c.a. Lu-177), NorthStar, SHINE, Eckert & Ziegler, plus cyclotron sites using Ni-64 and Zn-68. They are well capitalised, but they qualify suppliers slowly and prefer primary enrichers (Urenco Stable Isotopes, Isoflex/Russian supply, DOE NIDC, new US laser and EMIS enrichers). Some already recycle their own irradiated Yb-176 and Ni-64.
scored.ladder: Above this rung: recovering isotopes from customers' spent targets, then enrichment itself (EMIS, centrifuge or laser, which is very capital-heavy and already contested by Urenco, ASP Isotopes and DOE), then target manufacturing, then isotope production. The market is real but small. Global enriched stable isotope sales are roughly low-single-digit $B per year (my estimate). Legacy surplus cannot scale, so there is no compounding flywheel from the first rung.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no supply. Enriched stable isotopes are so expensive (thousands of dollars per gram) that they are tracked lot by lot, sold with certificates, and often DOE-loaned property. Ownerless, unlabelled, high-enrichment lots that can be bought cheaply exist only as rare gram-scale oddities, and proving them is already a cheap ICP-MS screen. ML has neither a large illegible search space nor an expensive proving step to work on.
scored.one_line_reason: The idea is clever but fails the rubric. The lots are accountably tracked and tiny, assay is already cheap, and GMP qualification plus repurification make up most of the rung, so the step-up is in small dollars with no ML lever.

scored.name: Shinsa Bridge (US WWII bring-back Japanese blades to NBTHK papers)
scored.one_line: Buys unpapered Japanese swords at US estate sales and militaria auctions, uses ML on tang signatures and blade photos to pick likely major smiths, sends them for NBTHK shinsa, and sells papered into Japanese and global markets.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of unpapered swords from heirs of US veterans sold as militaria
scored.proving_step: NBTHK shinsa with shipping/agent fees (~$1.5-3k, dated figure) plus polish; many signatures forged
scored.proven_buyer: Japanese and Western nihonto dealers and collectors pricing by paper level
scored.public_data: LiveAuctioneers and estate photos, scanned NBTHK Juyo zufu, mei reference databases
scored.rough_step_up: ~2-10x typically (up to $20-200k on major-smith hits); weak C2
scored.frame: The rung is: buy an unpapered blade, get it polished, get it judged at NBTHK shinsa, sell it papered. I estimate discovery is about 40-50% of the work, which is well below the 80% the rubric asks for. The physical and logistics steps are a large share. Traditional polish runs about $100-150 per inch, so roughly $3-5k per blade (my estimate). Taking a blade into Japan needs a Bunkacho registration (torokusho). Machine-made showato (WWII army-issue blades) cannot be registered, and shinsa usually runs in stages over several months. A capitalised buyer does exist: dealers and collectors who price by paper level.
scored.step_up: These are my estimates from memory of the dealer market; no searches ran. A typical unpapered, signed or unsigned blade sells for about $1-4k at US militaria auctions. The same blade with Hozon papers sells for about $3-8k, with Tokubetsu Hozon for about $5-20k, and with Juyo for about $25-150k+. So the usual step-up is 2-5x. A Juyo-level hit is 10-50x, but those are very rare among bring-backs. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are my estimates. A proving attempt costs about $1.5-3k for shinsa plus agent fees and shipping, plus $3-5k for polish, so roughly $4-8k per blade. Most WWII bring-backs are showato or gendaito (made around WWII) and have little paper upside. I estimate under 10% of bring-backs are older blades worth sending. Famous-smith signatures are very often forged (gimei); I estimate about 50% or more fail as gimei. The hit rate for Tokubetsu Hozon or Juyo on a major smith is perhaps 1-5% of submissions. So the lever exists, but each hit only pays 2-10x, and capex per attempt is fixed by polish and fees, not by finding.
scored.data: The signal is in public but semi-legible data: LiveAuctioneers and estate-sale photos, which are often poor shots of the tang (nakago) and the blade's hardening line (hamon). Grain (hada) and hamon detail usually needs the blade in hand. The scanned Juyo zufu and mei databases (Markus Sesko's references, for example) are curated, legible references, and human experts already use them. The outcome is not written into any legible field until papers are issued, which is a point in favour. The right is bought cheaply from heirs, but sellers and auction houses increasingly price signed blades with help from online communities. Incumbents already arbitrage this by eye: Japanese and US dealers who work the US sword shows (the San Francisco and Chicago shows), regulars on the Nihonto Message Board, and agents who arrange US-to-Japan shinsa.
scored.right_bought: Ownership of unpapered swords, bought outright from veterans' heirs, at estate sales and at militaria auctions. It is cheap per blade but supply is finite, and this is a shrinking stock of WWII bring-backs.
scored.buyer: Nihonto dealers and collectors in Japan and the West who price by paper level. They have money but it is a niche: I estimate the global nihonto market at well under about $500M a year.
scored.ladder: The ladder is very short. Possible rungs above are dealer, auction house and restoration (polish and mounts). There is no path to a large company. The market is small and set by collectors, and the supply of bring-backs is fixed and shrinking.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is only 2-10x per hit. The physical cost per attempt (polish, shinsa fees, getting the blade into Japan and registered) is a large fixed share of each attempt, so better discovery cannot produce Terranox-style returns. Expert human dealers already do this arbitrage in a market too small to climb.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a niche collectibles arbitrage, not a Terranox analog. The step-up is 2-10x, polish and logistics are not trivial, human experts already do the work, and there is no ladder to a large company.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared search budget for this turn was already used up, so every number here is an estimate from memory and has not been checked against a source.
Estimate: NBTHK shinsa fee and agent cost, $1.5-3k per blade including shipping, as given in the candidate.
Estimate: traditional polish at about $100-150 per inch (typical US and Japan polisher rates).
Estimate: price levels by paper grade (Hozon, Tokubetsu Hozon, Juyo) from dealer listings such as Aoi Art and Seiyudo.
Rule as recalled: a Bunkacho torokusho is required to bring a sword into Japan, and showato are not eligible.

scored.name: Mill Privilege Hydro (dormant US water-power rights at small private dams)
scored.one_line: Acquires small private dams and dormant 'mill privilege' water-power rights in New England and the Mid-Atlantic from owners who see them as liabilities; ML over scanned deeds and USGS records finds flow-rich ungauged sites, a flow study plus FERC exemption proves them, and the package goes to a hydro roll-up.
scored.unproven_right: Dam ownership plus attached historic water-power rights, often bought for $1-50k because owners face dam-safety repair liability
scored.proving_step: About $40-80k: ungauged-basin flow-duration study (StreamStats plus temporary gauge) and a FERC 10 MW exemption filing. Most dams lack enough head times flow.
scored.proven_buyer: Small-hydro consolidators and infrastructure funds (Eagle Creek/Ontario Teachers, Hull Street Energy, Brookfield Renewable)
scored.public_data: Scanned county registry deeds conveying mill privileges, National Inventory of Dams, state dam-safety inspection PDFs, FERC eLibrary surrendered/expired licenses, USGS historical gauge cards
scored.rough_step_up: About $10k (or negative) to $1-3M/MW permitted, roughly 50-300x, but the physical step (rehab plus turbine) is large, so it fails the trivial-physical-step test like the geothermal counter-example
scored.frame: The candidate's rung is a dam plus a flow study plus a FERC exemption, sold to a hydro roll-up. That rung barely sells on its own. Consolidators buy operating megawatts, not paper permits: the comparable deals (GMP/Enel, Hydro-Quebec/Great River) are all operating plants. Building out a non-powered or derelict small dam costs roughly $5,000-10,000/kW (my estimate from ORNL non-powered-dam cost work for sub-MW sites). For a typical 200-500 kW New England mill dam that is about $1-5M of turbine, penstock, powerhouse and dam-safety rehab, against a $40-80k proving step. Discovery and proving are about 2-8% of the work to reach the value buyers pay for, not 80%+. This is the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.step_up: Proven (operating) small hydro: GMP paid $20.3M for 14 New England plants totalling 17 MW in 2016, about $1.2M/MW. Hydro-Quebec paid $2B for 589 MW at Great River Hydro in 2022, about $3.4M/MW including about $750M of assumed debt. Unproven: a dam at $1-50k, often worth less than nothing because of dam-safety repair liability. Permitted but unbuilt: no market price found. My estimate is roughly $30-150k/MW as a developer fee, because a buyer must still spend $5-10M/MW to build. A typical 0.3 MW site therefore goes from about $10k to about $20-50k on a hit, about 2-5x. The 50-300x figure only applies after the large construction step, so it is not an immediate step-up.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: my estimate is that 10-20% of small private New England dams have enough head times flow, plus a plausible interconnection, to be worth a 100 kW+ project. ORNL's 2024 update kept only about 2,600 of roughly 90,000 non-powered dams as candidates above about 1 MW, averaging 1.5 MW, and 86% of that potential is at federal dams, so few private sites qualify. Cost per proving attempt is $40-80k (the candidate's own figure, plausible). The study is not the costly part; build capex is. A first-pass screen with free StreamStats plus NID dam height already does most of the filtering at near-zero cost. ML could improve a cheap step, and a step that is cheap and only moderately failing leaves little capex to cut. The lever's ceiling is about 1/0.15, roughly 7x, but on a small share of total cost.
scored.data: The outcome is largely already in legible fields. The National Inventory of Dams has dam height, purposes, hazard class and condition. USGS StreamStats gives ungauged flow-duration estimates for any New England pour point for free. ORNL HydroSource publishes per-dam potential capacity and generation for non-powered dams, with a Non-Powered Dam Characteristics Inventory alongside it. FERC eLibrary is searchable. The genuinely illegible part is the scanned deeds conveying mill privileges. In New England riparian law that right adds little value, because FERC jurisdiction, state 401 water-quality certification and fish passage decide whether a project can be built, not the historic deed. This repeats the prior-hunt pattern: the answer is already written into public datasets.
scored.right_bought: Yes: rights are bought, not claimed first-come. Owners do sell cheaply, often for $1-50k, because of dam-safety liability. But the cheap price reflects a real liability (repair orders, high-hazard classification, removal pressure from state fish and wildlife agencies and NGO dam-removal programs), not owners being unable to read the data. Buying the dam takes on that liability, so the purchase discount is mostly fair price rather than an information edge.
scored.buyer: Small-hydro consolidators and infrastructure funds: Eagle Creek (Ontario Teachers), Hull Street Energy, Brookfield Renewable, Green Mountain Power, KEI. They are capitalised, but they buy operating assets with cash-flow history and seldom pay for permitted, unbuilt sub-MW exemptions. Competitors on the development side include local developers and consultants who have long used StreamStats, NID and HydroSource, plus state low-impact-hydro programmes.
scored.ladder: Rungs exist above (build, operate, roll up, sell RECs and capacity in ISO-NE), but the total market is small. All New England small hydro is on the order of hundreds of MW, sites average well under 1 MW, and fish-passage, relicensing and dam-removal pressure are shrinking the base. Even full integration leads to a niche independent power producer worth a few hundred million dollars, not a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step dominates. Turning a proven site into what a buyer actually pays for takes about $5-10k/kW of construction and dam rehab, which dwarfs a $40-80k flow study. No sellable rung exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work. On top of that, the flow and head outcome is already summarised in free legible datasets (StreamStats, NID, ORNL HydroSource), so ML over scanned deeds has little edge.
scored.one_line_reason: Like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example, building and rehabbing the plant (about $5-10k/kW) dwarfs finding the site. A permitted but unbuilt micro-hydro site is worth only about 2-5x the cheap dam, and StreamStats, NID and HydroSource already make the flow answer legible.

scored.name: Altamont Legacy Repower Rights
scored.one_line: Buys fragmented legacy wind leases and land under decommissioned 1980s California/Hawaii wind farms, mines 30 years of CEC production filings to build a bankable modern-turbine P50, and sells the repowering package (resource plus existing interconnection) to a developer.
scored.unproven_right: Legacy leaseholds, small parcels and surface rights under old wind resource areas (Altamont, San Gorgonio, Tehachapi, Kahuku), held by heirs and defunct LLCs
scored.proving_step: About $50k: digitised historical production plus short LiDAR verification, giving a consultant-signed repowering energy-yield assessment; hit rate set by how many parcels combine into a buildable block
scored.proven_buyer: Repowering developers and IPPs (NextEra, Avangrid, Terra-Gen) needing contiguous blocks with grid access
scored.public_data: CEC Wind Performance Reporting System scanned quarterly reports (1985-2000s), county assessor and probate records, FERC QF filings
scored.rough_step_up: Grazing value ($1-3k/acre) to a repower-ready block at $50-150k/MW, roughly 10-50x; resource is semi-legible, so the edge is in title assembly
scored.frame: The rung would be a repower-ready site control package. Inside it, discovery (resource assessment) is maybe 10-15% of the work (my estimate). Wind at Altamont, San Gorgonio and Tehachapi has been known and measured since the 1980s. The hard parts are land assembly and permitting. Permitting means CEQA/EIR and avian mortality conditions: Alameda County ties repowering to a 2010 NextEra/Attorney General/Audubon settlement and its own EIR (acgov Golden Hills findings). Interconnection and deliverability retention are also hard. So no frame exists where discovery is 80%+. Capitalised buyers do exist (NextEra, Avangrid, Terra-Gen).
scored.step_up: Unproven: grazing land at about $1-3k/acre (candidate's figure), or wind option payments of $2-100/acre/yr (LandGate, ND legislature 2009). Proven: Enerdatics M&A data (Europe, July 2026) puts onshore wind early-stage premiums at about $20k/MW, rising to at least $100k/MW at ready-to-build, so roughly 5x between stages. Operating royalties run about $4-8k/MW/yr (SD PUC 2018 docket; LandGate). The landowner keeps the royalty stream, so a lease-assembler captures maybe 3-10x on its own cost (estimate). That gap only closes after permits and interconnection, not immediately on a data 'hit'. It is not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step costs about $50k per block (candidate's figure; consultant energy-yield assessments plus LiDAR typically run $30-100k, my estimate). The resource hit rate is near 100% because these are proven wind resource areas, so ML has nothing to raise. Failures come from title fragmentation, permitting (avian), and losing interconnection rights. Those are legal and political, not predictive. The lever is about 1x.
scored.data: CEC Wind Performance Reporting System data is semi-legible, and the incumbents who operated these turbines hold their own SCADA history. NextEra replaced about 2,400 Altamont turbines in 2010-2015 under the settlement (Alameda County). The outcome is summarised in legible fields: county planning staff reports list each repower project, its MW and its parcel owners. CAISO tariff and queue records show who holds the retained interconnection and deliverability. CAISO dropped the 3-year idle forfeiture rule in 2025, and its 2026 rule keeps rights with the existing generator owner. The data does not hide the answer; the public record already states it.
scored.right_bought: The rights are mostly not cheaply buyable from people who cannot read the data. Alameda staff reports name long-standing ranch families (Elworthy, Corbett Family LP, Vieux Family Properties) leasing directly to NextEra subsidiaries. Existing wind leases usually carry repower and extension clauses. The interconnection right, which is the scarce asset, belongs to the generator owner, not the landowner. So buying land under an old farm does not buy the grid position. Heir and defunct-LLC fragments exist but are small slivers.
scored.buyer: Repowering developers and IPPs (NextEra, Avangrid, Terra-Gen, Sand Hill Wind). But these buyers are also the incumbent leaseholders and interconnection owners, so they are competitors more than buyers.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: site control, then development (permits, interconnection), then build/own IPP, then a repowering platform. It is a large market, but crowded with well-capitalised incumbents who already hold the bottom rung in these specific areas. The geography is finite: four legacy wind resource areas, much of it already repowered (Golden Hills, Golden Hills North, Mulqueeney Ranch at Altamont; Tehachapi and San Gorgonio largely repowered).
scored.fatal_flaw: The value sits in the existing interconnection and deliverability rights and the permits. Incumbent generator owners hold those, not the fragmented landowners Terranox-style buying would target. The wind resource is already known and legible. ML has no hidden signal to extract, and buying parcels does not buy the grid position.
scored.one_line_reason: The resource has been known since the 1980s and is recorded in public filings. The value is in title assembly, permitting and interconnection rights the incumbents already hold, the step-up is about 5x rather than 10^4, and ML has no hit rate to improve.

scored.name: Gap-Wind Patagonia/Andes wind sites
scored.one_line: Buys cheap Argentine/Chilean estancia land or wind options in wind gaps lacking bankable met data, uses ML over scanned SMN/DGA station logbooks and aviation records to pick sites, proves them with an IEC/MEASNET campaign, and sells to IPPs entering LatAm.
scored.unproven_right: Freehold or long-dated options on low-value Patagonian grazing land, about $20-100/ha
scored.proving_step: About $150k LiDAR plus mast campaign and bankable P50/P90; many sites fail on turbulence or extreme gusts
scored.proven_buyer: IPPs (Enel, AES Andes, Genneia, Engie) paying for bankable-resource sites near transmission
scored.public_data: Scanned Servicio Meteorológico Nacional and Chilean DGA logbooks, old YPF/ENARSA camp weather logs, aerodrome METAR archives
scored.rough_step_up: $50/ha to roughly $2-5k/ha attributed project value, about 40-100x; grid access caps it
scored.frame: The rung is a wind site with land control and a bankable P50/P90 measurement. Inside that rung, finding the windy spot is maybe 20-30% of the work (my estimate). Grid access, PPA and offtake, permits, and 12-24 months of measurement are the rest. The physical step (a mast plus LiDAR) is cheap. But a site that has only been measured is not what IPPs buy. They buy sites that are ready to build or have secured grid access. Discovery is therefore not 80%+ of any rung that has a buyer.
scored.step_up: Unproven: Patagonian grazing land at about $20-100/ha (candidate's figure, plausible). Proven: wind development premiums are typically about $20-100k/MW at ready-to-build (my estimate, industry norm, not found for Argentina). At roughly 4-8 ha/MW of farm footprint, that is about $3-15k/ha, but only after grid, permit and PPA. A measured-only site is worth perhaps 10-30% of that, so about $500-2,000/ha, or roughly 10-40x (my estimate). The candidate itself says the grid caps it. No transaction prices for Argentine measured-only site sales were found. Capex reference: Enel's 100 MW Pampa (Chubut) is about $130M, or $1.3M/MW.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt is about $150k for mast plus LiDAR and 1-2 years of measurement (candidate's figure, consistent with industry norms). The base hit rate on resource is high, not low. Southern Patagonia averages 9-11.2 m/s (energypedia), and Chubut/Santa Cruz capacity factors are reported above 45%. Most measured sites clear on mean wind speed. Failures come from turbulence, extreme gusts (IEC class S) and icing, and I estimate 20-40% of sites fail (my estimate). With a base rate of about 60-80%, the lever is capped at 1/base rate, roughly 1.3-1.7x, nowhere near 10x.
scored.data: The resource outcome is already largely legible and free. Global Wind Atlas, ERA5/MERRA reanalysis, commercial mesoscale models (Vortex, 3TIER) and operating-farm output (CAMMESA dispatch) all map Patagonian wind. CONICET work notes that reanalysis is weak near the surface, so scanned SMN/DGA logbooks and METARs could add some signal on gusts and turbulence. But airport METAR archives are already digitised, and the incremental signal is narrow. Rights: the land is cheap and bought from ranchers, which is good. But ranchers in Patagonia know their land is windy, and the windiness is no secret.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Freehold or wind-lease options on estancia land can be bought or optioned from private owners at about $20-100/ha. Owners do not hold an information disadvantage about wind quality, and big IPPs typically lease rather than pay a large premium for raw land.
scored.buyer: IPPs including Enel, AES Andes, Genneia, Engie, YPF Luz, PCR and Total Eren/TotalEnergies. They buy ready-to-build projects or projects with grid access, not measured-only sites. Precedent: Mitsui took a 34% stake in Total Eren's Los Hercules project (97.2 MW, Santa Cruz).
scored.ladder: The ladder is decent: site, then permitted project, then grid/PPA, then build, then IPP operator, then green hydrogen/ammonia export (Patagonian H2 hubs). Each higher rung is capital- and grid-bound, and incumbents with balance sheets already hold those rungs.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Patagonian wind is world-famous and freely mapped. The proving step mostly succeeds, and value is gated by scarce transmission and offtake: published studies find the Patagonian grid already needs wind curtailment. ML over old logbooks can at best shave a modest share of failed met campaigns. It cannot create a 10^3-10^4 step-up, because a measured site without grid access is worth little more than the land.
scored.one_line_reason: The resource is already legible and abundant, the proving hit rate is high (lever about 1.5x), and transmission, not discovery, is what makes a site valuable. The rubric fails at C1-C4.

scored.name: Unclassified Meteorite Classification Arbitrage (Meteorix / Stone Ledger / Selene Stones) -- borderline mineral exclusion
scored.one_line: Buys unclassified NWA/Saharan/Atacama desert stones by the kilo from middleman dealers at ~$0.1-2/g (no field prospecting), uses ML over dealer photos (fusion crust, breccia texture, chondrule absence), density, magnetism and handheld XRF triage to pick probable lunar, martian or rare achondrites, gets Meteoritical Society classification, and sells type material. Reviewer should confirm it sits outside the mineral-exploration exclusion (purchase plus classification, not prospecting).
scored.unproven_right: Title to an unclassified stone bought from a dealer, value capped until classified
scored.proving_step: Thin section, microprobe and oxygen-isotope analysis at a recognised lab ($500-2,000), then Nomenclature Committee approval and Meteoritical Bulletin listing, the accepted standard that sets price class
scored.proven_buyer: Natural history museums, university collections, top collectors and dealers, Christie's/Bonhams/Sotheby's science sales
scored.public_data: Meteoritical Bulletin Database (70k+ labelled classifications with photos), dealer listings on eBay, Facebook groups and Tucson catalogues, published petrography
scored.rough_step_up: $0.5-1/g to $300-5,000/g lunar/martian/rare achondrite, ~500-5,000x on a hit; base rate ~0.1-1%. Small market (tens of $M), shallow ladder, export-law risk
scored.frame: The rung is buying an unclassified stone and getting it classified. Inside that rung, picking the right stone (discovery) is about 80-90% of the work. The physical step, cutting a thin section and sending it to a lab, is trivial and outsourced at $300-2,000. This fits the frame shape. It falls down on the buyer: collectors, small dealers and a few museums buy one stone at a time in a thin market. There is no capitalised developer-type buyer who can pay a large, repeatable premium. My estimate is that the whole planetary-meteorite market is tens of millions of dollars a year. I did not exclude it. Buying stones that have already been recovered and classifying them is closer to trading in collectibles than to mineral prospecting. But it is a borderline case, and anyone who does their own desert hunting would fall inside the exclusion.
scored.step_up: Unproven: bulk unclassified NWA sells for about $0.14/g (a 2 kg lot for $284), and single pieces run $0.20-1.20/g (ancientresource / napoleonexhibit listings). One collector blog puts unclassified NWA achondrites at $1-2/g direct from dealers on Facebook. Proven: lunar retail now runs about $41-57/g (Fossil Realm NWA 14685 at $41/g, NWA 15373 at $57/g). Wholesale lunar is about $8-12/g (collector page). Galactic Stone puts the lunar average at about $100/g in 2022, down about 90% from about $1,000/g in the early 2000s, and its 2025 report says planetary prices "continue to drop". On a real lunar or martian hit, the realistic step-up is therefore about 10-250x (wholesale to retail), not the pitch's 500-5,000x. The $300-5,000/g figures are outdated or apply only to a handful of famous stones. A more common hit, such as an HED or other achondrite, is about 3-20x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Classified stones are a pre-selected group, and even there Meteoritical Bulletin 112 (2023 approvals) shows 71 lunar and 27 martian out of 2,487, about 2.9% and 1.1%, with 77% ordinary chondrites. Stones that reach the labs have already been filtered by hunters and dealers. In unscreened dealer bulk, the planetary rate is likely well under 0.1% (my estimate). One proving attempt costs $300-350 per sample at the University of Alberta, or about $500-2,000 at other labs with oxygen isotopes (my estimate). It also uses 20 g or 20% of the stone, held as the type specimen, and the backlog runs to months. The ML lever is real in principle, at up to 1/base rate. But cheap triage (magnetism, density, handheld XRF, looking at the stone) already gets most of the gain, so ML adds little on top.
scored.data: The signal is not illegible. The Meteoritical Bulletin Database already sets out the outcome as a labelled class for 70k+ meteorites, so the answer sits in a legible field. Dealer photos are scattered, but the features that show (fusion crust, feldspathic breccia, no chondrules) are exactly what Moroccan and Mauritanian hunters look for by eye, in hand, on the actual stone. They read this signal better than a model working from photos can.
scored.right_bought: Yes, stones are bought cheaply ($0.1-2/g), with no free first-come claim. But the sellers are the expert screeners, so the cheap bulk is mostly what is left after the likely planetary stones have been pulled out. That is adverse selection, not owners who cannot read the data. Morocco and Algeria have export restrictions on meteorites, and Morocco passed a heritage law in 2021-22 (my recollection, not sourced here), which adds title and export risk.
scored.buyer: Collectors, dealers, university and museum collections, and Christie's/Bonhams science sales. The market is thin and fragmented, and price-sensitive in a falling market. None of these buyers is capitalised to absorb volume at a fixed premium the way a mine developer is.
scored.ladder: Shallow. The rungs above are retail, cutting and preparation, and auctions, all inside a market of tens of millions of dollars (my estimate). There is no path to a trillion-dollar chain. Space-resource or sample-return markets are not reachable from here.
scored.fatal_flaw: Adverse selection in a small, collapsing market. Saharan hunters and dealers already pick out likely lunar, martian and achondrite stones by eye and sell them at planetary prices, so the $0.1-2/g bulk is the leftovers. Meanwhile the price of the proven product has fallen about 90% (lunar from about $1,000/g to about $10-100/g) as supply has grown, so the real step-up is about 10-250x on a hit. The whole market is tens of millions of dollars, with no capitalised buyer and no ladder above it.
scored.one_line_reason: The frame shape fits (picking is most of the work and the lab step is outsourced), but expert sellers have already screened the cheap stones, the outcome already sits in a labelled public database, lunar prices have fallen to about $10-50/g, and the market is tiny with nothing above it to climb.

scored.name: Dormant Registry / Article6 Recovery (stalled CDM and registered carbon projects)
scored.one_line: Buys project-participant and issuance rights to registered but stalled carbon projects (Kyoto-era CDM projects in the Article 6.4 transition, Verra/Gold Standard projects with no recent issuance) from defunct or cash-poor developers; ML over scattered PDDs, monitoring reports, host letters and satellite/plant-operating evidence predicts which actually kept generating and meet new methodology, vintage and authorisation rules; one verification issues priced units for CORSIA, Article 6 and trading buyers.
scored.unproven_right: Issuance rights to registered projects with unverified backlog, bought for ~$10-50k (old CERs trade well under $1)
scored.proving_step: Monitoring report plus VVB/DOE verification and host letter of authorisation (~$20-80k); fails often on stopped plants, missing data, additionality or no host approval
scored.proven_buyer: Carbon trading desks, CORSIA Phase 1 airlines, Article 6 sovereign buyers (Singapore, Switzerland KliK, Japan JCM)
scored.public_data: UNFCCC CDM registry PDFs and Article 6.4 transition list (~1bn credits requested, ~13% approved by late 2025), Verra/Gold Standard document folders, host DNA gazettes, ICAO CORSIA decisions, Sentinel/VIIRS imagery. Caveat: approval status is a legible field and the host-approval deadline was 30 June 2026, so the edge must be operating evidence and seller illiquidity
scored.rough_step_up: ~$10-50k rights to 100k-1M+ units at $2-25 each, ~50x per unit and ~10^2-10^3x on purchase price when verification passes; policy-dependent
scored.frame: The rung is to buy issuance rights to a stalled registered project and get one verification and issuance through. I estimate discovery is only about 30-50% of the work inside it. The rest is reconstructing monitoring data, hiring a DOE/VVB, issuance fees and, above all, getting host-country letters of authorisation. That last step is political and bureaucratic, and a model cannot make it easier. Buyers exist (trading desks, CORSIA airlines, KliK/JCM), but sovereign and CORSIA buyers want authorised, recent-vintage, post-2016-start units, and legacy projects mostly do not qualify.
scored.step_up: Per unit, the move is from about $0.1-0.5 for old CER/legacy rights (my estimate; the candidate says under $1) to about $1-1.65 for legacy renewables (Sylvera: 2024-vintage renewables about $1.00, 2018-19 about $1.65). It reaches $10-16 only for CORSIA-eligible units (ICE CP1 Dec-26 at $16; a cookstove CEEU auction above $12, Jul 2026). Legacy CDM is largely shut out of that tier: ICAO eligibility needs a first crediting period from 2016 and 2021-26 vintages, plus authorisation. Worked example (my estimate): buy rights for $50k plus $50k to verify, issue 100k units at about $1, and you get $100k gross before issuance share-of-proceeds. That is roughly 1-3x on capital at risk, not 10^3. 10-50x appears only in the rare case of a large backlog that is also CORSIA or authorised.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step costs about $20-80k per attempt in the candidate's own figures, plus DOE time and host-letter lobbying. The base hit rate is not low. A UNFCCC survey of dormant CDM participants found the main reason for not requesting issuance was low CER prices (55%), followed by no buyers (24%) and high MRV cost (20%). Technical failure was not the main reason, so many dormant plants that are still running would verify. I4CE found 29% of expected CERs were never issued because the project failed. My estimate of the base hit rate, conditional on the plant still operating, is about 40-70%, which caps the ML lever at about 1.5-2.5x, not 10x. The binding constraint is policy (authorisation, vintage, methodology), not physical uncertainty.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: CDM PDDs, monitoring reports, Verra/GS folders, DNA gazettes, and Sentinel/VIIRS imagery of plant operation. The outcome, however, is mostly already in legible fields. The registry shows the CDM transition status. Host approval had to be submitted by 30 June 2026, and only 415 of 1,512 activities secured it (Fastmarkets). Credits that did not transition face administrative cancellation on 1 July 2027. Issuance histories and CORSIA eligibility lists are public tables. The only remaining edge is whether a plant kept operating, and the seller (the developer or plant owner) already knows that better than any satellite model. So there is no real information asymmetry against the owner.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought: project-participant status and issuance rights from defunct or cash-poor developers, plausibly for $10-50k (no market comps found; my estimate). However, changing project participants and the modalities of communication needs cooperation from the original participants and the host DNA, and the seller is not information-disadvantaged.
scored.buyer: Carbon trading desks (South Pole, Vitol, Mercuria), CORSIA Phase 1 airlines (demand about 200-250M units by Jan 2028, IATA), and Article 6 sovereign buyers (Singapore, Switzerland KliK, Japan JCM). The best-paying of these buyers require authorised, corresponding-adjusted, recent-vintage units, which legacy stalled projects mostly cannot supply. Incumbents already doing this include South Pole, Climate Impact Partners, Vitol/Mercuria origination desks, and CDM consultancies that have been sweeping the transition list since 2024.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak and capped. It runs from legacy issuance recovery to developing new projects to a carbon trading desk to owning abatement assets. The total VCM is about $1-2B a year and CORSIA Phase 1 is roughly a $2-4B cumulative opportunity. Climbing means becoming a project developer or trader, which is a crowded, low-margin, policy-whipsawed business, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is gated by policy, not by hidden information. The CDM-to-Article-6.4 host-approval window closed on 30 June 2026, and the result (415 of 1,512 approved) is published in a legible registry field. Units that did not transition are cancelled in July 2027. Legacy Verra/GS units sell for about $1 because buyers distrust their additionality and vintage, not because nobody can read the files. The seller already knows whether their plant ran. With no information asymmetry, a high base hit rate and about a 1-3x return on capital, there is neither a 10^3 step-up nor a 10x ML lever.
scored.one_line_reason: Policy deadlines and legible registry fields, not illegible data, decide the outcome. Legacy units clear at about $1, verification hit rates are already moderate, and sellers know their own plants, so the step-up is about 1-3x and the ML lever is about 2x.

scored.name: Article 6 Authorised Pipeline (LoA-predicted forward vintages)
scored.one_line: Buys forward vintages cheaply from small-project developers before host-country authorisation, using ML over untranslated host gazettes, NDC decrees and ministry PDFs to predict which projects will get Letters of Authorisation and CORSIA eligibility, which reprices units for airlines.
scored.unproven_right: Forward offtake or option contracts on unauthorised future vintages at ~$1-4/t
scored.proving_step: Host-country LoA plus registry CORSIA-eligible tagging; company assembles the file and lobbies; many never get one
scored.proven_buyer: CORSIA-obligated airlines and Article 6 sovereign buyers (Singapore ICS, Swiss KliK, Japan JCM)
scored.public_data: Host gazettes and environment-ministry PDFs, UNFCCC Article 6 database and CARP registry, Verra/Gold Standard pipeline documents. Once the LoA exists it is legible, so the edge is predictive timing only
scored.frame: The rung is a forward vintage turned into an authorised CORSIA-eligible unit. A capitalised buyer exists: CORSIA airlines, with Phase 1 demand of about 146-236M EEUs. But very little of the work in this rung is discovery, perhaps 20-30% (my estimate). The proving step is a sovereign political decision. Getting the LoA means lobbying, assembling the dossier, the host's corresponding-adjustment policy, and share-of-proceeds and price negotiations with the ministry. None of that is trivial or abstracted. It is the bespoke-plant problem in another form: the hard part is the authorisation, not picking the project.
scored.step_up: Unauthorised clean-cooking credits average about $4/t in 2026. Eligible (LoA plus CORSIA) cookstove credits trade above $14/t (MSCI 2026). ICE CORSIA futures are about $10-13/t (Dec-26 future $13.10, down from an $18.10 high). A July 2026 Cambodian EEU auction cleared above $12/t. One bilateral deal reached about $23/t. Analysts in Jan 2025 put the LoA premium at about 80%. Net step-up is about 2-4x, up to 6x at best if the forward is bought at $2. This is nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The premium is shrinking as more hosts issue LoAs, so the step-up is falling.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per attempt is the forward premium plus the legal and lobbying cost of the dossier. My estimate is $50k-300k per project file, plus the offtake price. That is cheap relative to a drill hole. I could not find a published base rate for LoA approval. My estimate is that it is moderate, perhaps 20-50% within a few years for credible projects in countries with an Article 6 framework: more than 80 countries report authorisation systems underway, and the CFME26 registry representative said the LoA pipeline is 'filling'. With a base rate of 0.2-0.5, the lever is capped at 2-5x, not 10x. Failure is also cheap: an unauthorised unit still sells into the VCM at $4. That keeps downside low but also kills the lottery-ticket shape.
scored.data: Gazettes and ministry PDFs are public and partly untranslated. But the outcome becomes a legible field the moment it happens: UNEP CCC Article 6 Pipeline (relaunched March 2026), the CARP registry, Verra/GS LoA tags and the ICAO TAB eligible-units list. The candidate itself admits the edge is timing only. More importantly, the information asymmetry runs the wrong way. The developer is the party applying for the LoA and talking to the ministry, so they know their odds better than any model reading gazettes. Sophisticated offtakers (Mercuria, Climate Impact Partners, South Pole, Respira, ACX, Xpansiv brokers) already write LoA-contingent price clauses, and Sylvera, Abatable and MSCI already rate LoA risk.
scored.right_bought: Yes, technically: forward offtakes and options are bought from developers. But they are not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. Developers know the LoA status of their own project, and current contracts already price LoA contingency. The cheap tail is mostly adverse selection: projects whose own developers expect no LoA.
scored.buyer: CORSIA-obligated airlines (Phase 1 2024-26, demand of 146-236M EEUs). Sovereign Article 6 buyers: Singapore ICS, Swiss KliK, Japan JCM, Sweden. These are real, capitalised and liquid buyers. ICE runs a CORSIA futures contract.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are trader/aggregator, then project developer, then a sovereign Article 6 deal broker. A large trading house (Mercuria-scale) is possible, but carbon markets are a regulatory construct with volatile policy. The rung above (developing projects) is real physical work with thin margins. There is no clear trillion-dollar chain. C5 is weak to moderate.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is only about 2-4x ($4/t to $10-14/t), and it rests on the developer's own government lobbying outcome, which the developer knows better than any ML over gazettes. Buying 'unproven' forwards is mainly adverse selection against better-informed sellers, in a market where traders already price LoA contingency and the outcome is published in UNEP, CARP and ICAO registries.
scored.one_line_reason: No exclusion applies, but it fails the rubric. The step-up is about 3x, not 10^4. The proving step is a political authorisation rather than discovery. The informational edge belongs to the seller. LoA status is published in legible registries once granted.

scored.name: Legacy Peat (drained-peat carbon rights)
scored.one_line: Leases carbon rights cheaply on drained peat farmers think is rough grazing; ML over scanned drainage grant records, legacy soil sheets and LiDAR ditch networks finds deep actively drained peat; probe survey and Peatland Code validation prove it; cheap ditch-block rewetting yields PIUs sold to UK corporates.
scored.unproven_right: 30-100 year carbon-rights leases at near-zero upfront (profit share)
scored.proving_step: Peat-depth transects plus Peatland Code validation (~£5-20k); many fail on shallow, rewet or eroded peat
scored.proven_buyer: UK corporates buying domestic units, water utilities and national park trusts
scored.public_data: Scanned MAFF/ADAS drainage grant maps, BGS/Soil Survey of Scotland legacy peat maps, EA LiDAR, UK Land Carbon Registry PDFs
scored.rough_step_up: ~£0-50/ha right to ~£5-20k/ha PIU value, ~10^2-10^3x on the right; modest absolute value per site
scored.frame: The rung is a validated Peatland Code project, which sells PIUs. Discovery is maybe 20-30% of the work in that rung (my estimate). The rest is getting landowner consent for a 30-100 year commitment, doing the restoration (median about £1,026/ha in Scotland, SEFARI 2022), validating before and after the works, verifying for decades, holding back buffer units, and selling the units. The physical step is not hard, but the "proven" output is a forward credit stream over 75-100 years, not an asset that changes hands once for a step-up price. Buyers exist (corporates, water utilities) but they buy credits per tonne, not proven land.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about £0-50/ha. The carbon lease is mostly profit share with near-zero upfront payment (Peatland Code terms; no published per-hectare lease rate). Proven: the registry averages about 180-217 tCO2e/ha (10.48M claimable units, or 12.8M tCO2e, over 58,861 ha; my arithmetic from IUCN stats). At £25-40/PIU (2024 VWAP £25.04, 2025 average £39.57, Ecosystem Marketplace via IUCN) that is about £4.5k-8.7k/ha gross. Taking off restoration (about £1-2k/ha), buffer and the landowner's share leaves the developer roughly £1-3k/ha net, spread over decades (my estimate). The headline multiple is about 10^2x because the base is near zero. In absolute terms it is roughly comparable to the land's own value, and it is not paid at once.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step costs about £5-20k per site (candidate's figure; I found no published peat validator fee). Registry issuance is £0.15/PIU and verification is at least £100 (IUCN registry fees). The base hit rate is already high (my estimate: more than 50% for sites screened with existing maps). England's peat map says about 80% of its peat is dry or degraded (Defra 2025), so drained deep peat is not rare. A 1/base-hit-rate cap of about 2x means ML cannot cut capex 10x, and proving is a small share of project cost anyway.
scored.data: This fails the "outcome not already legible" test. Natural England's England Peat Map (May 2025) is open data, itself built with ML/deep learning, and maps peat extent, depth, condition, gullies and man-made drainage channels. That is exactly the signal this candidate wants to extract. Scotland has the 2016 Carbon and Peatland Map, and the UK Land Carbon Registry publishes every project. The NFU says the map has inaccuracies, so there is some residual edge in ground-truthing, but it is incremental.
scored.right_bought: Rights are contracted from landowners, not taken first-come, so that part fits. But owners are not data-blind. Land agents (Strutt & Parker publish natural capital market guides), the NFU, and many developers and advisors (e.g. CLEVEL, Nattergal, Forest Carbon, Zulu Ecosystems) are actively marketing peat carbon to farmers. Grants such as Peatland ACTION and Nature for Climate fund restoration, which also complicates additionality. There is no structural information discount when owners sign.
scored.buyer: UK corporates buying domestic PIUs, water utilities, and national park or NGO trusts. Demand is thin. Only 28,679 peatland units were reported transacted in 2025, about £1.1M at £39.57, down from 187,291 in 2024 (Ecosystem Marketplace via IUCN). The whole registry is 408 projects and 58,861 ha (IUCN, April 2026).
scored.ladder: Possible rungs: carbon-rights aggregator, then restoration contractor, then owning peat land or a natural capital fund, then bundling biodiversity net gain and water-quality payments. But the total addressable value is small and policy-dependent. UK peat restoration is estimated at about £50bn in avoided emissions over very long horizons, mostly captured through public grants, and the voluntary PIU market is on the order of £1-10M a year. There is no credible path to a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The discovery signal is already public and legible. Natural England's 2025 England Peat Map (open, ML-built) and Scotland's Carbon and Peatland Map already give peat depth, condition and drainage ditches. Deep drained peat is common rather than rare (about 80% degraded), so ML has no hit-rate lever. And the buyer market is tiny (about 28.7k PIUs, roughly £1.1M, reported in 2025).
scored.one_line_reason: The government has already published an open, ML-built peat depth and drainage map. Drained peat is common, proving costs little and usually succeeds, and the PIU market is about £1M a year. So there is no hidden signal, no hit-rate lever and no capitalised buyer paying a step-up.

scored.name: Regrowth Vintage (retroactive-start ARR on naturally regenerated farmland)
scored.one_line: Buys carbon rights on abandoned farmland already regrowing naturally; ML over scanned historical aerials and land-use records proves eligibility (non-forest 10+ years before start, start within retroactive window); VVB validation plus plot inventory yields premium ARR removal units.
scored.unproven_right: Carbon-rights agreements on regenerating abandoned fields (US Southeast/Appalachia, Eastern Europe, Brazil Atlantic Forest) owners value at ~$0
scored.proving_step: Eligibility/additionality validation plus inventory plots (~$20-60k per aggregated project); usually fails on eligibility evidence, start date or title gaps
scored.proven_buyer: Removal buyers (Symbiosis Coalition, Frontier-adjacent corporates) paying $15-35/t ARR premiums
scored.public_data: USDA/USGS scanned aerial film archives, county agricultural census and land-use records, Landsat, Verra VM0047 pipeline PDFs
scored.rough_step_up: ~$0-20/ha right to ~$3-10k/ha forward removal units, ~10^2-10^3x on the right
scored.frame: The rung is a validated ARR project, from the carbon-rights agreement through VVB validation and a forward offtake. Discovery (finding eligible parcels and documenting history) is maybe 30-40% of the work; this is my estimate. Most of the cost and time goes to aggregating many smallholder rights, title cure, PDD writing, VVB validation and audit, 30-40 year monitoring, permanence buffers and leakage. A buyer pays mostly after verification, years later. This is not an 80%+ discovery frame and the physical step is not abstracted: the trees have to keep growing and be re-verified for decades.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: about $0-20/ha. This is the candidate's estimate, and I accept it as plausible for idle abandoned fields. Proven value: secondary regrowth is roughly 3-10 tCO2/ha/yr (my estimate). Net of the dynamic-baseline deduction (big for land that is already regrowing) and a 10-20% buffer, call it about 1-4 credits/ha/yr. At the market price for higher-rated ARR (about EUR 21.5 per AlliedOffsets Oct 2025; EUR 22-50 per Senken; BBB+ ARR averaged ~28.55 in H1 2026), that is roughly $30-150/ha/yr, or about $500-2,500/ha in present value over 30 years. Forward VM0047 pre-purchases above EUR 65 (Carbon Pulse Oct 2025) are for credits not yet issued, and no VM0047 credits had been issued at that point. So realistically the step-up is about 25-100x in present value, and it is not immediate: validation gets you a forward offtake, and the cash arrives per verified vintage. The claimed $3-10k/ha looks inflated.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: about $20-60k per aggregated project (candidate's figure). VVB validation plus plot inventory runs about $50-150k all-in (my estimate). Base hit rate of eligibility/validation: no published figure. My estimate is 30-60% for screened parcels, because 10-year non-forest history is easy to check from free Landsat, MapBiomas or Hansen layers before anyone spends money. The real failures are additionality and start date, and better ML over aerials does not fix those. Lever capped at about 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible already. Brazil's MapBiomas publishes annual land-cover classes back to 1985. Hansen Global Forest Change and Landsat are free and processed, and the USDA NASS Cropland Data Layer covers the US. Together these effectively summarise the "non-forest 10+ years ago, forest now" outcome in a public raster field, the same pattern seen with regulator status fields, so scanned aerials add little marginal edge. Competitors already do this screening at scale: Pachama, Chestnut Carbon (US Southeast), Mombak and re.green (Brazil Atlantic Forest/Amazon), NCX, Funga, Ponterra and Renoster.
scored.right_bought: Carbon rights can be bought or leased from landowners. Typical structures are 30-40 year easements or revenue shares, often with no upfront payment; that is my estimate from developer structures. Owners do not need to read historical aerials to sign, but many developers are competing for the same parcels, and long-tenure commitments plus title gaps make the rights neither trivially cheap nor clean.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist: Symbiosis Coalition (Google, Meta, Microsoft, Salesforce; up to 20 Mt by 2030, reportedly ~$50-55/t), Microsoft direct (~$70/t reported for Ponterra Panama), and Frontier-adjacent corporates. But Symbiosis criteria stress dynamic baselining for additionality, so they would discount or reject regrowth that happened without the project.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are weak. Integrated restoration developer, then timberland or land owner (Chestnut-style), then nursery or planting ops and a credit trading desk. These are a land and asset-management business with thin margins, not a trillion-dollar chain. Possible, but this path is capped by the size of the voluntary carbon market.
scored.fatal_flaw: The thesis contradicts itself on additionality and start date. VCS defines the start date as the first significant action by the project, and VM0047 uses a dynamic performance benchmark against matched control land. Fields that are already regrowing naturally with no intervention therefore have no creditable start date. Their matched controls are also regrowing, so the net removals for which credits issue are near zero. Retroactive windows are closing too: VCS v4 requires ARR validation within 8 years of start, and VCS v5 requires pipeline listing within 1 year of the crediting start for requests on or after 1 Jan 2027. The "vintage" being bought is exactly what quality buyers like Symbiosis are built to exclude.
scored.one_line_reason: Regrowth that has already happened passively fails VM0047's dynamic-baseline additionality and VCS start-date rules. Eligibility history is already legible in MapBiomas, Hansen and Landsat. Proving is a multi-year audit, not a trivial step. The realistic step-up is about 25-100x, paid slowly, and the hit-rate lever is around 2x.
sources: https://carbon-pulse.com/?p=445535 (VM0047 forward EUR 65-70, no issuances yet, ARR index EUR 12 / EUR 21.5)
https://verra.org/documents/vcs-version-5-overview-of-vcs-program-updates-and-effective-dates/ (VCS v5: pipeline listing within 1 year of crediting start from 1 Jan 2027)
https://verra.org/documents/vcs-program-clarifications-19-april-2022-rev (ARR validation within 8 years of start date)
https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240521133634/en (Symbiosis 20 Mt pledge, dynamic baselining for additionality)

scored.name: Orphan TC (abandoned FAA type certificates and STCs)
scored.one_line: Buys dormant TCs and STCs from defunct holders for out-of-production aircraft, engines and props with large active fleets, uses ML over scanned TCDS, ADs and SDRs to find fleets grounded by missing ICA and parts support, re-establishes design-holder obligations, and sells parts/ICA or the TC to consolidators. Next to the killed FAA PMA idea.
scored.unproven_right: Dormant TCs/STCs held by estates or dissolved companies, bought for $5-100k
scored.proving_step: FAA TC transfer plus reinstated production/parts approval (~$50-300k); ML ranks TCs with unmet AD and parts demand
scored.proven_buyer: Captive fleet owners/operators and aftermarket consolidators (Textron aftermarket, Heico, Ontic)
scored.public_data: FAA DRS (TCDS, STCs, ADs as scanned PDFs), SDR database, aircraft registry, Federal Register AD dockets
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x ($20k TC to $1-5M parts franchise); fleet counts are legible so ML edge is modest
scored.frame: The rung would be 'own a dormant TC/STC and turn it back into a supported design with ICA and parts approval'. In that rung, discovery (finding which orphan TC has a large grounded or under-supported fleet) is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The other 80%+ is physical and regulatory: the FAA transfer, keeping design-holder obligations (AD response, ICA, continued-airworthiness engineering staff), standing up a production approval or quality system, rebuilding tooling and drawings, and making certified parts. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mine pattern: running the bespoke parts and engineering operation is harder than finding the TC. Capitalised buyers do exist (Ontic bought the Twin Commander TCs in 2018 and the Fairchild Merlin/Metro TCs from M7 in 2022; Viking took the Shorts SC7/330/360 TCs from Bombardier). But they buy a support business with a working operation, not an unproven right.
scored.step_up: I found no published price for a standalone TC sale, and the deal values below come from asset sales and reserve prices. Bankruptcy packages that included TCs: Micco TC plus factory equipment >$1.1M (2004); Stoddard-Hamilton/GlaStar design rights plus assets $593k; Jetcruzer 450 TC lot reserve $500k; Adam Aircraft lowest opening bid $10M; Icon all assets $15.79M (2024). Dormant TCs held by estates (the candidate says $5-100k; my estimate is plausible for small STCs, while airframe TCs with fleets go for $0.5-1M+). The proven side is a parts and ICA franchise worth maybe $1-5M (candidate's estimate, unverified). That gives about 10-50x, and it is not immediate: the value only shows up after years of engineering and manufacturing build-out. Ontic, Viking and McFarlane deal prices were not disclosed.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step (TC transfer plus re-establishing parts support) does not mostly fail. A TC transfer is an administrative FAA action that succeeds whenever the buyer can meet the holder's obligations, so the base hit rate is high (my estimate: >50% of attempted transfers go through). Cost per attempt is the candidate's ~$50-300k for transfer and approval, plus my estimate of $1M+ to actually stand up production. Because the base hit rate is high, the ML lever is capped at under 2x (1/base rate), nowhere near 10x. The commercial risk is whether demand covers the fixed engineering cost, and fleet size answers that.
scored.data:
Partly illegible: TCDS, ADs and SDRs are scanned or unstructured. But the outcome-relevant fields are legible:
- The FAA aircraft registry gives exact active fleet counts by make and model.
- Each TCDS names the current holder.
- The FAA publishes Federal Register 'Notice of Intent to Designate as Abandoned' lists, with a public abandoned-TC page. Recent 2026 notices covered 765 Century Flight Systems STCs and 30 New Systems Engineering STCs.
Two things weaken the edge further. Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2012 and Order 8110.120, once a TC is declared abandoned the FAA can release its engineering data on request. That makes the right non-exclusive and nearly free instead of a cheap purchased monopoly. And the sellers (estates, Bombardier, M7) know their fleets and route the TCs to known specialists. So the regulator writes the answer into public status fields and fleet counts, which is the known failure mode.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought: TCs and STCs transfer by private sale or bankruptcy auction, for example McFarlane buying P. Ponk's STCs after the co-owner's death (2025), and Ontic, Univair and Viking deals. But the sellers are not data-blind. They are informed OEMs and trustees, the deals are bilateral or run by trustees, and in abandonment cases the FAA itself releases the data, so the right comes free and non-exclusive.
scored.buyer: Ontic (CVC-backed, a serial buyer of legacy TCs: Twin Commander 2018, Fairchild Merlin/Metro 2022), Viking Air (Shorts and DHC legacy TCs), Univair (Stinson 108, Ercoupe, Forney/Alon, Mooney M10), McFarlane (Cessna STCs plus PMA), HEICO and TransDigm-style aftermarket consolidators, and fleet operators (e.g. C-26/Metro military operators). These buyers are capitalised, but they are also the direct competitors already doing the rung.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder: TC and ICA holder, then PMA and parts manufacturer, then MRO and upgrade STCs, then a production restart. Viking restarted Twin Otter production after acquiring the DHC legacy TCs, so the path exists. The ceiling is a niche aftermarket roll-up (Ontic/HEICO scale, $1-10B), and incumbents already occupy each rung. It is not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no hidden-discovery step. Which orphan TCs are valuable is legible from public fleet counts in the FAA registry and the FAA's own abandoned-TC notices. Experienced serial buyers (Ontic, Univair, Viking, McFarlane) already harvest them. The value comes from the costly engineering, quality and manufacturing operation needed to meet design-holder obligations, not from finding the asset. So ML neither cuts capex 10x nor finds mispriced rights.
scored.one_line_reason: Buying orphan TCs is a real niche business, but discovery is a small share of the work, the proving step is administrative and mostly succeeds, fleet value is legible from the registry, and incumbents like Ontic and Univair already do it, so the ML edge is about zero.

scored.name: Post-Sackett Wetland De-designation (Sackett Land Co. / Drylands)
scored.one_line: Buys rural and exurban parcels priced near zero because NWI maps flag them as wetland, uses ML over LiDAR flow connectivity, hydrography, SSURGO and the USACE ORM2 JD archive to pick those failing the post-2023 'continuous surface connection' test, obtains a 'no WOTUS' Approved Jurisdictional Determination, and sells developable land to homebuilders, logistics and data center developers. Owns the land, unlike the killed mitigation-bank idea.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title or 12-24 month options on NWI-encumbered parcels at ~$300-2,000/acre from owners who assume the land is undevelopable
scored.proving_step: Wetland delineation (~$3-15k) plus USACE AJD, a binding, appealable federal determination valid 5 years that title, lenders and appraisers rely on; must exclude states with their own wetland programs (CA, NY, NJ, MA, MN)
scored.proven_buyer: Production homebuilders (Lennar, D.R. Horton land arms), industrial/logistics developers, data center site selectors, land bankers
scored.public_data: USACE ORM2 public JDs and scanned JD memos (pre- and post-Sackett labels), NWI polygons, USGS 3DEP LiDAR, NHD/NHDPlus HR, NRCS SSURGO, historical aerials
scored.rough_step_up: ~20-200x per acre ($500 to $20-100k at metro edges), low 10^3 in hot exurbs; estimates say 60-84% of wetlands lost federal protection but NWI and prices have not caught up
scored.frame: Rung: option on an NWI-flagged parcel, plus a delineation and a 'no WOTUS' AJD, sold to a homebuilder or land banker. Inside that rung, discovery (picking parcels that fail the continuous-surface-connection test) is perhaps 40-50% of the work (my estimate). The rest is zoning, utilities, access, floodplain and hydric-soil constraints, state and local wetland ordinances, and getting the Corps to issue an AJD at all. Taft and Kimley-Horn report districts pausing AJDs after Sackett, and the Nov 2025 proposed rule leaves the AJD's future uncertain. The physical step is cheap (a $3-15k delineation), but it is not the binding constraint. Buyers exist: Lennar and D.R. Horton land arms and industrial developers.
scored.step_up: The candidate's '$500 to $20-100k/acre' confuses location and entitlement value with wetland status. Measured wetland discounts are 25-80% per wetland acre. In North Dakota a wetland acre sold for $192 vs a $262/acre average, 27% less (NDSU, Kendall/Goltz/Leitch). A Hudson NY appraisal took an 80% cut: about $5,185/acre down to $1,050/acre. In a Middleton MA appeal it was about $2,000 vs $13,500/acre developable, roughly 6.75x, and that gap includes buildability. Texas A&M TRERC found a tract that is half wetland sells only about 1% below a comparable tract. So removing the federal wetland label typically yields 1.3-5x, rarely about 7x. Getting to 20-200x still needs rezoning, utilities and entitlement, which are separate rungs that take years. Realistic score: 2-10x, not 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is high, not low. The Berkeley WOTUS-ML team (trained on about 150,000 Corps JDs) estimates Sackett deregulates about one third of previously regulated waters. The candidate itself cites 60-84% of wetlands losing federal protection. With base rates of about 33-80%, the lever is capped at 1/p, about 1.25-3x, far from 10x. A proving attempt costs about $3-15k (delineation plus AJD; candidate's figure, consistent with consultant pricing, unsourced). That is trivial next to land carry, so ML saves little capex. The money at risk is the option or land price and the holding time, not the proving shots.
scored.data: The data is public: ORM2 JDs, NWI, 3DEP LiDAR, NHDPlus, SSURGO. But the outcome is already written in legible fields. Post-Sackett Corps AJD memos list each feature as 'Non-Jurisdictional' with acreage (Vicksburg District memos), and the EPA has already analysed ORM2 at both the AJD and the aquatic-resource level. Worse, the Berkeley WOTUS-ML model's predictions of which waters the CWA regulates are published free on Dryad. North Carolina DEQ is building an ML-plus-LiDAR map of the probability that land is jurisdictional. The illegibility edge is small and shrinking, and a free public model already exists.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Fee title or 12-24 month options on encumbered rural parcels can be bought from owners. Prices of about $1,000-5,000/acre for wetland-heavy tracts are documented in NY and MA appraisals and appeals. But discounts are only 25-80%, not near-zero. Sophisticated land bankers and homebuilders already order delineations and read Sackett, so the mispricing is thin at metro edges where the value sits. It is larger in remote rural land, where the uplift is small in dollars.
scored.buyer: Production homebuilders (Lennar and D.R. Horton land-banking arms), industrial and logistics developers, data center site selectors, and land bankers such as Millrose and Varde-backed vehicles. They are well capitalised, but they pay for entitled, serviced lots, not for a parcel that merely lacks federal wetland status.
scored.ladder: The path runs option, then AJD, then entitlement and rezoning, then horizontal development (utilities, roads), then vertical building or a build-to-suit data center or industrial site. It is a real but commodity land-development ladder with thin margins and a fragmented field of competitors, and the asset is nonrenewable once Sackett-driven mispricing is arbitraged away. A large regional developer is plausible; a trillion-dollar path is not.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is not a discovery step-up. A no-WOTUS AJD removes only a 25-80% wetland discount (about 1.3-5x). The 20-200x the candidate claims comes from entitlement, utilities and location, which are slow non-discovery rungs. The base hit rate is already about one third or more, a free public ML model (Berkeley WOTUS-ML on Dryad) and legible 'Non-Jurisdictional' fields in Corps memos already summarise the outcome, and AJD issuance itself is paused or politically unstable.
scored.one_line_reason: Weak: removing the federal wetland label yields about 2-5x, not 10^3. The base hit rate is high (about 33%+), so the ML lever is under 3x. The outcome is already legible in Corps JD memos and in a free public ML model, and state, local and entitlement constraints dominate.

scored.name: Pre97 (EU Novel Food status determinations for traditional ingredients)
scored.one_line: Takes exclusive supply contracts for traditional botanicals blocked from the EU as presumed Novel Foods, uses ML/OCR over historical trade, retail and customs records to prove significant pre-15 May 1997 consumption, gets an Article 4 'not novel' determination, and signs offtake with food majors.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive long-term supply or offtake rights from origin-country growers bought while EU demand is legally zero
scored.proving_step: Article 4 consultation under Regulation 2015/2283 (~€20-50k) producing a published status determination
scored.proven_buyer: Food and ingredient majors (Nestle, Givaudan, IFF, Symrise)
scored.public_data: EU Novel Food Catalogue and consultation outcomes, Eurostat/Comext, Europeana, Delpher, Gallica archives
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x on the supply right; ruling is non-exclusive so competitors free-ride (weak right)
scored.frame: The rung is 'get an EU Article 4 not-novel determination for a botanical, then sell supply'. Inside the determination itself, finding the evidence is close to 100% of the work: it is a paper file of pre-1997 EU consumption records, and there is no physical step. But that is not a sellable rung. The determination is a public, non-exclusive legal status, not an asset Pre97 owns. What actually gets sold is commodity ingredient supply, where sourcing, quality control, processing, logistics and contaminant compliance are most of the work. So discovery is perhaps 20-30% of the sellable rung (my estimate). The buyers (Givaudan, Symrise, IFF, Nestle) are well capitalised, but they buy the ingredient at commodity-plus prices, not the right.
scored.step_up: Unproven: exclusive offtake from origin growers at roughly local-market prices, so the contract premium is near $0 (estimate). Proven: once the status is published, any EU importer can buy from any grower, so the exclusive contract is worth only what can be enforced against growers who will sell to others. Realistic gain is a supply-margin uplift of about 2-5x on a small volume (estimate). The one-line pitch claims 10-100x, but that applies to market volume, not to a right Pre97 captures. Baobab is the precedent: the EU authorised it in 2008 (Decision 2008/575/EC) after a PhytoTrade Africa application. The market later grew about 4-5x (B'Ayoba, anecdotal), and the benefit went to all suppliers, not to whoever held the ruling. No price series was found, so the step-up is unquantified and an estimate.
