scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: in one reported batch of Article 4 consultations, 2 of 8 were found not novel (about 25%; NutraIngredients/FoodNavigator, 2019). This is a single small sample and applicants self-select. Cost per attempt: about EUR 20-50k for consultancy work and the dossier. This is the candidate's own figure and I could not verify it; I found no official fee. At a 25% base rate the lever is capped at 4x, and the attempt is already cheap. A 10x capex cut is impossible and saves only tens of thousands of euros. There is also a fallback route: the Article 14 traditional-food-from-third-country notification (25 years of safe use in the origin country, 4-month EFSA objection window). It goes around the pre-1997 evidence question altogether.
scored.data: Partly fits. The evidence is genuinely illegible: digitised newspapers and catalogues in Delpher, Gallica and Europeana, old retail price lists, customs lines in Comext. That is the ML/OCR-friendly part. But the outcome is often already in a legible field. The EU Novel Food Catalogue gives a status for each species (novel, not novel, food supplement only), and consultation outcomes are published by member states and the Commission. This is the same failure mode as earlier hunts. Incumbents already do this as a paid service: novel-food regulatory consultancies, plus ingredient firms' own regulatory teams.
scored.right_bought: Yes, cheaply: exclusive offtake or supply contracts with growers or cooperatives in the origin country, bought while EU demand is legally zero. But the right is weak. It is a contract, not title, so growers can defect or sell side volumes once demand appears. The species usually grows across several countries, so other suppliers exist. And the regulatory status, which is the step-up event, attaches to the food, not to Pre97. Anyone can free-ride on it right away. Only a full Article 10 authorisation backed by proprietary new data gets 5 years of data protection (Art. 26 of Reg. 2015/2283), and that route costs far more and is not an Article 4 determination.
scored.buyer: Ingredient and flavour houses and food majors: Givaudan, Symrise, IFF, Nestle. They are well capitalised, but they buy volume at commodity-plus prices and can source from any grower once the status is public. They have no reason to pay a premium for Pre97's contract.
scored.ladder: Modest. Possible next rungs are processing and extraction in the origin country, a branded or standardised ingredient (a patented extract or a full novel-food authorisation with data protection), and then consumer brands. Specialty botanical ingredients form a multi-billion-dollar niche at best, not a trillion-dollar chain. Each rung is ordinary CPG or ingredient-processing work, where discovery confers no edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step produces a public, non-exclusive status that attaches to the food, not to the company. Pre97 pays for the determination, and every competitor and grower captures the step-up for free. The asset Pre97 actually holds, a grower supply contract, sees only a few-x uplift and cannot be enforced against defection.
scored.one_line_reason: Pre97 can buy grower supply contracts cheaply, but the step-up event is a public, non-exclusive legal status that competitors free-ride on. The base hit rate (about 25%) caps the ML lever near 4x on an already cheap EUR 20-50k step, and the Novel Food Catalogue often already states the answer.

scored.name: Dark Strand (certified spare fibre from utility OPGW and orphaned IRUs)
scored.one_line: Buys spare dark-fibre strands from utilities/coops and orphaned IRUs from bankrupt carriers at near-scrap prices, tests to ITU/TIA standards, and sells certified route-diverse IRUs to hyperscalers and AI-cluster builders.
scored.unproven_right: IRUs or strand purchases for fibre of unknown condition and route
scored.proving_step: OTDR plus CD/PMD certification to ITU-T G.652/G.655 and TIA-568 (a few hundred dollars per span); ML over PUC dockets and bankruptcy schedules finds likely-continuous scarce paths
scored.proven_buyer: Hyperscalers, neoclouds, fibre wholesalers (Zayo, Crown Castle Fiber)
scored.public_data: State PUC dockets, utility rate-case exhibits, PACER schedules, FCC National Broadband Map, HIFLD
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-30x; old fibre often passes so base hit rate high; adjacent to killed telco copper
scored.frame: The rung would be buying an untested strand or IRU, testing it, and reselling it as a certified IRU. The buyers are real and have money: Lumen signed about $8.5B of private-fibre deals with hyperscalers in 2024-25, and Zayo is buying long-haul capacity (from memory, not searched). But discovery and proving are maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). Most of the work is commercial and legal: easement rights for third-party telecom use on utility rights-of-way (landowner suits against utilities over fibre on power-line easements are well known), splicing and access to OPGW, which needs line outages, building laterals and handoffs at data centres, maintenance and SLA obligations over 20-year IRUs, and negotiating with utilities. The OTDR test is cheap, but the testing is not the hard part.
scored.step_up: Unproven: fibre from bankrupt carriers or utility spares, my estimate roughly 10-30% of replacement value, about $300-1,500 per fibre-mile. Proven: certified long-haul dark-fibre IRUs historically about $1,000-3,000 per fibre-mile for 20 years, and possibly a few times more on scarce AI-driven routes (estimate from memory, not verified this run). That is about 2-10x, and most of it comes from packaging, route assembly and selling, not from the test result. It is nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is high. My estimate is that 80-95% of installed G.652 strands pass OTDR and loss tests. Old G.652/G.655 fibre can fail CD/PMD checks at 400G+ coherent rates, but coherent DSPs compensate for most of that. So the lever is capped at 1/0.85, about 1.2x, not 10x. Each test costs a few hundred to a few thousand dollars per span (estimate), which is trivial next to asset value. ML does not cut capex by any meaningful amount.
scored.data: Route data partly sits in illegible public sources: PUC dockets, rate-case exhibits and PACER schedules. But commercial fibre-route databases already map the routes (FiberLocator, GeoTel, and Zayo/Lumen's own maps), and the FCC map and HIFLD are already structured. The outcome, whether a strand is lit, spare or working, is not in a public field, but the owners know it from their own records and cheap tests. Utilities run fibre monetisation programmes and use brokers, and bankruptcy trustees run auctions with bankers. These are not owners who cannot read the data, so there is little information asymmetry for ML to exploit.
scored.right_bought: Bought: strand purchases or IRUs from utilities and co-ops, and orphaned IRUs from carrier bankruptcy estates (sec. 363 sales). They are bought rather than free, but sellers are fairly well informed, and easement scope can block third-party telecom use.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Meta, Google, AWS), neoclouds, and wholesalers (Zayo, Lumen, Crown Castle Fiber, now owned by Zayo). They have plenty of money, but they mostly buy from incumbents that can build to order and give SLAs.
scored.ladder: There are plausible rungs above: route aggregation, lit wavelength services, building new long-haul, data-centre interconnect, then owning AI campus connectivity. This is a mid-sized infrastructure path that Zayo and Lumen already occupy, not a clear path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not where the value is or where the uncertainty lies. Old fibre mostly passes testing (base hit rate about 85%, so the lever is about 1.2x), and the step-up is about 2-10x, driven by legal rights, easements, splicing and access, and sales rather than discovery. It is the same failure pattern as the killed telco-copper idea.
scored.one_line_reason: Testing is cheap and nearly always passes, owners already know what they hold, and the value comes from rights, access and sales, so there is no 10^4 discovery jump for ML to unlock.
sources: Web search was not run: the shared per-turn search budget was already used up, so no figures were checked this run.
My estimate, from memory: long-haul dark-fibre IRU prices of about $1,000-3,000 per fibre-mile over 20 years
From memory, not verified this run: Lumen announced about $8.5B of private connectivity fabric deals with hyperscalers in 2024-25
From memory, not verified this run: FiberLocator and GeoTel are commercial fibre-route databases
From memory, not verified this run: landowner suits against utilities over fibre on power-line easements
My estimate: 80-95% of installed strands pass OTDR and loss tests

scored.name: Western Surface Water Rights Historic-Use Decrees (CoolRight / Decreed)
scored.one_line: Buys senior but unquantified, sporadically used or abandonment-listed surface water rights and ditch shares from irrigators and heirs, uses ML over scanned diversion records, water-commissioner field books, ditch ledgers and decades of aerial/OpenET imagery to reconstruct historic consumptive use, wins a water-court or state engineer change-of-use decree, and sells the quantified transferable volume to Front Range municipalities, homebuilders and data center campuses. Surface water only, no groundwater exploration.
scored.unproven_right: Decreed surface diversion rights and ditch shares priced low (~$2-5k per share) because owners cannot prove historic use
scored.proving_step: Change-of-use decree or state engineer approval quantifying transferable consumptive use; litigation plus engineering, not cheap or instant; many rights quantified near zero or cut back
scored.proven_buyer: Front Range municipalities and utilities (Aurora, Thornton, Denver Water), homebuilders needing water dedication, data center developers in AZ/NV/UT/CO, water funds
scored.public_data: Colorado CDSS/HydroBase, Utah water rights DB, scanned water court decrees and field books, state engineer abandonment lists, OpenET, NAIP and Landsat irrigation history, ditch company records
scored.rough_step_up: ~3-10x on agricultural-to-industrial value generally; up to ~10-100x where a near-zero unproven share becomes $30-80k per consumptive acre-foot
scored.frame: The rung is "buy an ag water right or ditch share, win a change-of-use decree, sell the quantified consumptive-use acre-feet to a municipality." Discovery (reconstructing historic consumptive use) is maybe 20-30% of the work inside that rung, and that is my estimate. Most of the work is adversarial water-court litigation: 3-10 years, statements of opposition from many other water users, engineering experts on both sides, plus decreed terms and conditions (revegetation, return-flow maintenance, dry-up covenants). The physical/legal proving step is the hard part, the same failure pattern as the geothermal counter-example. A capitalised buyer does exist (Aurora, Thornton, Greeley, Denver Water, homebuilders).
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified this session: Front Range municipal and C-BT-equivalent water trades at about $30-80k per acre-foot (C-BT units are widely reported at roughly $70-100k per unit of about 0.7 AF in 2023-2025). Senior South Platte and Arkansas ag shares are already priced on expected historic consumptive use, at about 30-60% of the municipal value per consumptive AF, so the realised step-up is about 2-5x (estimate). The "$2-5k unproven share to $30-80k" case only happens where the share really has little historic use. In that case water court quantifies it near zero, so there is nothing to step up. Neither end of the market sits near zero.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Change cases mostly succeed, but with cutbacks. I estimate (not verified) that most decrees issue, at about 50-80% of the volume the applicant claimed. Cost per change case is about $200k to over $1M in legal and engineering fees, over 3-10 years (estimate from the Colorado water-law practice I know of). The base hit rate is not low, so ML cannot multiply the number of successful attempts much: the lever is capped at about 1.3-2x by 1/base rate. ML can help pick which shares to buy, but it cannot remove the litigation cost, which is most of the capex.
scored.data: The data is partly legible already. Colorado HydroBase/CDSS has digitized structure-level diversion records back decades, and the state engineer publishes decennial abandonment lists. OpenET publishes field-level ET publicly, and NAIP/Landsat irrigated-acreage layers already exist (CDSS irrigated-parcel GIS for 1956-2020s). Consulting engineers (Leonard Rice, Helton & Williamsen, Spronk, Wilson Water) already run historic-consumptive-use analyses for both buyers and opposers. Scanned field books and ditch ledgers are the illegible remainder, and they matter mostly for pre-1950 use. The outcome is not written into a single status field, but the main inputs are already structured. The ML edge over existing HCU methods is likely incremental.
scored.right_bought: Yes, ditch shares and decreed rights are bought from irrigators and heirs, and the market is real and fairly active. The sellers are not uninformed, though. Brokers, ditch-company boards and municipal acquisition teams all know the going rates. The bigger problem is Colorado's anti-speculation doctrine (High Plains A&M v. Southeastern Colorado Water Conservancy District, 2005; the Pagosa line of cases). A change application generally needs a specific end user or need, so a speculator cannot cleanly prove a right on spec and resell it. The buyer usually has to be under contract first, and that hands the step-up to the municipality.
scored.buyer: Front Range municipalities and utilities (Aurora, Thornton, Greeley, Castle Rock, Denver Water), homebuilders meeting water-dedication requirements, and data center developers. All are well capitalised and most run their own acquisition and change-case programs.
scored.ladder: Moderate. The rungs go from rights aggregation to augmentation plans, storage, wholesale water utility and municipal supply. There is precedent: Vidler Water was sold to D.R. Horton (2022, roughly $290M, from memory), and Pure Cycle, Water Asset Management, Renewable Water Resources and Greenstone are other examples. Water is politically capped (buy-and-dry backlash, AZ/CO legislation) and regionally fragmented. It is a path to a company worth hundreds of millions of dollars, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is multi-year adversarial water-court litigation, not discovery. The anti-speculation doctrine stops a non-user from proving a right on spec and reselling it. The unproven shares are already priced on expected consumptive use, so the real step-up is about 2-5x and the hit-rate lever is capped near 2x.
scored.one_line_reason: This has the geothermal counter-example's shape. Litigation and decree conditions dominate the rung. The asset only steps up about 2-5x from an already-efficient market, and the base success rate is high, so ML has little hit rate to improve. HydroBase, OpenET and incumbent HCU engineers already make the key data mostly legible.
sources: Web search budget for this turn was used up (shared limit hit) before any results came back. All numbers are estimates from prior knowledge and need verifying.
Colorado Decision Support Systems / HydroBase (cdss.colorado.gov): digitized diversion records and irrigated-parcel GIS (prior knowledge)
Northern Water C-BT unit market prices, about $70-100k per unit, 2023-2025 (prior knowledge, unverified)
High Plains A&M, LLC v. Southeastern Colorado Water Conservancy District, 120 P.3d 710 (Colo. 2005): anti-speculation in change cases (prior knowledge)
Pagosa Area Water & Sanitation District v. Trout Unlimited, 170 P.3d 307 (Colo. 2007): anti-speculation (prior knowledge)
D.R. Horton acquisition of Vidler Water Resources, 2022 (prior knowledge)

scored.name: Survivor Shares (lost-security reclamation)
scored.one_line: Buys antique and lapsed stock/bond certificates and dormant registered positions at scripophily prices, uses ML over scanned corporate-action records to trace live successor companies, and validates with the transfer agent to collect market value.
scored.unproven_right: Certificates and assignment rights held by owners who think they are worthless paper ($5-100)
scored.proving_step: Transfer-agent validation and re-registration (Computershare, Equiniti); cheap, usually fails
scored.proven_buyer: The public equity market (validated position instantly liquid)
scored.public_data: Scanned Moody's/Mergent manuals, Capital Changes Reporter, SEC EDGAR, state registries, digitised newspaper notices
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-10,000x on a hit but few hits, niche market, escheatment limits supply; weak C5
scored.frame: The rung is buying a certificate, tracing its successor and re-registering the position. Inside that rung, discovery (tracing corporate actions through mergers, reverse splits and bankruptcies) is roughly 80-90% of the work, and the physical step is paperwork at the transfer agent. The buyer is the public equity market, which is liquid and fully capitalised, so that part fits. What breaks the frame is that the 'physical' step is not trivial in practice. A registered certificate does not pass to whoever holds the paper. The transfer agent needs the registered owner's endorsement, or the estate's, with a Medallion signature guarantee, plus estate or probate documents for a dead holder and often an indemnity bond. Buying the paper is not the same as buying the right. That legal step, not tracing, is the gating work. Estimate, not sourced.
scored.step_up: From memory, not sourced this run: unproven certificates trade at scripophily prices of about $5-100 each, and the rare live successor positions are worth about $1k-$100k. So a hit gives roughly 100-1000x on purchase price, and occasionally more. The candidate's '10,000x' fits only outliers. One more catch: once an heir knows the paper may be live, the price stops being a scripophily price. Holders of large positions are usually traceable heirs who can pay $50-100 for a search themselves.
scored.hit_rate_capex: From memory / my estimate, not sourced this run: old-certificate research services (Scripophily.com/OldCompany research, Stock Search International) charge about $50-150 per certificate. By industry lore, most certificates they research turn out to have only collectible value, and perhaps about 1-5% still have redeemable value (estimate). Re-registration costs about $25-200 in transfer-agent fees and Medallion guarantee, plus an indemnity bond of about 2-3% of value for lost certificates. The proving step is already cheap, about $100 per attempt. So even a 10x hit-rate gain saves dollars per shot, not millions. There is no large proving capex for ML to collapse, and the lever does not matter economically.
scored.data: Partly illegible: scanned Moody's/Mergent manuals, Capital Changes Reporter and old newspaper notices are hard to read. But the outcome is often already summarised in legible fields. First, dormant positions get escheated to the states after about 3-5 years of lost contact. The states liquidate them and list owner name, holder and amount in public, searchable unclaimed-property databases (MissingMoney.com and state sites). Second, transfer agents and DTC/CUSIP records already map successor issues. Third, incumbents already sell this lookup: certificate research firms charge about $100 each, and heir finders and asset locators work state unclaimed-property lists on 10-35% contingency, with fees capped by many state statutes. The right also cannot be bought cleanly. Beneficial ownership follows the registry, not the paper. Escheated value goes to the registered owner or heirs, and states restrict or cap finder assignments. The candidate itself notes that 'escheatment limits supply'.
scored.right_bought: Mostly no. Collectors can buy the physical paper cheaply, but the claim to the shares stays with the registered owner or estate unless it is properly endorsed and assigned with a Medallion guarantee. After escheatment, the claim is against the state and belongs to the owner or heirs. Finder agreements there are often capped by statute at about 10-35% and sometimes barred for a waiting period. So the company ends up with a fee-capped heir-finder contingency rather than owning the asset and keeping the step-up.
scored.buyer: The public equity market for traced live positions, and state unclaimed-property programmes, which pay cash to the rightful claimant, for escheated ones. Both are capitalised and liquid, but the capped finder fee limits what the company keeps.
scored.ladder: Weak. Possible next steps are general unclaimed-asset recovery (dormant bank accounts, insurance demutualisation shares, class-action settlement claims) or litigation-finance-style claim buying. These are fragmented, fee-capped, regulated markets in the low billions at most, already served by heir finders and claims aggregators. There is no path toward owning a large physical chain the way a mineral right leads to a mine.
scored.fatal_flaw: Owning the paper does not mean owning the shares. Registered ownership and escheatment send the value to the registered owner or heirs, and states write the outcome into public, legible unclaimed-property listings. That leaves a fee-capped heir-finder business, not an asset the company owns and marks up 1,000x.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is already cheap (about $100), hits are rare and small, and the right cannot be bought from paper holders. The value follows the registry or escheats to the states, whose public lists already name it, and incumbents already sell the lookup.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared search budget for this turn was already used up, so every number here is from memory or my own estimate and needs checking.
Recalled, unverified this run: Scripophily.com / OldCompany.com certificate research service (about $50-150 per certificate)
Recalled, unverified this run: MissingMoney.com / NAUPA state unclaimed-property databases (escheated securities listed by owner name)
Recalled, unverified this run: state unclaimed-property statutes capping finder fees (typically 10-35%)
Recalled, unverified this run: transfer-agent (Computershare/Equiniti) rules requiring Medallion signature guarantee and indemnity bond for lost certificates

scored.name: Fallrett (Norwegian/Alpine waterfall-right aggregation)
scored.one_line: Options privately owned waterfall rights (Norwegian 'fallrett', Swiss/Austrian small water rights) from farmers, uses ML over scanned NVE hydrology and river-regulation archives to pick reaches with underestimated runoff, proves them with a 12-month gauged flow study plus NVE-standard hydrology report, and sells to small-hydro developers.
scored.unproven_right: Riparian waterfall rights owned by fragmented landowners, typically optioned for a revenue-share promise at near-zero upfront cost
scored.proving_step: About $30-60k: temporary gauge plus scaling against the NVE regional regime, giving a bankable flow-duration curve and concession application. Many reaches fail on flow or environmental grounds.
scored.proven_buyer: Small-hydro aggregators (Småkraft/Statkraft, Clemens Kraft, Norsk Grønnkraft), paying lump sums or 10-20% revenue leases for licensed falls
scored.public_data: NVE scanned historic concession files and 'Samlet plan' archives, NVE HYDRA II gauge archive, 19th-century mill and sawmill records, Kartverket lidar DEM
scored.rough_step_up: Near $0 upfront to a licensed fall worth about NOK 2-10M, roughly 100-1000x on cash out; the right is optioned not bought, so the 'buy cheap' leg is weak
scored.frame: The rung would be selling a licensed fall (fallrett plus NVE concession) to a developer. Inside that rung, finding the reach is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The rest is permitting: environmental surveys, the concession application, hearings and appeals. The Riksrevisjonen review (2013) put average NVE processing at about 3.5 years, plus about 2 more years when a decision is appealed, which happened in about a third of cases. So proving takes years and is mostly regulatory, not a 12-month gauge study. Capitalised buyers do exist (Småkraft AS, owned by Aquila Capital; Clemens Kraft; Fossberg/Eqva). But they already run this origination themselves.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the right is optioned to the developer for a revenue share. Landowners typically keep more than 10% of gross turnover on 40-60 year leases (NVE file and lease-tax submissions), so the company never owns the upside it creates. Proven: the Skjeggfoss project (5.6 GWh/yr, under construction) sold for about NOK 45M, roughly NOK 8 per kWh of annual output (Eqva, 2022). That price includes construction capex of about 3.8-4.7 NOK/kWh (NMBU thesis). By my estimate, the licensed-but-unbuilt right alone is worth about NOK 1-3 per kWh/yr, so NOK 2-10M for a typical 2-5 GWh fall. That looks like 100-1000x on near-zero cash. But the step-up is on a revenue-share promise, not on an asset bought at a discount, and most of the value is shared with the landowner. Realistic captured step-up: about 3-10x (my estimate).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate of the proving step is high, not low. In 2010/11 NVE granted 78 of 101 small-hydro cases (about 77%). In 2012 it granted 61 and rejected 36 (about 63%). In 2024 so far, 17 of 23 decisions were positive (about 74%) (Storting written answer). The lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, so ML can improve capex by at most about 1.3-1.6x. Cost per attempt: about $30-60k for the gauge and hydrology work (candidate's figure). Adding environmental surveys and consultant fees for the concession application, my estimate is NOK 0.5-1.5M, spread over 3-5 years.
scored.data: The outcome is already in a legible public field. NVE publishes an open (NLOD) digital resource map of small-hydro potential: dataset 'Småkraftverk ressurskartlegging', updated 2026, REST endpoint kart.nve.no/enterprise/rest/services/Smakraftverk1/MapServer. It covers every candidate reach from 50 kW to 10 MW, with modelled flow, output and build cost per kWh (threshold 8 kr/kWh at 2025 prices). Earlier versions (2004-06) identified about 10,000 sites and 25 TWh. Gauge records (HYDRA II) and concession decisions are also digital and searchable. Developers have been canvassing farmers for 20 years with this same map, so landowners are not unaware. Rights are not bought cheaply: farmers lease them on revenue-share terms and keep ownership.
scored.right_bought: No. The fallrett belongs to the riparian landowner and is leased on a revenue share of more than 10% of gross over 40-60 years, not sold at a discount. Developers already compete for these leases on the standard 'småkraftmodellen' terms. There is no purchase discount from information asymmetry, because NVE's potential map tells the farmer what the fall is worth.
scored.buyer: Småkraft AS (Aquila Capital, 45+ plants, 500+ GWh), Clemens Kraft, Norsk Grønnkraft, Fossberg Kraft/Eqva, UK infrastructure funds (bought Skjeggfoss for about NOK 45M), and utilities such as BKK and Statkraft. They are capitalised, but they originate these sites in-house.
scored.ladder: Licensed fall, then construction, then an operating IPP, then a portfolio sale or grid-scale aggregation. A ladder exists, but it is short and capped. Remaining Norwegian small-hydro potential is a few TWh of economic sites, and Swiss/Austrian small water rights are similarly saturated and politically constrained. Aquila Capital already ran this roll-up to Europe's largest small-hydro operator. This is not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The answer is already a public legible field. NVE's open digital small-hydro resource map gives modelled flow, output and build cost for every candidate reach, and concessions are granted at about 65-77%. So there is no illegible-data edge and no low hit rate for ML to lever. On top of that, the right is leased on revenue share from informed landowners, not bought cheap.
scored.one_line_reason: NVE already publishes a reach-by-reach small-hydro potential and cost map, about 70% of concessions succeed, and farmers lease falls on 10%+ revenue share. So there is no illegible-data edge, the ML lever is at most about 1.5x, and the right is never bought cheap.

scored.name: Flow-Proven Pumped Storage Sites (private land, closed-loop)
scored.one_line: Options private ranch land pairs with large head and enough inflow for closed-loop pumped storage; ML over scanned USBR/USACE studies and geologic maps picks pairs, a hydrology/head survey and FERC preliminary permit prove them, and storage developers buy.
scored.unproven_right: Land options on upper and lower reservoir sites (FERC preliminary permits are first-come, so the bought right is the land)
scored.proving_step: About $200-500k: water-availability study, desktop geotech and FERC preliminary permit; most fail on geology or water rights
scored.proven_buyer: Pumped-storage developers (rPlus Hydro, Brookfield, utilities)
scored.public_data: Scanned USBR/USACE 1970s-80s pumped-storage reconnaissance studies, USGS geologic quadrangles, state water-rights adjudication PDFs
scored.rough_step_up: About $500/acre land to development rights at $10-50k/MW, roughly 20-100x, but the physical build is enormous
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "optioned land plus a desktop study plus a FERC preliminary permit". That is not a discrete rung that anyone buys at a step-up. The step that makes a pumped-storage project valuable is getting the FERC license plus an offtake or interconnection agreement. That takes about 5-10 years and (my estimate) $10-50M of environmental, geotech and licensing work, plus drilling and a water-rights adjudication. Inside that real rung, finding the site is maybe 10-20% of the work (estimate). The rest is permitting, stakeholder work and engineering. Above it, building a $2-4B plant is the overwhelming share of the work. This is structurally the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: the bespoke build dwarfs the finding.
scored.step_up: The proven price has no public benchmark. CIP's 2020 purchase of Rye Development's Swan Lake (393 MW) and Goldendale (1,200 MW) was at undisclosed terms, and both projects were already licensed or near licensing. Buyers do not pay a premium at the preliminary-permit stage: permits are first-come, cost roughly nothing to file, and many are surrendered or cancelled. Examples are Cabin Run, Mineral Run, Chandler Mountain (Alabama Power surrendered it after filing a notice of intent) and Don Pedro (cancelled). The candidate's own figure is land at ~$500/acre against $10-50k/MW. That $/MW range applies to late-stage, licensed rights, not to a desktop-proved site. My estimate is that a permit-stage site sells for about 1-3x the land option cost, if it sells at all.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rate (from what the search found): FERC preliminary permits covered over 12,000 MW in effect plus about 6,000 MW pending in 2017, and about 30 GW of permits by May 2023 (Statista citing FERC). Against that, only 3 new projects totaling 2,100 MW were licensed in 2014-2017, and only one small project was built in the US after 1995 (Van Ness Feldman, 2017). Permit-to-build conversion is therefore probably under 5% (estimate). But the failures come from offtake, financing, cost and opposition, not from picking the wrong site, so better site selection by ML barely moves that rate. Cost per desktop attempt is about $200-500k (the candidate's figure, my estimate agrees). Real proving (licensing) is $10M+ (estimate). The ML lever applies only to the cheap desktop slice.
scored.data: The data is largely legible already. NREL publishes a national closed-loop pumped storage siting atlas: GIS of thousands of candidate reservoir pairs with head, volume and cost class (from memory, not re-verified here). FERC eLibrary and the Federal Register list every permit, including location and capacity. USGS geologic maps are already digitized. The scanned 1970s-80s USBR/USACE studies add some value, but closed-loop design mostly removes the need for inflow history, which is a large part of what those studies contain. Water-rights adjudication PDFs are truly illegible, but the outcome (whether water is available) gets settled through a public process, not by reading old files.
scored.right_bought: Partly. Ranch land options can be bought cheaply, and owners do not know the value of the pumped-storage pairing. But FERC priority is first-come and nearly free, and established developers already blanket the best sites with permits: Premium Energy Holdings (Walker Lake 2,000 MW, Intermountain 1.2-2 GW), rPlus Hydro, and Alabama Power. Developers also often option the land only after they hold the permit, so the land is not the binding scarce right.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist: CIP, Brookfield, utilities such as Alabama Power, and rPlus Hydro. But they buy licensed or late-stage projects. At desktop or permit stage they can file their own permits for nearly nothing, and they have the NREL atlas.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: site, then license, then interconnection and offtake, then a $2-4B construction, then operating long-duration storage. The market is large. But each rung up is dominated by civil construction and permitting, not by information. Winning the smallest rung gives no compounding edge on the rungs above.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value of a pumped-storage site is only created at FERC licensing plus offtake, which takes 5-10 years and $10M+ (estimate), and is then dwarfed by a multi-billion-dollar bespoke build. Meanwhile, the desktop-plus-preliminary-permit rung that ML could speed up sells for roughly nothing. Permits are first-come and nearly free, NREL already publishes the closed-loop siting atlas, and about 30 GW of permits sit unbuilt. This is the geothermal counter-example again: the build is far harder than the find.
scored.one_line_reason: Not excluded, but weak (6/25 total). Discovery is a small share of the work, no buyer pays a step-up at permit stage, permits are first-come and nearly free, NREL already maps the sites, and project failures come from financing and build, not siting.

scored.name: Superemitter Rights (idle and orphan well methane credits) -- oil/gas-adjacent, flagged
scored.one_line: Takes over idle or orphaned wells from marginal operators and bankrupt estates for ~$0 plus plugging liability; ML over scanned state well files picks the rare super-emitters, a cheap flow measurement proves baseline under the ACR plugging methodology, routine contracted plugging produces ACR credits, and corporate offset buyers pay. This is plugging, not exploration or drilling, so it was kept, but the reviewer should confirm it is outside the oil/gas exclusion.
scored.unproven_right: Operatorship and carbon rights to idle/abandoned wells with unknown emission rate, acquired for ~$0 net
scored.proving_step: ACR-protocol wellhead methane flow measurement (~$500-2k per well); most emit near zero; hits are plugged (~$50-150k commodity service) and credits verified
scored.proven_buyer: Voluntary-market corporate buyers and offtake funders paying premiums for domestic measurable ACR credits, plus state orphan-well programmes co-funding plugs
scored.public_data: State commission scanned well files (PA DEP, OCC, TX RRC, WV DEP), USGS/EPA orphan well inventories, ACR registry project documents
scored.rough_step_up: Effectively unbounded on the ~$0 right; a ~10 kg CH4/hr well yields ~20k+ credits (~$0.5-1M) against a ~$100k plug, so ~5-10x net per hit
scored.frame: The rung is one plugging-credit project: get operatorship of a well, measure its baseline, plug it, get credits issued, sell them. Discovery is maybe 1-5% of the work and cost inside that rung (my estimate): a measurement costs ~$500-2k and a plug costs $33k (PA budget) to $150k (deep ND wells). The plug, bonding, regulatory transfer of operatorship, verification and the monitoring tail are most of the work. That is the inverse of the Terranox frame: the physical step is the hard, expensive part, not the trivial one. Exclusion check: plugging is not exploration, prospecting or drilling, so by the letter it falls outside the hard exclusion and I did not exclude it. But it means taking operatorship of oil and gas wells, so it is plainly oil/gas-adjacent and the reviewer should apply the exclusion in spirit if in doubt.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: ~$0 nominal but net negative, because the operator takes on the plugging liability ($33k-150k per well; sources: PA budget and ND figures cited in the ACR/Zefiro coverage). Proven value: credits sell for ~$7 (WDF, which had other funding) to $25-30/tCO2e (ZeroSix, CarbonPath), and Grist's experts suggest $10-30 (QCI, Grist/Yahoo). My estimate for a 10 kg CH4/hr well: ~88 t CH4/yr x ~28 GWP = ~2,450 tCO2e/yr, so ~10-25k credits over the crediting period, worth ~$150k-750k at $15-30. Against a ~$100k plug that is roughly 1.5-7x gross. ACR itself estimates that less than 10% of orphaned wells pay for themselves on credits alone. The step-up is ~2-7x, not 10^3-10^4, and nearly all wells are underwater.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: the 2014 Kang et al. PNAS study found 3 of 19 PA wells were high emitters (~15%), and the 2016 study of 88 wells found a 'small proportion' of high emitters dominate emissions. ACR's primer says high emitters dominate, and ACR says <10% of wells self-fund. Most unplugged wells emit only 10-30 g/hr (Colorado study average 586 g/hr; one super-emitter at 76 kg/hr). So the base hit rate is ~5-15%, which caps the ML lever at ~7-20x on measurement cost. But each proving attempt costs only ~$500-2k. ML would save roughly $5-15k of measurement per hit, against a $100k plug per hit, which is under 10% of rung capex. Aerial and satellite methane surveys (Carbon Mapper, Bridger, MethaneSAT-class) and the 2016 Kang predictors (unplugged gas wells, coal areas) already do the screening cheaply. The lever is real but immaterial.
scored.data: The data is public and illegible: scanned state well files (PA DEP, OCC, TX RRC, WV DEP) plus USGS/EPA orphan inventories. But the outcome (emission rate) is a cheap direct physical measurement and is increasingly written into legible public fields. IIJA orphan-well grants ($4.7B federal programme) require states to measure and report methane on wells they plug, and remote sensing finds super-emitters without any document mining. So the ML-over-files edge is weak. Fields like well type, plug status and coal-area location already predict high emitters (Kang 2016).
scored.right_bought: Mixed. Orphan wells belong to state programmes, so operatorship is not bought from naive owners; it is a regulatory transfer that needs bonding, and states plug the worst wells with federal money first. Idle wells from marginal operators and bankrupt estates can be taken for ~$0, but the seller is offloading a liability, not mispricing an asset. The 'cheap' price reflects the plugging obligation, not illegibility. Competitors already aggregate inventories: Zefiro Methane (public, an inventory of 900 priority wells, first ACR issuance of 92,956 t, pre-sale to Mercuria), Rebellion Energy Solutions (first ACR issuance), CarbonPath, ZeroSix, WDF. ~5M ACR orphan-well credits have been issued since 2023.
scored.buyer: Voluntary-market corporate buyers and commodity traders such as Mercuria (Zefiro pre-sale) pay ~$7-30/t, with prices not public and widely dispersed (QCI, Aegis). State orphan programmes co-fund plugs. The buyer is real but thinly capitalised for this use and price-sensitive. Not a 10^4-paying developer.
scored.ladder: Short. The rungs above are scaled plugging services, methane MRV and perhaps gas capture, which is a small, subsidy-bounded niche (finite well count, credits ~5M to date). There is no path to a trillion-dollar chain; the top of the ladder is a plugging contractor plus carbon developer, which is roughly what Zefiro already is.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step is the business. Inside the rung, plugging ($33k-150k per well) dwarfs proving (~$1k measurement), so discovery is a few percent of the work, not 80%+, and ML cuts the trivial part. The step-up on a hit is only ~2-7x, credits are $7-30 with <10% of wells self-funding, and super-emitters are already found cheaply by direct measurement and remote sensing.
scored.one_line_reason: This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode: the hard and expensive part is the physical plug, not finding the leaky well, and a hit yields only ~2-7x in a thin, subsidy-dependent credit market that Zefiro and others already serve. It is also oil/gas-adjacent.

scored.name: Listed-Species Bank Sites (eDNA-proven conservation bank land)
scored.one_line: Options cheap grazing and fallow parcels in species-bank service areas; ML over scanned survey notes, CEQA appendices, museum records and old aerials predicts unrecorded listed-species presence; a cheap eDNA or protocol survey proves it, enabling a USFWS/CDFW conservation bank whose credits sell to infrastructure developers. Close to the previously weak wetland-banking idea.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase options on low-value agricultural parcels (~$3-10k/acre) with no recorded listed-species occupancy
scored.proving_step: eDNA sample or protocol survey (~$1-5k); most negative; positive supports a bank enabling instrument
scored.proven_buyer: Highway, rail, solar and housing developers needing take-permit credits (Caltrans, high-speed rail, utility solar)
scored.public_data: CNDDB, USFWS RIBITS ledgers, scanned county biological surveys in CEQA/EIR appendices, GBIF/VertNet, historical USDA aerials
scored.rough_step_up: ~$5-10k/acre land to $50-300k per credit-acre, ~10-50x; entitlement takes 1-3 years so price is not immediate
scored.frame: The sellable rung would be "species-proven parcel under option", but no capitalised buyer pays for that by itself. Developers buy approved bank credits, not occupancy data. So the real rung is the full bank: buy the land, then get the banking agreement, the conservation easement, a management plan and an endowment. Fox's survey of bank sponsors found 2.18 years on average to a signed agreement (range 8 months to 6 years), and 67% named that bureaucracy as their biggest challenge. Endowments ran $81k (a Utah case) to about $1M (a planned Montana bank). On my own estimate, discovery is about 5-15% of the work in that rung, and entitlement, land capital and long-term management are the rest. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern again: the bespoke part is harder than the finding.
scored.step_up: Unproven: farmland at about $3-10k/acre (the candidate's figure; I did not verify it). Proven: credit prices of $1,505-$205,055 per credit across 137 US banks (2015 dollars, Auburn dissertation and Springer 2019), or $3k-$125k per acre (Fox and Nino-Murcia). One 2023 Swainson's hawk sale worked out to about $40k per credit (my arithmetic: $54k for 1.35 credits). Credits are often issued 1 credit per acre. Gross step-up is about 3-30x, but it is not immediate. It comes only after 1-6 years of entitlement plus the endowment, and only when credits actually sell. Through 2015 about 71k of 520k generated credits had sold, roughly 14% (my arithmetic), and 12% of banks had no transactions at all. Realised step-up is maybe 2-5x (my estimate).
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap and accurate. eDNA for California tiger salamander detected the species in 0.96 of samples (WSU thesis), and a sample or protocol survey costs about $1-5k (the candidate's estimate; I found no published price). Base hit rates on well-chosen grassland or vernal-pool parcels inside a species' range are plausibly 20-50% (my estimate), which caps the ML lever at about 2-5x. More importantly, a survey costing $1-5k is noise next to roughly $1M+ in land, endowment and entitlement per bank. Raising the hit rate cuts almost none of the real capex. Also, credits are often granted for suitable habitat inside a service area, not only for proven occupancy.
scored.data: The outcome is partly in legible public sources already. CNDDB records occurrences, RIBITS and the CDFW list of approved banks show where banks exist and what credits they have left, and habitat-suitability models and HCP maps define the service areas. The scanned survey notes in CEQA/EIR appendices are genuinely hard to read and could add some unrecorded occurrences. But incumbent bank sponsors (RES, Westervelt, Wildlands) employ in-house biologists, and RES already benchmarks eDNA against seining for tiger salamander and red-legged frog. The advantage over them is thin.
scored.right_bought: Yes in principle: options on private farmland can be bought from owners. The catch is adverse selection. Owners generally know that a listed species on their land cuts its development value, and many already carry CNDDB records or past surveys. Optioning at farmland prices is possible, but there is no hidden-deposit discount comparable to a mineral claim.
scored.buyer: Capitalised permittees exist (Caltrans, California High-Speed Rail, utility-scale solar, housing developers). But they buy approved bank credits, and only inside one bank's service area for one species. Demand is limited by local permitting volume: many banks have sold out (Sand Creek, North Suisun, Grasslands) while others go years without a sale (Fitzgerald Ranch's last recorded sale was 2010). Credits are not a liquid market where whatever you prove gets sold.
scored.ladder: Short ladder: species bank, then a mitigation-banking company at the scale of Westervelt or RES, then perhaps advance-mitigation contracts with state agencies. It caps out at a multi-hundred-million-dollar niche tied to regulatory demand. There is no path to a whole value chain worth trillions.
scored.fatal_flaw: The thing ML improves, finding the species, is not the bottleneck. The proving step is a $1-5k eDNA test that is already 96% sensitive. The value is set by 1-6 years of entitlement, roughly $0.1-1M of endowment and land capital, and buyer demand within one service area that is already thin (only about 14% of generated credits had sold through 2015). So discovery is a small share of the rung, and a higher hit rate saves almost no capex.
scored.one_line_reason: The wetland-bank problem again: finding the species is cheap and is not what limits value. Entitlement, endowment and thin service-area demand dominate the rung, so the ML lever and the step-up are both small and slow.

scored.name: Recert Switchgear (certified-reconditioned obsolete breakers)
scored.one_line: Buys obsolete LV/MV breakers and switchgear from scrappers and demolitions at scrap weight, uses ML to match them to installed bases with no OEM replacement, recertifies under NETA/PEARL, and sells into the switchgear shortage.
scored.unproven_right: Title to scrap-grade legacy breakers (GE AK, Westinghouse DB, ITE K-line) at ~$0.50/lb
scored.proving_step: NETA/PEARL reconditioning, primary-injection and dielectric testing ($500-3,000 per unit); ML over scanned catalogues, FERC Form 1, rate cases and demolition permits predicts passing units with unmet demand
scored.proven_buyer: Utilities, hyperscale/colo data center builders, industrial plants facing 2-4 year lead times, paying $10-80k per breaker
scored.public_data: Scanned GE/Westinghouse/Square D catalogues, FERC Form 1, PUC rate cases, demolition permits, GovDeals
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x per unit ($300 scrap to $10-40k certified). Ladder: recertifier, retrofit kits, switchgear OEM
scored.frame: The rung is a reconditioned-breaker reseller: buy used legacy breakers, recondition them, sell them certified. Discovery inside this rung is about 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The real work is physical: teardown, replacing parts, retrofitting trip units, primary-injection testing, NETA/PEARL paperwork, warranty and logistics. Knowing which breaker models are in demand is already common trade knowledge. Dealers list stock by exact model (Westinghouse DB-25/50/75, GE AK-2A-25, ITE K-600), and buyers search by model number. This is the geothermal counter-example again: the physical step is the business, not a trivial one.
scored.step_up: The $0.50/lb starting point is false: owners already sell these units to surplus dealers at well above scrap. Used and rebuilt prices: a 600A DB-25 with 125VDC control is listed at $2,500 and the same frame at $9,210 (Surplus Record). A rebuilt DB-50 1600A is $3,320 and a rebuilt ITE K-600 is $2,850 (eBay). A new or new-surplus GE AK-2A-25 600A EO/DO is $7,920 (IPS store). The real step from used-as-is (my estimate: $500-2,500 dealer buy price) to certified ($3-10k) is about 2-6x. The candidate's $10-40k figure applies only to rare large frames or urgent outage buys. The 10-100x story holds only if you could buy at true scrap weight, and the existing dealers make that rare.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost is $500-3,000 per unit for reconditioning and testing (the candidate's figure; it matches typical NETA shop rates, my estimate). The base hit rate is high, not low: most complete legacy air breakers can be reconditioned with parts. My estimate is a 70-90% pass rate on mechanically complete units, with failures caught by inspection before money is spent. The lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, about 1.1-1.4x, nowhere near 10x. Demand matching also needs no ML: dealers already know which frames sell.
scored.data: The proposed data (scanned catalogues, FERC Form 1, rate cases, demolition permits) is public, but the outcome is already summarised legibly. Model numbers, ampere frames and interrupting ratings are printed on nameplates and in dealer listings. Surplus Record, eBay and the IPS and BCS stores publish asking prices by model. Installed-base demand shows up directly as buyers searching for a part number. ML over FERC Form 1 and rate cases would at best estimate how many legacy units are installed, which helps marketing but does not uncover hidden value. No illegibility edge.
scored.right_bought: Units can be bought, but not cheaply from sellers who don't know the value. Demolition contractors and plant owners already sell to established surplus and reconditioning dealers, who pay well above scrap for complete drawout breakers. Scrap yards that do get breakers usually flip complete units to those dealers. Some mispricing exists at GovDeals-style auctions and small demolitions, but it is thin and other buyers bid on it.
scored.buyer: Utilities, industrial plants, data centers and colos, mostly as emergency replacements for installed legacy gear. New switchgear lead times are 44-84+ weeks, and data-center-spec MV gear takes 2-3 years at peak. That demand is real, but new data center builds buy new gear; legacy reconditioned breakers mainly serve existing installed bases. Incumbents serving this already: OEM service arms (GE Vernova, Eaton, Siemens and ABB all sell recon and roll-in retrofill kits), IPS, BCS Switchgear, Circuit Breaker Sales/CBS, Southern States Toyota-style regional shops, and many NETA-accredited testing firms.
scored.ladder: Recertifier, then retrofill/roll-in kits, then new switchgear OEM. The ladder exists, but each rung is a crowded manufacturing business that the OEMs already own (OEMs sell retrofill kits for their own legacy lines). Winning recon gives some installed-base data and customer relationships, but no protected path to an OEM-scale company. Recon is a fragmented services market, plausibly a few hundred million to low single-digit billions of dollars (my estimate).
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no hidden value to discover. A liquid, mature surplus market with posted prices for each exact model already prices these breakers well above scrap, and most units pass reconditioning. The step-up is only about 2-6x, ML has under 1.5x of hit-rate lever, and the physical reconditioning, not discovery, is the bulk of the work.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a crowded, physical-labour resale business: posted model-level prices, high pass rates and OEM and dealer incumbents leave no illegible signal, no low hit rate to improve, and no 10^3+ step-up.
sources: https://bcsswitchgear.com/?p=113052 (reconditioned GE AK-2A-25, PEARL/NETA, 1-yr warranty; incumbent)
https://surplusrecord.com/m/westinghouse-db-75 (liquid used market, multiple sellers, 10 units available)
https://www.marketsandmarkets.com/Market-Reports/data-center-switchgear-market-18764388.html (MV switchgear 2-3 yr lead times at peak)

scored.name: FEMA LOMA on Mis-mapped Flood Lots (Floodway Out / Uplandco)
scored.one_line: Buys vacant lots and teardowns mapped in FEMA SFHAs or floodways and priced as unbuildable, uses ML comparing 1m 3DEP LiDAR to BFE profiles on scanned FIRM/FIS panels to find ground above BFE, gets an elevation certificate and FEMA LOMA/LOMR-F, and sells buildable lots or mandate-free homes.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to flood-mapped lots at ~$500-5k from absentee or tax-delinquent owners, ideally floodway acreage near zero
scored.proving_step: Elevation certificate (~$500-1,500) plus LOMA (no FEMA fee), decided within ~90 days; binding on lenders
scored.proven_buyer: Regional homebuilders and lot aggregators (Lennar/DR Horton land arms), infill developers, any mortgage-backed home buyer
scored.public_data: USGS 3DEP LiDAR, FEMA NFHL, scanned historical FIRM/FIS PDFs, FEMA LOMC issued-letter archive (labels), county parcel and tax-delinquency rolls
scored.rough_step_up: ~3-30x per lot, ~20-100x on floodway acreage; many LOMAs are approved and 3DEP makes the check easy, so the hit-rate lever and data edge are modest; outside floodway the gain is mostly an insurance discount
scored.frame: The rung is buying a flood-mapped lot, getting the LOMA, and reselling the lot as buildable. Inside that rung, discovery (finding ground above the BFE) is maybe 50-70% of the work (my estimate). The physical step is cheap and abstracted: an elevation certificate for about $500-1,500 and no FEMA fee (Boulder and Venice, FL guidance). The rest is buying land from scattered owners, clearing title and selling into local lot markets. Buyers exist (builders, infill developers), but builders buy entitled, serviced lots in volume, not scattered $5k parcels. For floodway acreage, the true value unlock, the proving step is not a LOMA. FEMA's LiDAR-LOMA guidance excludes floodway buildings, and removing a floodway needs a hydraulic-model LOMR plus community concurrence. That costs tens of thousands of dollars (my estimate), so the step is no longer trivial.
scored.step_up: Outside the floodway, the market discount for being inside the SFHA is small. Studies find about 17% for vacant land (La Plata), muted SFHA discounts nationally, and even a roughly 2% premium inland in a Texas regression-discontinuity study. So a hit on non-floodway land is worth about 1.05-1.3x, mostly the avoided insurance mandate. The candidate's own 3-30x is generous. Lots priced at $500-5k are usually cheap for other reasons (no access, too small, rural, tax-delinquent), and a LOMA does not fix those. Floodway or truly unbuildable land could go 20-100x, but that requires a LOMR, not a LOMA (my estimate, no transaction data found). Typical outcome: below 3x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published FEMA LOMA approval rate. Practitioners report that near-edge properties 'the vast majority of the time' sit above the BFE and qualify (rpls.com forum, anecdotal). LiDAR screening already filters well, using West Virginia's rule to look further when the BFE-to-LAG gap is 2 ft or more. So the base hit rate for screened candidates is high, perhaps 50%+ (my estimate), which caps the ML lever at about 2x. Each attempt costs about $500-1,500 for the elevation certificate plus a $0 FEMA review, so capex is already small and a 10x cut buys little. An Esri abstract notes most LOMA submissions need extra data, which is friction, not a low hit rate.
scored.data: The signal is largely legible already. NFHL polygons and BFEs are digital, 3DEP 1 m LiDAR is a free raster, and comparing them is a GIS overlay, not illegible-data extraction. FEMA Region V, Minnesota DNR (abbreviated LiDAR LOMA) and the WV Flood Tool already publish free LiDAR-for-LOMA tools and guides. Dewberry ran a 'LiDAR for LOMAs' pilot for FEMA. FEMA's LOMC archive records the outcome of every past case. Scanned historical FIS profiles are the one illegible piece, but the effective BFE is what lenders use, and it is mostly digital.
scored.right_bought: Fee title can be bought, and some absentee or tax-delinquent owners are cheap. But any owner can get the same LOMA for about $1k and no FEMA fee, and the free state tools make that easy to check. Sellers' information gap is small, and the price discount you could capture is small (about 0-17%).
scored.buyer: Infill developers, small builders and owner-occupiers with mortgages. Large builders (Lennar, DR Horton land arms) want entitled, serviced subdivisions in volume and do not buy scattered single lots. The buyer's own payoff from a non-floodway lot is mainly lower insurance (Preferred Risk can cut premiums up to 90%), which is worth thousands, not orders of magnitude.
scored.ladder: The ladder is lot entitlement, then spec homebuilding, then floodplain-aware land development. That is a real but fragmented, low-margin path, and nothing makes the LOMA rung a moat for it. Map updates can also supersede a LOMC (Maine template letter), which erodes the asset.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no real step-up. Outside the floodway, SFHA status cuts land value only about 0-17%, so a LOMA hit gives roughly 1.1-1.3x. Where the step-up is large (floodway or unbuildable land), a LOMA cannot do it: FEMA's LiDAR guidance excludes floodways, so it needs a costly hydraulic LOMR with community concurrence. Meanwhile the LiDAR-vs-BFE check is already a free, legible overlay that FEMA and the states publish.
scored.one_line_reason: The proving step is cheap and usually succeeds, but it unlocks roughly a 1.1-1.3x value change. The data is already legible (NFHL plus 3DEP plus free state LiDAR-LOMA tools), and owners can do it themselves for about $1k. That leaves no 10^3-10^4 jump and no hit-rate lever.

scored.name: Clean Corner (stigmatised former-gas-station parcels to state NFA)
scored.one_line: Buys tax-foreclosed or abandoned corner parcels avoided for a suspected REC (old gas station, dry cleaner on Sanborn maps) with no confirmed release, uses ML to pick likely-clean sites, runs a Phase II, gets a state NFA letter, and sells to retail/QSR developers.
scored.unproven_right: Tax-deed or land-bank parcels at ~$1-20k vs $150-500k clean value
scored.proving_step: ASTM E1903 Phase II (~$8-25k) plus state voluntary-cleanup NFA
scored.proven_buyer: QSR, convenience-retail, net-lease and municipal redevelopment buyers
scored.public_data: Library of Congress/ProQuest Sanborn maps, city directories, scanned state UST/LUST files, EPA ECHO, historical aerials, tax-foreclosure lists
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x; risk: LUST status fields often already record releases, and powered brownfields was killed for cleanup costs exceeding uplift; only works if ML screens to no-release sites
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a stigmatised corner parcel, run a Phase II, get a state NFA letter, and resell. Discovery (picking the site) is perhaps 30-50% of the work and value in that rung (my estimate). The rest is physical and legal: tax-deed title clearing (quiet title), removing or closing in place any abandoned USTs, demolishing canopies and buildings, and the state VCP process. In the Ozaukee WI case the assessor valued removing the building, tanks and canopies at a ~$350k drop in assessed value ($748k to $401k), which shows how much physical work sits inside the rung. QSR and net-lease buyers do exist and have capital. But the physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted. When the site turns out dirty, the job becomes remediation, which is exactly the powered-brownfields failure.
scored.step_up: The pitch claims ~$1-20k going to $150-500k (10-100x). Real cases are more modest. A Clarion County PA former truck stop had a $1,300 minimum bid but sold for $60k, so auctions bid stigma parcels up. Lake County OH: assessed at $39,860 with ~$55k of back taxes, and the land bank called it cost-prohibitive. Ozaukee WI: bought at a sheriff's sale for $760k against a $1.09M assessment, later resold for $365k. Retail Petroleum Consultants found the market applies no material discount where a major oil company indemnifies the site, and that is the case for most former branded stations. My estimate is a realistic 2-5x on all-in cost (purchase + back taxes + Phase II + tank closure + title). That is not 10^3-10^4. Most tax-foreclosed parcels are in weak markets, where a clean value is well below $150k.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published aggregate rate of former-station Phase IIs that come back clean. EPA says ~half of 450k US brownfields are petroleum-impacted, mostly by old gas-station USTs. My estimate: among stations with no recorded release, 40-60% would pass a Phase II, so ML can raise the hit rate at most ~2x (the lever is capped at 1/base rate, about 2). A Phase II costs ~$8-25k (the candidate's figure, consistent with industry ranges), which is cheap next to the parcel, so cutting discovery capex 10x does not matter. The real cost of a miss is the remediation tail (often six figures, per Inside Self Storage) plus liability. A cheap test with a modest failure rate is the opposite of the Terranox profile.
scored.data: Sanborn maps and city directories are public and partly illegible (scanned), and EDR/ERIS already extract them commercially for every Phase I. That is an incumbent dataset, not an unread one. The outcome is largely already in a legible field. State LUST databases and EPA UST performance measures (from memory, not looked up: ~570k cumulative confirmed releases nationally) list confirmed releases and closures by facility. UST registration lists record tank status. Unregistered pre-1980s tanks are the only truly illegible part. The right is bought: tax-deed and land-bank sales are cheap. But auctions are competitive and bid parcels up (Clarion $1,300 to $60k). Land banks often pair parcels with state brownfield grants, which erodes the information edge.
scored.right_bought: Bought at tax-deed or sheriff auctions or from land banks. Nominal minimum bids run ~$1-2k, but clearing prices are much higher in decent markets ($60k Clarion PA; $760k Ozaukee WI). The parcel often carries back taxes ($55k Lake County OH) and a weak, quiet-title-needed tax deed.
scored.buyer: QSR chains, convenience-retail operators, net-lease developers and municipal redevelopment authorities. All are capitalised and do buy NFA'd corners. Some redevelopers (e.g. Weston) already buy, clean and redevelop such sites.
scored.ladder: Above this rung: ground-up QSR or net-lease development, then a portfolio of net-lease assets. That is ordinary real estate development: fragmented and capped, with no proprietary step that compounds and no trillion-dollar chain. It leads to a mid-size infill developer or REIT at best.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is cheap, and failure is common but not dominant (~50% clean, estimated). So there is no high-cost, low-hit-rate search for ML to collapse. Release outcomes are already recorded in legible state LUST and UST status fields. And the value of a hit is eaten by physical work (tank closure, demolition, title clearing) and by competitive auction pricing. The result is a 2-5x real-estate flip, not a 10^4 discovery jump. It is powered brownfields again with a different data source.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a low-multiple, physically heavy real-estate flip. The Phase II is cheap with an estimated ~50% pass rate, the release outcome is already in state LUST fields, and auctions and oil-company indemnities erase most of the stigma discount.

scored.name: Parcellaire (Champagne AOC delimitation arbitrage)
scored.one_line: Buys arable or non-AOC vineyard plots in the ~40 candidate communes for the Champagne zone revision, using ML over scanned INAO delimitation files, BRGM geology, cadastre, slope and aspect to predict which parcels the expert commission will include; inclusion reprices them for Champagne houses.
scored.unproven_right: Freehold land at ~EUR 5-15k/ha from farmers who cannot read INAO parcel criteria
scored.proving_step: INAO expert-commission parcel delimitation; a third-party decision, political and slow (8+ years since 2008), effectively one big event not many shots
scored.proven_buyer: Champagne houses and co-ops (LVMH/Moet, Pernod Mumm, Laurent-Perrier, Centre Vinicole), SAFER-mediated buyers
scored.public_data: INAO/CNAOV commune lists and expert reports, 1927 delimitation scanned annexes, BRGM BD Charm-50, DVF land prices, PCI parcels, IGN RGE ALTI
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-200x (EUR 5k/ha to EUR 1M+/ha); lever ~3-5x and a single decision cycle
scored.frame: The rung is buying land in candidate communes and having it classified as Champagne AOC. Choosing parcels is maybe 30-50% of the work. The rest is out of the company's hands: an INAO decision that is political, collective and slow, and still no final ruling since 2005/2008. After that comes planting, which needs planting authorisations the Champagne trade rations, plus 3-4 years before the vines produce. The physical and regulatory steps are not trivial or abstracted, so discovery does not reach the 80% the rubric requires. The buyers (Champagne houses, co-ops) do have capital.
scored.step_up: Proven: Champagne AOC vineyard averages about EUR 1.13M/ha (FNSafer 2025; Marne about EUR 1.18M/ha in 2023). That figure is for planted, producing land. Bare land that is classified but unplanted would sell for less (my estimate: well below EUR 1M/ha, because planting rights are rationed). Unproven: ordinary farmland in the area is about EUR 10k/ha, but land in the candidate communes has already traded at about EUR 70k/ha on speculation (Reussir, Laines-aux-Bois, Aube). Buying today at a marked-up price, the realistic step-up is about 10-15x (EUR 70k to roughly EUR 0.7-1M). From true farmland prices it would be about 100x, but the market has already priced that in.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no repeatable proving attempt. The process is one INAO decision for the whole region, covering a 2008 list of 40 communes added and 2 removed. The company cannot buy more shots, and the base rate for a parcel inside a candidate commune is not published (my estimate: a fairly high share, since commissions include most suitable slopes). Each attempt costs nothing extra to "drill", but holding land costs time: the process has run 18+ years. In February 2025 the SGV (the growers' union) asked INAO to suspend the parcel delimitation work, and Meininger reports no new boundaries are likely this decade. ML can at best rank parcels within an already public list of communes. It does not cut the cost of discovery 10x.
scored.data: The 2008 commune list is public and has been widely reported, which is the legible summary of most of the answer. The parcel criteria and the 1927 annexes exist only as scans, and BRGM, IGN and cadastre data are public, so some parcel-level information is illegible. However, the delimitation experts work in the open: there are public inquiries and a final list of parcels is published.
scored.right_bought: Freehold land is technically buyable, but SAFER can pre-empt sales and ask a court to revise the price to curb speculation. Local growers and the SGV are actively fighting speculation (there was a framework agreement at Viteff). Sellers in candidate communes already know about the revision, which is why prices sit at about EUR 70k/ha versus EUR 10k/ha for farmland. The company cannot buy cheaply from owners who cannot read the data, because the owners already know.
scored.buyer: LVMH/Moet, Pernod/Mumm, Laurent-Perrier and co-ops such as Centre Vinicole would pay. However, the growers' unions control whether the expansion happens and are hostile to outsiders capturing the gain. Planting rights after classification are rationed by the trade.
scored.ladder: The ladder is modest: plant the vines, sell grapes to the Champagne houses (about EUR 8/kg, 10-12t/ha), then possibly a négociant brand. The prize is capped at roughly a few thousand hectares of new area (my estimate: EUR 2-5B of land value at most). This is a single appellation with no repeatable second region, so there is no trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a single, political, indefinitely stalled regulatory event the company cannot repeat or speed up: no decision in 18+ years, the growers' union asked to suspend the work in February 2025, and no new boundaries are expected this decade. On top of that, candidate-commune land is already priced at about 7x farmland, SAFER can block speculative purchases, and planting rights are rationed. There are no repeated shots for ML to improve.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a bet on one stalled, politically controlled regulatory decision that is already public knowledge. Land in the candidate communes already trades at about EUR 70k/ha against EUR 10k/ha for farmland. ML gets no repeated shots and almost no information edge, and the frame lacks the 80% discovery and trivial physical step the rubric requires.

scored.name: Gesha Hunter (specialty-coffee microlot discovery to auction)
scored.one_line: Buys or long-leases small high-altitude farms or microlot options in Panama, Colombia, Ethiopia and Yunnan, using ML to pick farms likely to score 90+ in Cup of Excellence or Best of Panama; the jury score sets the auction price the same week.
scored.unproven_right: Farm freehold or exclusive multi-year microlot options at commodity-coffee land values from smallholders who never enter competitions
scored.proving_step: Q-grader or CoE/Best of Panama jury cupping score ($100-500 per entry); most lots score 84-87
scored.proven_buyer: Specialty roasters and auction buyers (Julith Dubai, JD.com, Japanese and Korean roasters, Starbucks Reserve); Best of Panama 2025 washed Gesha sold at $30,204/kg
scored.public_data: Decades of CoE and Best of Panama results PDFs, WorldClim/CHELSA, SoilGrids, SRTM, Colombian FNC SICA registry, ECX washing-station records
scored.rough_step_up: Per kg $5-8 to $100-30,000, 20x to ~4000x; land re-rates ~10-50x with a proven score history
scored.frame: The rung is to own or option a farm and get a competition score. Inside that rung, discovery (picking the land) is perhaps 20-30% of the work, which is my estimate. A 90+ score is mostly made, not found. You need the right variety (Gesha takes 3-4 years to first harvest), careful picking, fermentation and drying, and producer skill. Hacienda La Esmeralda and the Lamastus family win again and again because of what they do, not because of where they are. The physical step (growing and processing) is the hard, bespoke part, which is the same shape as the geothermal counter-example. There is a capitalised buyer (Julith, JD.com, Asian roasters), but they buy coffee, and only in lots of about 20 kg.
scored.step_up: Per kg, the jump is real but applies to tiny volumes. Commodity green coffee is about $5-8/kg. The Best of Panama 2025 average was $2,861/kg, and the top washed Geisha (GW-01, Esmeralda, 98 points) sold for $30,204/kg, but for only 20 kg ($604k in total). The whole auction made about $2.8M. Land does not show a 10^3 step-up. In Boquete, asking prices are about $47-50k/ha for unproven highland land (341 ha La Esperanza, Palmira 20 ha). Established Geisha farms ask about $200-320k/ha (encuentra24 listings). That is about 4-6x, and much of it is the value of planted trees and infrastructure rather than proof. So land re-rates 3-10x, not 10^4x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap and is not the bottleneck. Under CoE rules the first sample entered is free. Entries run about 300-1,848 per country (Ethiopia set a record of 1,848), and at most 30 win. That is a base win rate of about 2-10% (my calculation), so the lever is capped at roughly 10-50x in theory. But each extra shot costs a cheap sample, not a $1M drill hole. What costs money is 3-5 years of planting and processing per farm before you can enter at all. ML cannot cut that cost, and it cannot cut the score variance that comes from processing.
scored.data: The outcome is already summarised in legible public fields. CoE and Best of Panama publish every winning farm, producer, score, price and buyer, and the tables are easy to scrape. The terroir inputs (WorldClim, SoilGrids, SRTM, altitude) are clean global rasters, not illegible scans. The one missing piece is entries that lost: CoE does not publish full scores for every entry, but that gap is thin. Incumbents already read the signal: the famous Boquete microclimates (Jaramillo, Cañas Verdes) are priced in, and Gesha seed and know-how have spread. Buying the right: Colombian smallholder land can be bought. Ethiopian land is state-owned and cannot be freehold, so you would need contracts with a washing station. Yunnan land use is collective and leased. Smallholders do not hold a hidden asset that ML can see and they cannot.
scored.right_bought: Freehold farmland ($47-50k/ha for unproven Panama highland land, my figure from listings; cheaper in Colombia), long leases, or microlot purchase options from smallholders. Freehold is not possible in Ethiopia or, in practice, in Yunnan.
scored.buyer: Specialty roasters and auction buyers: Julith Coffee Dubai (GW-01, $30,204/kg), JD.com (natural Geisha, $23,608/kg), and Japanese, Korean and Taiwanese roasters. The pool of buyers is deep, but total spend at the top is small, about $2.8M a year for all of Best of Panama.
scored.ladder: The rungs go farm, then processing (wet mill), then exporter or importer, then roaster or brand, then retail. A specialty-coffee roll-up is possible, but the whole specialty green market is worth billions, not trillions, and lots above 90 points are a niche worth tens of millions of dollars a year. Nobody has climbed this ladder to a very large company (Ninety Plus Gesha Estates and Esmeralda stayed boutique).
scored.fatal_flaw: The score is made by years of cultivation and processing, not found by picking land. That makes the physical step most of the work, like the geothermal counter-example. The outcome and terroir are already public and priced into the land (about $50k/ha unproven against about $250k/ha established Geisha farms, only about 5x). The 10^3 per-kg price applies to 20 kg lots, so the auction pool is only about $2.8M a year.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the frame test: a 90+ cup comes from 3-5 years of farming and processing skill, not from discovery. The proving step is nearly free and is not where the cost sits. Results and terroir are public and legible. Land re-rates about 5x, not 10^4x, and the high per-kg prices apply to tiny volumes.

scored.name: Leptospermum Estates (high-MGO manuka land)
scored.one_line: Buys or leases Leptospermum-covered scrub in NZ/Australia, using ML over satellite imagery, vegetation databases and published DHA nectar surveys to pick high-MGO stands; one season of hives plus MPI manuka testing and UMF/MGO grading reprices honey and land.
scored.unproven_right: Freehold or 10-20 yr apiary-exclusive leases on land valued as low-grade grazing, often from Maori trusts or sheep farmers
scored.proving_step: MPI monofloral manuka test plus UMF/MGO lab grade (~$100-300; nectar DHA pre-screen <$100); most stands grade low
scored.proven_buyer: Comvita, Manuka Health/Egmont, Oha, Capilano/Hive+Wellness paying $50-150+/kg for UMF 15-20+
scored.public_data: NZ LCDB v5, LINZ titles, Landcare and university DHA nectar surveys, MPI science data, NSW/QLD vegetation mapping, Atlas of Living Australia
scored.rough_step_up: Honey ~$5/kg to $50-300/kg (10-60x), land ~5-20x; moderate C2
scored.frame: The rung would be "hold a manuka-access right and prove it with a season of honey plus MPI/UMF grading". Discovery is well under 80% of the work in that rung. Finding manuka is easy: it is visible scrub, mapped in LCDB, and beekeepers have known for decades where high-MGO regions are (East Cape, Northland, Taranaki). Most of the work and cost is the physical step: running hives for a season, which is apiary labour, transport, varroa control and theft risk, and supplying sugar if the flow fails. My estimate, not sourced: discovery is about 10-20% of the work and beekeeping is 80%+. That is the geothermal counter-example in miniature. There are capitalised buyers (Comvita, Manuka Health), but they buy graded honey or sign JVs directly with landowners. They do not buy a 'proven stand' as an asset.
scored.step_up: Honey: non-manuka bulk is about NZ$3-6/kg, and one bulk report put it at NZ$3.50-4/kg against a NZ$6-7 break-even (Farmers Weekly; MPI 2020-21). Manuka bulk ran about NZ$12-135/kg in 2017/18 and NZ$8-120/kg in 2020-21, depending on grade (MPI Apiculture Monitoring). So a high grade gives roughly 2-30x on honey. Land: the realisable value is a hive-site rental or profit share. Industry arrangements are per-hive-per-season, per-kg or profit-share (NZFFA 2017; Ngati Hine/Manuka Health). My estimate, unsourced: rental of NZ$10-50 per hive per season on scrub hill country worth about NZ$1-5k/ha, which gives a land uplift of perhaps 1.2-3x, not 10^3. On a hit, the right goes up about 3-30x, nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The lab proving step is cheap: about NZ$100-300 per MPI/UMF test, and the DHA nectar pre-screen is under $100 (candidate's figures, consistent with commercial labs such as Analytica). The real proving cost is one season of hives, which I estimate at NZ$300-800 per hive per year (not sourced). For base hit rate, the only figure I found is a 2017 industry claim that up to 20% of manuka honey failed the MPI monofloral test, and one MPI submission said over 50% of drums previously labelled manuka failed (MPI dmsdocument submissions, 2017; ODT). Even if the base hit rate on reaching high UMF (15+) is low, say 10-30% (my estimate), the lever is capped at 3-10x. It applies to a cost that is mostly fixed beekeeping opex, which better site selection does not remove. Also, the cheap DHA nectar pre-screen already does most of the de-risking without ML.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible, and the outcome is largely known already. Manuka cover is in LCDB v5 as a legible class (manuka/kanuka scrub). Landcare Research and university DHA nectar surveys are published and already used by the industry. Regional MGO potential is common knowledge among about 9,000 registered beekeeping enterprises and 900k hives (MPI 2018/19). Hive-site competition was intense enough during the 'manuka gold rush' to cause hive theft and site wars. There is no large scanned, illegible corpus that incumbents fail to read. On the right itself: it is bought or leased, which is good, but owners are not unable to read it. Maori trusts already strike JVs and profit shares with Comvita and Manuka Health. The Miere Coalition is pushing landowners to capture more value, and DOC has a formal hive-placement fee schedule. The landowners know what manuka is worth.
scored.right_bought: Freehold scrub or hive-site leases (per-hive-per-season, per-kg or profit-share) from sheep farmers and Maori trusts. These are bought rather than first-come, but the market is informed and competitive.
