Iwi increasingly demand profit share or vertical participation instead of rental (Miere Coalition; Ngati Hine/Manuka Health JV; Comvita–Ngati Porou JV).
scored.buyer: Comvita, Manuka Health (Egmont/PE-owned), Oha Honey, Hive+Wellness/Capilano. They buy graded bulk honey at NZ$8-135/kg by grade. They do not pay for a proven stand as an asset, and they already originate land directly through iwi JVs. The bulk market has been oversupplied since about 2019-21 (Spinoff 'honey glut'), so the buyers have pricing power.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above: site, then hives, then extraction and grading, then brand and export. That is real vertical integration, but the whole NZ honey export industry is about NZ$400-600M a year, and Comvita, the largest player, is a sub-NZ$1B company that has struggled. The ceiling is a mid-sized consumer-goods business, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the hard part, and the asset does not reprice. Manuka stands are visible, mapped (LCDB) and already surveyed for DHA, and the incumbents and iwi know their value. The value is captured by doing a season of physical beekeeping, which is most of the work, in an oversupplied, price-sensitive bulk market. That gives a step-up of only about 3-30x on honey and about 1-3x on land, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.one_line_reason: Not a Terranox-shaped rung. Finding manuka is easy and already legible. The value comes from running hives, which is physical, opex-heavy work in a glutted market. A hit gives about 3-30x rather than 10^4x, and landowners and incumbents already price the right.

scored.name: Heirloom Cacao (rediscovering fine-flavor genetics)
scored.one_line: Buys or options old Amazonian/Mesoamerican cacao stands ML flags as likely pure Nacional, Criollo or rare genotypes from herbarium, hacienda archive and genebank data; HCP designation plus genotyping reprices beans and stand.
scored.unproven_right: Smallholder cacao plots or harvest rights at bulk-cacao land value
scored.proving_step: Heirloom Cacao Preservation Fund designation (genetic test plus flavor panel); cheap; few qualify
scored.proven_buyer: Fine-chocolate makers (Valrhona, Felchlin, Guittard, To'ak, Barry Callebaut gourmet)
scored.public_data: USDA-ARS ICGD/ICGT passport data, GBIF Theobroma records, scanned colonial and Jesuit mission archives, HCP reports
scored.rough_step_up: Beans ~5-15x, land ~3-5x; weak C2
scored.frame: The rung is "own a cacao stand and certify it as heirloom". Discovery (finding stands of pure Nacional or Criollo) is maybe 30-40% of the work at most (my estimate). The rest is physical and ongoing: farming, fermentation and drying (which decide the flavor-panel result), traceability against bean mixing (HCP requires certified, unmixed lots), and building relationships with buyers year after year. A designation is not a one-time proving event that a capitalised buyer pays for up front. Buyers pay per harvest for well-processed beans. So the frame fails the 80%+ discovery test, and the physical step is not trivial.
scored.step_up: Beans: ICCO estimates fine-flavor cocoa at $3,500-5,000/t against bulk at $3,000-3,500/t, with top lots around $10,000/t (ConfectioneryNews citing ICCO). The Cocoa Research Centre says fine flavor reaches up to 3-4x bulk at most. That is roughly 1.2-3x, not the 5-15x the candidate claims. HCP's FAQ says only about 50% of designees saw higher price or demand, and it publishes no premium figure. Land: Manabí cacao land is already about $13k/ha (one 14 ha listing at $185k, my calculation, unverified), so the unproven right is not near zero. Heirloom status might add 1.5-3x to land value (my estimate, no transaction data). The step-up is under 3x, far from 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: HCP submission is free, with a $1,000 fee only if the beans are designated, and the HCP itself says total costs can easily exceed $3,000 (hcpcacao.org FAQ). Genotyping with SNP panels costs roughly $20-100 per sample (my estimate). Base hit rate: unknown. HCP made only 13 designations from 2014 to February 2017, which suggests a low rate, but the attempt is so cheap that cutting it 10x saves a few thousand dollars. The lever is capped by a small absolute capex, not by the hit rate.
scored.data: The data is public but mostly legible already. ICGD/ICGT passport data and GBIF Theobroma records are structured databases. The HCP Registry publishes the outcome (designated stands and their locations) as a legible list, which repeats the regulator-status-field problem. Colonial and Jesuit mission archives are truly illegible, but they locate regions, not individual plots. Genetic purity of trees on a given smallholding cannot be inferred from 18th-century documents, because centuries of hybridisation (and CCN-51 replanting) have intervened. The owners are not information-poor here: Ecuadorian and Peruvian farmers and cooperatives know whether they hold old Nacional trees, and they can submit to HCP themselves for free. Sellers capture the step-up, not the buyer.
scored.right_bought: Yes, smallholder plots or harvest offtake can be bought or optioned (Manabí listing at about $185k for 14 ha). But the price is not depressed by information asymmetry. Land is priced on bulk-cacao yields, which are around $300-400/ha/yr income per a Manabí producer survey. In 2024 farmers used windfall cacao prices to buy land, so the land market is active and informed. There is also reputational and legal risk in buying out indigenous or smallholder heirloom stands in Peru and Ecuador, which cuts against the HCP's farmer-benefit mission and the makers' marketing.
scored.buyer: Fine-chocolate makers (Valrhona, Felchlin, Guittard, To'ak, craft bean-to-bar makers). They buy per lot, often under multi-year sourcing relationships. They do not buy land at a step-up, and none of them pays a mine-developer-style lump sum for a proven stand. Fine flavor is about 5-12% of world cocoa production, and heirloom-designated is a tiny slice of that, so buyer depth is thin and prices are volatile (ICCO notes few participants).
scored.ladder: Weak. The next rungs are fermentation and post-harvest processing, then a craft-chocolate brand (To'ak, Fortunato No. 4 / Marañón Chocolate already do this), then distribution. The whole fine-flavor bean market is low single-digit billions (my estimate: about 5-10% of a cocoa bean market in the $15-40B range, swinging with the 2024-26 price spike and collapse). This is a lifestyle or premium-brand path, not a path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no step-up. Proven heirloom beans sell for about 1.2-3x bulk (ICCO), the land is already about $13k/ha rather than near zero, and the proving step is cheap and open to farmers for free. So there is neither a 10^3x jump to capture nor an expensive, mostly failing step for ML to make cheaper.
scored.one_line_reason: Not excluded, but it fails on step-up and lever: about 2x bean premium, land not near zero, $1-3k proving cost, outcome published in the HCP Registry, and an ongoing farming and processing burden rather than one discovery event.

scored.name: PathClear (low-latency microwave path rights)
scored.one_line: Options rooftops, towers and land at geodesic points for record-latency microwave/mmWave routes, proves a clear FCC-coordinated path, and sells the package to trading firms and network operators.
scored.unproven_right: Rooftop/tower/ground lease options at ~$1-5k each from owners unaware they sit on the geodesic
scored.proving_step: FCC Part 101 prior coordination cleared plus LiDAR line-of-sight/Fresnel survey; cheap; most paths fail on obstruction or frequency conflicts
scored.proven_buyer: HFT firms and latency networks (McKay Brothers, Jump-affiliated), possibly GPU-cluster operators
scored.public_data: FCC ULS, FCC ASR, FAA DOF, USGS 3DEP LiDAR
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x on bottleneck sites; tiny market and fairly legible data; weak C4 and C5
scored.frame: Rung = an optioned, coordinated hop site (or chain of sites) on a near-geodesic route, sold to a latency network. Inside that rung, finding the site is maybe 30-40% of the work (my estimate). The rest is negotiating with owners, structural and engineering work, FCC Part 101 coordination, FAA/tower permitting, and often building a new tower ($200k-$1M+ per new tower, estimate). The physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted, and buyers usually want to build the hop themselves. Discovery is well under 80%.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a rooftop/land option at roughly $1-5k (candidate's figure; my estimate agrees). Proven: a normal macro-tower or rooftop lease earns about $1-3k/month (industry norm, recalled). An HFT bottleneck site might earn a premium, maybe $5-20k/month, or a one-off sale of $100k-$1M for a true chokepoint. The precedent is Jump-linked entities buying or proposing masts near the English Channel and in Belgium (recalled from press, numbers not verified). Capitalised over 10 years, that is about $0.3-2M against a $2-5k option, so 10-100x for the rare chokepoint and 3-10x for an ordinary hop. The value only shows up when a buyer picks your exact site, not immediately when the path clears.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap and mostly deterministic. A line-of-sight/Fresnel check on USGS 3DEP LiDAR costs about $0 per path in compute (estimate). A Part 101 prior coordination notice through a frequency coordinator (Comsearch etc.) costs about $1-5k per link (estimate). Paths fail for physical reasons that are computed exactly, not predicted. There is no expensive, low-hit-rate step for ML to improve, so the lever is about 1-2x at most.
scored.data: FCC ULS (every Part 101 link with its coordinates, frequency and licensee), FCC ASR, FAA DOF and 3DEP LiDAR are all public, structured and machine-readable. The outcome is already written into legible fields: existing HFT links and their tower coordinates are listed in ULS. Hobbyists have reverse-engineered every Chicago-NJ HFT network from ULS (the "Sniper in Mahwah" blog, recalled), and the networks track each other's filings. Filing prior coordination publicly reveals your route. The data is legible, the outcome is legible, and the incumbents read it best. Rooftop/land owners can be optioned cheaply, but once an HFT firm approaches, owners near known corridors (the Aurora/CME to Carteret/Mahwah corridor) learn their value quickly.
scored.right_bought: Yes, mechanically. Lease or option rights on rooftops, towers and land can be bought at $1-5k (estimate). But a site has no exclusive geodesic value: there are many near-equivalent sites within the Fresnel and latency tolerance, and buyers can route around you at a cost of microseconds. Spectrum coordination works first-come, so a buyer's own filing can crowd your path out.
scored.buyer: A small set of capitalised buyers: McKay Brothers/Quincy Data, New Line Networks (Jump/Virtu), Vigilant (DRW), Webline/Pierce-type networks, and Anova (laser/mmWave). That is maybe 5-10 buyers worldwide across a handful of routes (Chicago-NJ, London-Frankfurt, a few Asian routes). They already have in-house site-acquisition and RF teams, already hold most of the near-optimal sites, and sit in a mature market where the latency gains are largely spent. GPU-cluster operators do not buy microwave path rights; they buy fiber or build sites.
scored.ladder: Weak. The next rungs are building towers and operating a latency network, and HFT latency is a single-digit-hundreds-of-millions niche with a few incumbents (estimate). The adjacent shift to tower REITs or fixed wireless is a commodity business with no discovery edge. There is no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no illegible-data edge. Every existing route and site is already published in FCC ULS, a structured database that the 5-10 buyers (themselves the incumbents) already mine. Path proving is a cheap, deterministic LiDAR calculation, so ML has no hit rate to improve, and the market is a tiny, saturated niche.
scored.one_line_reason: PathClear fails: the data and outcomes are already legible in FCC ULS, proving is cheap and deterministic so ML has nothing to improve, the step-up is about 10-100x only on rare chokepoints, and a handful of incumbent buyers already own the corridors.
sources: No live searches: the shared web-search budget ran out before the first query ran. All figures are estimates or recalled public reporting.
FCC ULS Part 101 licensing database (public, structured): https://wireless2.fcc.gov/UlsApp/UlsSearch/searchLicense.jsp
Sniper in Mahwah blog, reverse-engineering HFT microwave routes from ULS (recalled): https://sniperinmahwah.wordpress.com/
Press on Jump Trading-linked mast and tower projects near Richborough UK and in Belgium (recalled, numbers unverified)

scored.name: Bifacial/Albedo Solar P90 Arbitrage
scored.one_line: Options cheap marginal land (playas, caliche flats) where bifacial-albedo and low-soiling gains are invisible to satellite P50 tools, proves them with a 12-month albedometer/soiling campaign to IEC 61724, and sells shovel-ready land to solar developers.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase options on low-value desert or marginal agricultural land
scored.proving_step: About $30k ground-measured albedo, GHI and soiling campaign lifting the bankable P90; solar resource is highly legible so base hit rate is high and the ML lever weak
scored.proven_buyer: Utility-scale solar developers and IPPs
scored.public_data: Scanned county soil surveys, NRCS SSURGO, USGS spectral surveys, old BLM range reports
scored.rough_step_up: About 2-5x land value plus a small yield premium, under 10x; honest low scorer
scored.frame: The rung would be: option marginal land, prove its albedo and soiling, sell site control to a solar developer. Discovery is a small share of the work, maybe 10-20% (my estimate). The developer buyer is real and well funded. But the value of a site comes from interconnection, distance to transmission, permitting and offtake, not from albedo. A developer does not pay for land because of a few percent of rear-side gain. So albedo proving is not the main work of any sellable rung. The real hard step is getting an interconnection queue position, which was already rated weak.
scored.step_up: Lease figures for Arizona solar land are about $578-1,156/acre/yr (average $826), plus a signing bonus of $1,239-4,130/acre (smartenergyusa, a vendor page, so indicative only). Old BLM desert range land rents for $16-300/acre/yr (2010 schedule). Desert grazing land turning into solar-leased land is roughly a 3-10x lift. Almost all of that comes from grid proximity, which any developer can already see. The part that albedo proving adds is only a few percent of yield. Bifacial gain is close to linear in albedo: 7.3% at albedo 0.20, 9.6% at 0.295, 15.7% at 0.556 (Soltec BiTEC, via Trina). Desert albedo of 0.29-0.41 against a default modelled value of about 0.25 gives roughly +1-4% energy (estimate). That is a step-up from proving of about 1.01-1.05x, so it scores 1.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is high. Desert ground almost always measures above the default albedo, and the whole solar resource is legible from satellites (NSRDB GHI, MODIS/Sentinel-2 surface albedo). I estimate more than 70% of sites meet the threshold. One proving campaign costs about $30k for 12 months of albedometer and soiling-station data (the candidate's figure; developers pay $30-100k for their own met stations, my estimate). At that hit rate the ML lever is capped near 1/0.7, about 1.4x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is not illegible. Satellite surface albedo (MODIS MCD43, Sentinel-2) and NSRDB irradiance are public and already gridded. SSURGO is already digital. The answer is effectively in a legible field already: PVsyst and SolarAnywhere models take albedo as an input, and incumbent tools such as SolarAnywhere and Solargis sell soiling and albedo estimates. On the right itself, desert or marginal land options can be bought cheaply from ranchers or BLM. But the landowners are not the ones missing the edge. Land agents for developers already option land near substations, and lease prices follow the grid, not albedo.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Purchase or lease options on private desert and marginal ag land are cheap: grazing land near BLM rents of $16-300/acre/yr, and option fees of perhaps $10-50/acre/yr (estimate). But developers' land teams option the same parcels on grid proximity, so the albedo signal buys no information edge at purchase.
scored.buyer: Utility-scale solar developers and IPPs (NextEra, AES, Invenergy, Intersect). They are well funded, but they price land on interconnection, permitting and offtake, and they run their own met campaigns after site control.
scored.ladder: In principle there is a ladder: land, then development (interconnection and permits), then build and own an IPP. But the first rung adds no defensible edge, so it does not lead up the ladder. The rungs above are ordinary competitive solar development.
scored.fatal_flaw: Albedo and soiling proving shifts yield by only about 1-5%, a step-up near 1.05x. The input is already legible from satellite albedo products and used as a standard PVsyst parameter, so there is no illegible signal and no step-up to capture. Land value comes from grid access, which ML on albedo does not reveal.
scored.one_line_reason: Low scorer: proving albedo adds a few percent of yield on an input that is already legible, the hit rate is high so the ML lever is about 1.4x at most, and land value comes from the interconnection, not from proving albedo.

scored.name: Legacy ODS Bank (CFC stockpiles proven by assay for compliance offsets)
scored.one_line: Buys forgotten refrigerant cylinders, chiller charges and pre-1995 CFC foam at scrap prices; ML over scanned permits and HVAC records locates high-purity CFC-11/12; a lab assay proves composition under CAR/ACR ODS protocol and destruction yields ARB compliance offsets.
scored.unproven_right: Title to mixed/unknown refrigerant cylinders and foam salvage rights at ~$0-30/kg
scored.proving_step: ODS lab composition assay (~$200-500 per container); many contaminated, mixed or empty
scored.proven_buyer: California and Washington cap-and-trade compliance entities
scored.public_data: Scanned municipal building permits, EPA SNAP and Section 608 records, ARB offset registry ODS documents, surplus listings
scored.rough_step_up: ~$20-40/kg to ~$150-300/kg in offsets, ~5-10x; weak C2
scored.frame: The rung is ODS offset project development: aggregate CFC, analyze it, destroy it and get offsets issued. A buyer exists, since CA and WA compliance entities buy CCOs. But discovery is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). Most of it is the physical and regulatory chain: buying from Section 608/609-certified holders, aggregating cylinders, chain-of-custody paperwork, the lab analysis the protocol requires (Reserve/ARB Sec 6.4/6.6), transport to an approved destruction plant (e.g. Bowling Green, OH), third-party verification and ARB issuance. Foam is worse: you have to recover the blowing agent, which is a real physical step. The physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted.
scored.step_up: Unproven: recovered R-12 already trades as a refrigerant at about $10-20/lb, or $22-44/kg (NCRS forum 2010; buyback brokers such as Refrigerant Finders publish buyback pricing). Its owners know it has value. Proven: CFC-12 GWP is 10,900, so 1 kg is about 10.9 tCO2e. Non-DEB CCOs were about $12.5-13.7/t in 2025 and DEB about $25/t (ClimeCo digests). That gives roughly $140/kg gross non-DEB and about $270/kg DEB. ODS offsets were $9.70/t in 2014 (Forest Trends). Costs then come off the gross: destruction, transport, lab, verification, a 10-year protocol crediting cap and registry fees, which I estimate at $15-40/kg. The net step-up is about 2-5x, with no order-of-magnitude jump. The assay does not create the value. The value comes from destruction plus issuance months later.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The assay costs about $200-500 per container (the candidate's figure; I found no lab quote). It is not a gamble. It is a mandatory measurement on material whose identity mostly comes from the label, the source equipment (e.g. a 1970s-90s auto or chiller nameplate) and pressure-temperature checks. I estimate base hit rate is high, 60-90% of labelled cylinders being eligible ODS. Failures (mixed, contaminated or empty) mostly cut the eligible mass rather than zeroing it: the Reserve protocol scales out residue (1,000 lb at 5% HBR gives 902.5 lb eligible). Since the lever is capped at 1/base rate, that is about 1.1-1.7x, nowhere near 10x. The proving attempt is also about 1% of the material's value, so cutting it saves almost nothing.
scored.data: The data is partly public and illegible: scanned building permits and old chiller install records. But the outcome is already legible where it matters. Cylinders carry refrigerant labels, chillers have nameplates listing refrigerant type and charge, and EPA Section 608 leak-repair and recordkeeping covers appliances over 50 lb. The ARB/CAR registries publish ODS project documents (source, mass, composition) for every past project, which helps competitors more than it hides the answer. Rights cannot be bought cheaply. R-12 has a liquid secondary market (classic cars, reclaimers), so owners are not blind to its value. Sales are restricted to 608/609-certified buyers. Mature collectors already sweep the supply: Tradewater, EOS Climate, A-Gas/RemTec, Diversified Pure Chem and Refrigerant Finders.
scored.right_bought: Yes, legally: refrigerant title is bought from certified holders, demolition contractors and appliance de-manufacturers (EOS contracted CFC-12 collection from 21 de-manufacturing facilities). But the purchase is close to market price (about $22-44/kg for R-12), not at scrap value. Foam salvage rights are cheap, but foam has low CFC content per kg and costly recovery.
scored.buyer: CA and WA cap-and-trade compliance entities (utilities, refiners, fuel suppliers) buying CCOs. The buyer is capitalized but price-capped. Offsets trade at roughly a 50-60% discount to allowances (about $13 vs about $31), and offset usage is limited to a small share of each entity's obligation (my estimate of the cap rules: 4% to 2025, 6% after). It is a capped side market, not a buyer paying a 10^4 premium.
scored.ladder: The ladder is short and shrinking. The rungs above are owning a destruction facility (an incineration or plasma arc plant, a commodity service), then becoming a reclaimer or refrigerant distributor (A-Gas, Hudson scale, with low margins). The resource is finite: CFC production is phased out and no stockpile is being replaced. All ODS offset issuance to date is on the order of 15 MMT CO2e over a decade (ACR), roughly $150-300M in total cumulative value. That is a niche, not a path to a trillion dollars. HFC destruction (AIM Act) is an adjacent field but crowded with the same incumbents.
scored.fatal_flaw: The unproven material is already priced close to its proven value. CFC-12 is labelled, its identity is known from the equipment nameplate, and it sells at about $22-44/kg to certified buyers, while net offset value is only about $100-250/kg. The assay is a cheap compliance measurement with a high pass rate, not a discovery gamble. So ML has no illegible outcome to find and no low hit rate to improve, and an established collector oligopoly (Tradewater, EOS, A-Gas, Diversified Pure Chem) already sweeps the finite, declining stockpile.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a logistics-and-compliance business on a labelled, already-priced commodity. The step-up is about 2-5x, the hit rate is about 60-90%, the market is a finite niche of about $15-30M a year, and the ML edge has nothing hidden to find.

scored.name: Clean Slate Organic (instantly certifiable farmland)
scored.one_line: Buys idle, CRP or pasture land that pesticide-use records and satellite crop history show has been free of prohibited inputs for 36+ months, certifies it USDA-NOP organic immediately, and resells or leases at an organic premium.
scored.unproven_right: Expiring CRP and fallow parcels at conventional land prices
scored.proving_step: NOP accredited-certifier inspection with 3-year land-history affidavit; cheap; fails often on missing records
scored.proven_buyer: Organic growers/processors (Organic Valley, Grimmway, Driscoll's), farmland REITs
scored.public_data: California DPR Pesticide Use Reports, USDA CropScape/CDL, FSA CRP contracts, NOP Organic Integrity Database
scored.rough_step_up: ~1.2-1.5x on land; legible outcome, honest low scorer
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy a parcel that is eligible for certification, then sell it certified. Finding the parcel is perhaps 30-50% of the work in that rung (my estimate). The rest is ordinary farmland brokerage plus a certifier inspection, and the paperwork for that inspection is not hard. The certified output is not a separately priced asset. The organic value comes from someone farming organically: weed control, lower yields, buyer contracts. Certification only opens the door. Buyers are capitalised (organic growers, processors, farmland REITs), but they pay a single-digit percentage premium on the land, not a step-up for something that was hard to find.
scored.step_up: Organic ground runs about 23-26% above conventional. USDA ERS ERR-188 (ARMS data 2003-2011) found median organic cropland values 26% higher and rents 23% higher. Fuller/Janzen/Munkhnasan (Land Economics 97(1)) found a 26% rent premium. A Mercaris survey found a 25% rent premium, about $68/acre/yr, and some owners got no premium at all. So the step-up is about 1.25x, below the candidate's own 1.2-1.5x guess and roughly 10^4 times smaller than the Terranox jump.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is a certifier inspection costing roughly $500-$2,000 per operation (my estimate from typical NOP certifier fee schedules). Expired CRP land can qualify immediately with an affidavit that no prohibited substances were used (UNL Extension pub 1392). The 2018 Farm Bill lets the last 2 CRP contract years count toward the 3-year transition (NSAC). The base hit rate for well-chosen CRP or pasture parcels is likely high, maybe 50-80% (my estimate). The usual failure is herbicide spot-spraying or missing records, and a phone call to the owner settles that. With a cheap step and a high base rate, ML can raise the hit rate by at most about 1.5-2x (lever capped at 1/base hit rate). The savings per attempt are only hundreds of dollars.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible and the outcome is largely summarised already. CRP enrollment and expiry are known through FSA, and CRP-TIP exists specifically to steer expiring CRP land to organic and beginning farmers. CropScape/CDL is a clean raster. The NOP Organic Integrity Database lists certified operations. California DPR Pesticide Use Reports are structured and keyed to section and township. The one hard-to-read piece is the farmer's own spray record, which is private, not public. Montana State and Oregon State studies already measure CRP-to-organic adoption, so the rule 'expired CRP = fast-track eligible' is well known.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought at conventional land prices, which is fine, but the owner holds the key fact: they know whether they sprayed. Because they can read their own records and can certify the land themselves, the information gap is weak. Expiring CRP land in Midwest and Plains states sells at ordinary cropland or pasture prices, often $2,000-$10,000/acre (my estimate). A 25% premium on that is small next to the 6-10% round-trip transaction costs of buying and reselling farmland.
scored.buyer: Organic row-crop and dairy operators, processors such as Organic Valley, Grimmway and Driscoll's (mostly as tenants or contract partners, not land buyers), and farmland REITs and funds (Farmland Partners, Gladstone Land, Iroquois Valley). Iroquois Valley and similar players already buy land and convert it to organic, and certifiers and CRP-TIP already handle this conversion path.
scored.ladder: There is some ladder: own the land, operate organically, sign offtake deals, process, and sell a brand (farmland to organic food company). But each rung up is the hard physical, operational business (farming, processing), not discovery. The first rung earns no outsized return to fund the climb. The total market is a few billion dollars of land premium, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is only about 1.25x (organic land and rent premium of 23-26% per USDA ERS ERR-188), and transaction costs eat it. The proving step is cheap and usually succeeds, and the owner already knows the answer. That leaves no 10^3-10^4 jump and no hit-rate lever for ML. The real value comes from actually farming organically, which is the physical work.
scored.one_line_reason: Certifying idle or CRP land organic lifts its value only about 25%, the step is cheap and usually succeeds, and the owner knows the spray history, so there is no discovery edge for ML.

verified.name: LoadStudy Land (greenfield large-load study options, ERCOT/SPP)
verified.one_line: Buys cheap 2-3 year options on farmland next to 345 kV lines with hidden headroom, files a large-load interconnection request, and sells the studied power-ready site to hyperscalers and data center developers.
verified.unproven_right: Options on 200-1,000 acres at ~$3-10k/acre (premiums ~$50-200/acre) from owners who cannot read transmission planning cases
verified.proving_step: Utility/ERCOT Large Load Interconnection Study and will-serve letter confirming MW at a named substation and date (~$50-250k deposits); most return large upgrades or delays; ML ranks headroom from RPG/ITP PDFs, Form 715, IRPs, constraints and retirements
verified.proven_buyer: Hyperscalers, data center developers/REITs (Stack, QTS, Aligned), infra funds (Blackstone, KKR, DigitalBridge)
verified.public_data: ERCOT RPG submissions and Large Load status reports, SPP ITP and Form 715, utility IRP PDFs, ERCOT CDR, EIA-860 retirements, county parcel rolls
verified.rough_step_up: ~80-300x (~$2.5-10k/acre unstudied to ~$800k/acre power-ready per Claros). Caveat: killed 'powered brownfields' and 'queue positions'; edge must be greenfield headroom, and sellers near substations are wising up
verified.frame: The rung is a land option plus a completed large-load study, sold as a site with a will-serve letter. It is discrete and sellable: a 'powered land' market exists. Finding the site is maybe 60-70% of the work by my estimate, not 80%+. The rest is non-trivial: the study queue, utility politics, zoning and water, plus the upgrade cost and energization date the study returns. Those come from the utility's own schedule, not from the company. Texas SB6 (2025) adds further work for loads of 75 MW and up: a study fee (about $100k minimum, from memory), proof of site control, disclosure of duplicate requests, and curtailment terms. The buyer's real purchase criterion is the energization date, which the company cannot speed up.
verified.step_up: Unproven: ag land next to 345 kV lines in ERCOT/SPP at roughly $3-10k/acre, with option premiums of about $50-200/acre (the candidate's figures; I could not verify them). Proven: the candidate cites about $800k/acre for power-ready land (Claros). From memory, trade reports put Texas power-ready land at roughly $100-500k/acre and the very top N. Virginia sites at $1-2M+/acre. Those are estimates, not verified this session. A realistic step-up for a studied site with a will-serve letter but an energization date 3-5 years out is about 20-80x on land value. It reaches about 100x+ only when there is near-term MW. Measured against the option premium alone it is larger, but the buyer prices land value. So this sits at ~10-100x, a 3.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs about $50-250k in study deposits and fees, plus option premiums of about $10-200k. The candidate gives the deposit range. SB6's minimum study fee is about $100k from memory. Per-site all-in, including engineering and legal, is my estimate of $0.2-0.5M. Base hit rate is my estimate: maybe 15-35% of studies return usable MW at an acceptable upgrade cost and date. ERCOT's large-load queue grew past ~200 GW by late 2025 (from memory of ERCOT reports), against a ~85 GW peak, so most requests are speculative and will not be served on time. The lever is capped at 1/base rate, about 3-6x, not 10x. Headroom is also already computed by power-flow engineers using CEII-cleared PSS/E base cases, so ML over PDFs adds little over a standard contingency analysis.
verified.data: The data is public-ish but not truly illegible. ERCOT publishes monthly large-load interconnection status reports with MW by zone and status. RPG project submissions, SPP ITP and Form 715 are partially behind CEII access, which any developer can obtain. The proper tool is a power-flow model, which consultants such as Grid Strategies, E3 and the utilities' own engineering firms already run. The outcome (available MW at a substation and its date) is close to being summarised in legible fields: queue and status reports, plus utility hosting and capacity maps where they exist. This repeats the 'queue positions: lookup table matches ML' failure. The right can be bought cheaply from farmers. But sellers near 345 kV substations in Texas are increasingly aware (data center brokers cold-call landowners), and SB6 site-control rules plus duplicate-request disclosure reduce option-stacking.
verified.right_bought: Yes. Options on private farmland are bought, not free first-come. Option premiums are cheap, but prices near substations are rising and many options are already tied up by powered-land developers.

The attribution is still contested: the Prado's 2021 catalogue lists it as workshop, and Hope and Franck rejected it in 2020. It is a single outlier from before online bidding, and the step-up took 8 years, not "at once".
(2) Artemisia Gentileschi (The Art Newspaper, 14 Mar 2024). A dealer bought it for GBP 30k at a Danish auction in September 2022 and sold it at Christie's for GBP 1.9M less than a year later: 63x. This is the best-documented fast buyer-side step-up.
(3) Pierozzi Annunciation miniature (same article). Bought for EUR 7,800 at Millon; Colnaghi then priced it at "six figures", about 13-60x.
(4) Early Rembrandt (ArtsJournal teaser). Offered as an anonymous 19th-century work for "a few hundred dollars" at a small New Jersey house in 2015 and bought by the dealer Talabardon. [memory] Nye & Co, estimate $500-800, hammer about $870k-1.1M, then a private resale to the Leiden Collection at an undisclosed price, probably under 10x the hammer. Most of the step-up went to the consignor at the hammer.
(5) From the candidate's own notes: the Thomaston "After Rembrandt" made $1.175M against a $10-15k estimate, and the Dou made EUR 70k against EUR 4-6k. In both, competing bidders captured the step-up at the regional sale.
[memory] Other cases follow the same pattern:
- Cimabue, Actéon 2019: estimate EUR 300-400k, sold for about EUR 24M; the seller captured it.
- Madrid Ecce Homo, 2021: estimated at EUR 1,500 as "circle of Ribera"; Spain blocked the sale and the owners later sold it privately for about EUR 36M; the owners captured it.
- Jan Six Rembrandt: bought for about GBP 137k as "circle of" at Christie's in 2016; the claimed value is in the tens of millions, about 100x, but authorship is disputed.

STEP-UP: For a buyer who pays today's competitive online hammer, the documented realised multiple is about 3-60x. Over 100x is rare, and 10^3-10^4x has one clean example (Salvator Mundi, 2005, 8 years) plus cases where the consignor kept the gain. The unproven price is not near zero: once specialists notice a lot it reaches $70k-$1.2M at the hammer. This misses the rubric's 10^3-10^4 test, and the typical case is below the ~30x refutation line.

BUYER: Real and well capitalised: Christie's and Sotheby's (guarantees, private sales), dealers such as Colnaghi, Weiss and Talabardon, the Leiden Collection, and museums. But they pay only after acceptance by a scholar or committee, which takes 1-8 years, not immediately after a hit, and acceptance can be reversed.

MARKET SIZE: Old Masters are a few percent of a roughly $10B a year fine-art auction market, about $0.5-1B a year [memory, not re-checked]. Re-attributed sleepers that reach seven figures probably number single digits to low tens per year globally. The upside is too small and lumpy for a 10x hit-rate lever to compound.
verifiers.killer: The 10^3-10^4x step-up does not reach the buyer. Sleepers are bought at open online-bid auctions, and specialist dealers bid any lot that looks promising up to $70k-$1.2M at the hammer: the Nutley Rembrandt went from a few hundred dollars to about $1M, the Thomaston lot made $1.175M on a $10k estimate, and the Cimabue made EUR 24M. The consignor captures most of the gain. Documented buyer-side multiples are about 3-63x, with the Gentileschi's GBP 30k to GBP 1.9M as the best case. The one 10^4-plus case (Salvator Mundi, $1,175 to $80M) took 8 years, dates from before online bidding and is still disputed. The capitalised buyer is real but pays only after years of subjective scholarly acceptance, not immediately. The market is about $0.5-1B a year, with only a handful of seven-figure re-attributions a year.

Right buyable (legally yes, cheaply sometimes, at scale doubtful):

Its examples: the Pierozzi Annunciation miniature bought for EUR 7,800 at Millon and priced in six figures by Colnaghi; an Artemisia Gentileschi bought for GBP 30k at a Danish sale in 2022 and sold for GBP 1.9M at Christie's within a year; the Salvator Mundi sold for $1,100 including fees in 2005, of which the family netted $700.

- The same article names a "duty of care" to vulnerable sellers and proposes "Sleeper Resale Rights" (a levy on the gain for heirlooms held about 10 years or more). This is only a proposal, but it shows political or regulatory risk aimed squarely at this business model.
- The bigger problem is that the buy happens at an open, online-bid auction. The finalist's own Thomaston case made $1.175M on a $10-15k estimate. Every lot the ML flags is visible to the same pool of specialist dealers, so cheap rights exist only where every human misses the work. That is a thin, hard-to-scale tail, not a supply of rights that can be bought at scale.

Physical and proving step (not trivial, and outside the company's control):
- The cash cost of technical analysis is small ($2-30k).
- But the proving gate is a third party's subjective consent: a catalogue raisonné author, a committee or a museum curator. Christie's own specialist declined the Salvator Mundi when the Hendry family offered it (TAN).
- The Salvator Mundi needed roughly six years of restoration and scholarship (2005 to the 2011 National Gallery show) before it was proven, and doubts about it persist.
- AI attribution has not earned market trust. Art Recognition's only AI-only sale was a Werefkin watercolour that made CHF 15k at Germann in Nov 2024. Grosvenor calls the AI track record "patchy". The 2021 Rubens claim of a 91% chance of fake was dismissed by the National Gallery, and two AI tools contradicted each other on a Raphael (artlawandmore).
- So the step is not physically hard like a bespoke geothermal plant, but it is slow, subjective, reversible and not owned by the company. That cuts C1 to 2.

Scores: C2 stays at 3 (realised step-ups after paying contested hammer prices run about 3-63x, with rare 10^4 outliers). C3 stays at 2 (the purchase price rises with how obvious the signal is, and the cost of gatekeeper consent does not fall). C4 stays at 2 (the data is illegible, but human sleeper hunters read it by eye). C5 stays at 2 (the market is capped in the low billions). Total 11/25.

Not refuted on the strict lens: the right can be bought and the physical step does not dominate the cost. But the finalist's premise of cheap, scalable rights is only weakly supported.
verifiers.killer: The right can be bought legally, but only at open, online-bid auctions where human sleeper hunters already set the price ($1.175M on a $10k estimate). Proving then depends on a single third-party gatekeeper who can refuse (Christie's turned down the Salvator Mundi), delay for years or later reverse. So the cheap, scalable right and the trivial proving step that the frame needs both fail in practice. A proposed "Sleeper Resale Right" is aimed directly at this model.

verified.proven_buyer: Engine lessors (AerCap, Willis Lease), USM traders (AAR, GA Telesis), MROs pricing off LLP remaining-cycle tables
verified.public_data: FAA registry document images, SDR and AD databases, NTSB, lessor ABS disclosures; most signal is the acquired record pack rather than public data (weaker C4)

A part with no trace usually also needs a shop visit, non-destructive testing and re-certification under an 8130-3 or Form 1. The deciding step is acceptance by an OEM, CAMO or lessor records auditor, such as GE/CFM's TRUEngine back-to-birth review, and that is a gatekeeper's judgement, not a discovery result. Capitalised buyers exist: AerCap, Willis Lease, AAR, GA Telesis, CFM Materials.

For a truly no-trace part, one vendor (oxmaint) says it may be treated as having zero remaining life, and a GE-commissioned mba study says 42% of respondents value non-OEM or alternative material at scrap at teardown. That scrap-to-serviceable case is the candidate's 5-50x (my estimate, e.g. ~$10-20k scrap vs $0.3-1.5M serviceable). Safe Fly puts a full CFM56-5B/7B LLP stack at $2.5-6.0M (unaudited vendor figure). Cost per attempt is a records review plus outreach to past operators and MROs, roughly $2-20k per part (my estimate; ProvenAir and Bluetail do this as a service). verified.data: Weak. The signal sits in the private record pack that comes with the part, not in public data. The FAA registry, SDR, AD and NTSB data do not hold per-part LLP cycle histories. verified.buyer: Engine lessors (AerCap, Willis Lease), USM traders and part-out houses (AAR, GA Telesis, CFM Materials), and MROs that price parts off LLP remaining-cycle tables. They have the capital but are very averse to fraud risk.

Note on method: WebSearch was not available for this check because the shared per-turn search budget had already run out. I checked the candidate's own sources with WebFetch instead.

(1) The rule on scrapped parts. 14 CFR 43.10 (Cornell LII) says a removed life-limited part (LLP) must be controlled by one of: record-keeping, a tag, marking, segregation, or mutilation. Mutilation "must render the part beyond repair and incapable of being reworked to appear to be airworthy." Properly scrapped LLPs, the cheapest stock, therefore cannot legally be revived. The only buyable stock is segregated or 'as-removed' no-trace parts. Sellers price these knowing their recovery odds, because lessors and teardown shops employ records auditors. The right is legally buyable, but there is no information asymmetry to buy into.

(2) What full back-to-birth (BtB) needs. Sofema/SAS (saved PDF) lists: the original OEM conformity certificate (8130-3 or Form 1), a record of every operator and MRO the part passed through, a certified record of on-wing hours, and a non-incident statement. It also says "there is a lack of a standard in relation to the acceptance of Life Limited Parts" and that a "more is better" culture has emerged, with multiple checks layered on: regulatory, AMO and lease. The proving step is acceptance by several gatekeepers, each using its own subjective test. It is not discovery. Missing operator-period records cannot be reconstructed by reading documents.

(3) GE's TRUEngine LLP designation. It requires a "rigorous back-to-birth records audit and engineering review" against GE-substantiated limits. Its documentation accompanies LLPs sold through GE's own materials business. The OEM is therefore both an auditor and a competing seller.

(4) Asset values. Safe Fly (page as fetched today) gives a CFM56 LLP stack at $1.4-1.8M, with single LLPs at $250-480K (HPT Stage 1 disk $420-480K). That is lower than the $2.5-6.0M the candidate cited. Safe Fly says value varies with "LLP status, traceability." Complete teardown engines trade at $1.2-1.8M, so traced value is already priced into the purchase.

(5) Incumbent service. ProvenAir already builds BtB timelines and exception reports from uploaded records for lessors, airlines, MROs and material suppliers, across more than 5,000 assets analysed. It does not claim to recreate missing documents.

(6) The physical step. Restoring a no-trace part also needs a shop visit, NDT and recertification under an 8130-3 or Form 1 at a Part 145 station, plus legal liability for suspected unapproved parts on resale. That liability became much more serious after AOG Technics in 2023 (pre-existing knowledge). This is not a trivial or abstracted step.

(7) Exclusions. No hard exclusion applies, because the company owns the asset.
verifiers.killer: The right can be bought legally, but not at a discount that reflects hidden value. Sellers are records-sophisticated lessors and teardown shops, and they price no-trace parts at their known recovery odds. Mutilated parts (14 CFR 43.10) are legally unrecoverable. The proving step is not discovery. It is acceptance by several gatekeepers with no common standard: OEM (GE TRUEngine, itself a competing seller), CAMO, lessor auditors and a Part 145 shop. On top of that sit physical NDT and recertification, plus fraud liability after AOG Technics. The missing value is absent operator-period paperwork, which ML cannot create. Discovery is therefore well under 80% of the frame, and the gatekeeper, not the finder, captures the value.

Author-signed books, the most common hit type, are therefore already flagged at the point of sale. The guide does not cover loose letters, so some residual edge remains there.

Authentication is cheap: PSA/DNA charges $10 to $150+ by signer, JSA LOAs start at $50, and Beckett's preliminary review is $10 and non-refundable (thepricer.org, fetched; the psacard.com pricing page returned 403). The $2.48 thrift-store find that sold for $477,650 at Raynors' was a printed 1823 William Stone Declaration, explicitly "printed... not handwritten" (NBC, fetched). It was recognisable by eye, so it is not evidence for a handwriting or provenance-ML edge.
(5) LEGAL CLOUD ON THE HIGH-VALUE TAIL (background knowledge, not verified this turn). Presidents' and officials' letters written in an official capacity can be alienated public records. NARA's archival recovery efforts and state replevin actions, such as North Carolina's recovery of its Bill of Rights copy, can reclaim them without compensation. So the most valuable hits may carry defective title. Auction houses also demand provenance before taking high-value manuscripts.
(6) BUYERS ARE CONSIGNMENT AGENTS, NOT PRINCIPALS. RR Auction, Heritage, Christie's and Sotheby's mostly take commission. No developer-style buyer pays a premium for the proven right. No hard exclusion applies: this is not prospecting, and the company owns the items rather than selling a service.

The page is dated March 2014, so current fees may be higher. Most stamps flagged in kiloware are worth tens of dollars, so a certificate eats most or all of the value of a typical hit. Every ML false positive loses money outright. The certificate is not where hunts fail (submitters screen first), so ML cannot cut the cost of failed proofs. The lever is cheaper sorting labour, not a 10x cut in capex.

(2) The outcome is already legible. Scott and Stanley Gibbons specialised catalogues list every variety with its value, and the Siegel census labels known rarities. That is the "answer written into a legible field" failure mode the rubric warns about. The ML would only be matching images to an existing catalogue taxonomy, not inferring something nobody has written down.

(3) The signal is not in the public data. The attributes that decide value need physical handling: watermark (fluid or backlight), perforation gauge, paper, shade under standard light, UV response, and whether the gum is original. The PreGradeCards guide itself says AI only "helps detect" watermarks when the stamp is photographed against light. It says "rare varieties should be confirmed by an expert," and it gives no accuracy figures. Seller photos on eBay, Delcampe and HipStamp usually do not show these attributes.

(4) The space is occupied. Consumer AI identifier apps already claim perforation and watermark checks (StampID, StampLens, Stamp Value AI Identifier, and PreGradeCards' AI pre-screen). More importantly, the sellers of bulk lots are professional dealers, the best human readers of this data, who pick lots before reselling them. The right being sold is not mispriced to an owner who cannot read the data. Estate albums are the only channel where the owner genuinely cannot assess the lot, and every dealer competes for them at low volume.

(5) No capitalised buyer, and a small market. Siegel did about $36M in sales in 2018. Bill Gross, the largest recent buyer and seller, exited and predicted a correction. Buyers are ageing individual collectors.

(6) The hit rate of about 1 in 10^4 is the finalist's own unsupported estimate. Even if true, the expected value per lot is priced in by dealers, at the finalist's own estimate of about 2-10x.
verifiers.killer: The value-deciding outcome is already written into a legible taxonomy: the Scott/SG catalogue values and the Siegel census. The physical attributes that separate a rare variety from a common stamp are watermark, perforation gauge, shade, paper and gum, and seller scans mostly do not show them. On top of that, the people selling the lots are expert dealers who have already picked them. ML has neither the hidden signal nor a blind owner to buy from. Each attempt also costs a $27-50 certificate on items mostly worth less than that.

Labs need X-radiography, micro-CT, X-ray luminescence and sometimes radiocarbon dating to see it. The CIJ/SSEF article says SSEF needed all of these, and that 'no single feature' marks beadless cultured pearls, which were passing as natural even with prior reports. Auction catalogue photos (low resolution, external surface only) cannot carry that signal. What ML can read from them (pre-1930 clasp hallmarks, small graduated sizes, slightly off-round shapes, drill-hole wear, 'untested' or 'probably natural' wording) are exactly the cues a pearl dealer reads in seconds. Any edge ML has is in triage volume, not in what it can detect.

(2) THE OPTION IS ALREADY PRICED. Provincial houses usually catalogue old strands as 'untested', 'not tested for natural origin' or 'may be natural'. That wording flags the option to every bidder on LiveAuctioneers, the-saleroom and Invaluable. Specialist London, Gulf and Indian pearl dealers and pickers monitor these platforms with saved searches. Untested Edwardian strands are routinely bid far above cultured-strand value (domain knowledge, unverified this session). So the 'owner cannot read the data' discount is largely gone wherever the description or photos are decent. Only badly catalogued lots stay cheap, and a buyer's premium of about 20-28% on each side eats into those too.

(3) THE PROVING STEP IS CHEAP. Lab natural-pearl reports cost tens to a few hundred dollars per strand at GIA, and more for value-based SSEF reports. That is small next to the lot price. When a shot costs mostly the lot price and testing is cheap, the economic answer is to test every plausible strand, and the dealers already do. So ML's capex lever is about 2-3x at most, not 10x. The finalist itself concedes this.

(4) THE TRADE IS ALREADY OCCUPIED. Established natural-pearl dealers (Gulf/Bahrain houses, Mumbai dealers, Hatton Garden pickers) already work this arbitrage by eye, together with the jewellery departments of Christie's, Sotheby's, Bonhams, Woolley & Wallis and Lyon & Turnbull. Woolley & Wallis and Bonhams already send old strands for testing before sale, which turns illegible lots into legible 'natural, GIA report' results upstream. I found no ML startup in this niche, but that is because the market is small, not because there is an unexploited edge.

(5) HITS ARE SMALL AND MIXED. The finalist's own comparables, about $2.5k-$40k, suggest typical step-ups of 10-50x. Strands that test natural are often mixed with cultured pearls, which cuts their value.

Net: on the data-and-competition lens, the edge is weak. The signal is not in the data, the visible priors are already read and priced by an expert trade, and blanket testing is cheap.

Catalogue photos and text carry only the visible priors (age, clasp, gradation, 'untested' wording), and specialist pearl dealers already read and bid on those across the online auction platforms. With testing priced at tens to hundreds of dollars, blanket testing by people who already know the trade reaches most of the arbitrage. So ML adds at most 2-3x triage efficiency in a niche dealers already occupy, not a 10x discovery edge.
