The web search budget ran out after the tool loaded, so no new search queries were run. The evidence below comes from fetching two primary sources directly, plus the finalist's own cited figures.

(1) DLA Land and Maritime SAR briefing (NDIA 2018), PDF text extracted locally. In FY17 it received 282 packages: 111 approved, 114 rejected, 144 pending. Approval rate is about 49% of decided packages, so the hit-rate lever is capped near 2x.
- Those 111 approvals gave "$35.5M potential annual savings", about $320k/yr of savings to DLA per approved NSN.
- Approval means "Company cage/part number added as approved source". The procedure (DAG 17.7501-6, June 2014) is "Sole Source Breakout": a multi-source award clause for at least 1 year, and "40% of the award may be given to the newly approved source" if its price is fair and reasonable rather than lowest.
- So a SAR does not create a sole-source franchise. It breaks one, makes you a second source at lower prices, and caps your guaranteed share at about 40% for a year. In 7 cases the item went fully competitive.
- Implied value per approval: if $320k/yr of savings is roughly 25-35% of NSN spend, spend is about $0.9-1.3M/yr. A 40% share is about $0.4-0.5M/yr of revenue at competitive margins (estimate 15-25%), so about $60-125k/yr EBITDA. At 8-12x that is about $0.5-1.5M of value against $50-150k all-in (package, SAR/FAT, tooling). Step-up is about 5-30x, not 10^3-10^4.
- Market size: about 111 approvals/yr at this DLA center. Even scaled across DLA Aviation and the other centers, it is a few hundred approvals per year worth roughly $0.3-1M/yr each.

(2) BizTimes: Extant Aerospace paid $27M cash for the Astronautics electromechanical HSI/ADI/BDHI line (production, repair, spares). No revenue or EBITDA was disclosed. This shows that real legacy lines are sold for full value to specialist buyers, not for $5-100k. The $5-100k bankruptcy-package price remains unverified.

(3) The buyer is real but does not pay at once. DLA pays per part order over time. TransDigm, Heico, Ontic and Extant buy on proven EBITDA after years of profitable manufacturing, not on a SAR approval letter.
verifiers.killer: DLA's own SAR procedure ("Sole Source Breakout", DAG 17.7501-6) makes an approved SAR an ADDED source that is guaranteed only about 40% of awards for about a year, at lower prices. The 111 FY17 approvals were worth about $320k/yr each in savings to DLA. So a proven right is worth roughly $0.5-1.5M against $50-150k invested, about 5-30x, with value realised slowly through manufacturing rather than paid at once by a capitalised buyer. Real legacy lines (Astronautics, $27M to Extant) already sell at full price to specialists.

verifiers.evidence: Web search was unavailable: the turn's shared search budget was used up, so this check rests on direct fetches of primary sources. (1) DLA Land and Maritime SAR briefing (NDIA 2018, text extracted from the PDF): FY17 shows 111 packages approved and 114 rejected, about 49% approval. Rejections are mostly for incomplete packages, so the failure is procedural rather than a mispick a model could avoid. The hit-rate lever is therefore capped at about 2x. The cited DLA Casting and Forging data (40 approved, 4 rejected, about 91%) would cap it near 1.1x. (2) The same briefing gives the targeting method contractors are told to use: 'Identify potential items (NSNs) of interest - Search DIBBS, Haystack, SERVA (PTACs can help)' and 'DLA candidate list's - Obsolescence / limited competition'. It also links a published 'SAR Candidate List'. So DLA itself publishes which NSNs it wants new sources for. Commercial NSN data vendors (Haystack, SERVA) already sell the sole-source and demand view, and free government-funded advisors (PTACs) help small shops run the same search. The outcome sits in legible fields and published lists: AMSC/AMC codes, award history, the candidate list. That fails C4's rule that the answer must not already be written into a legible field. (3) The same briefing says the SAR route also accepts 'Reverse Engineering (OEM Part)'. Competitors can qualify on an NSN without buying any orphan data package, so the bought right is not exclusive. (4) Retention of Newly Approved Sources (DAG 17.7501-6, since June 2014) works through 'Sole Source Breakout' and a multi-source award clause. It guarantees the new source a share for at least 1 year, with up to 40% of an award when its price is fair and reasonable but not lowest. An approved SAR therefore makes you an added source in a competition DLA is deliberately opening, not a sole source with TransDigm pricing. That shrinks the step-up to roughly 3-30x on a share of a contested NSN. (5) TransDigm FY2021 10-K: about 90% of net sales are proprietary and about 80% sole source. The ladder is real, but that franchise comes from OEM-designed proprietary parts, not from SAR-won second sources. (6) The proving step is not the expensive, mostly-failing shot the rubric needs. The SAR process is administrative (5/15/30/90-day review steps). The real cost is manufacturing, quality systems and FAT, which ML does not reduce.
verifiers.killer: DLA publishes its own SAR candidate list of limited-competition and obsolescent NSNs, and it tells contractors to target them with DIBBS plus the commercial NSN databases Haystack and SERVA. The discovery answer is already legible and handed out, with free PTAC help. Approval runs about 49-91%, so the lever is 2x or less. A win makes you a breakout second source with about a 1-year, up to 40% share guarantee, not a sole source.

verifiers.evidence:
The web search budget ran out after the first call, so this rests on fetches of primary sources the finalist already cited, plus the finalist's own research.

1) The right is not exclusive, so buying it gives no moat. The DLA Land and Maritime SAR briefing (NDIA 2018, text pulled with pdftotext) lists two SAR routes: 'OEM Data' and 'Reverse Engineering (OEM Part)'. Any shop can reverse-engineer a part and file a SAR without buying any package. A bought package is just one way to file, not a right anyone has to pay for. The briefing also says that once a package is closed 'Technical data is available for viewing (competitive)'.

2) Approval adds you as a source; it does not make you the sole source. SARs only apply to AMSC B (source controlled) and AMSC C (source restricted) items, which already have an approved source. On approval the 'Company cage/part number [is] added as approved source', and the stated goals are 'Sole Source Breakout' and a 'multi-source award clause for a minimum of one (1) year'. So the proving step breaks the very sole-source pricing the TransDigm-style model needs.

3) The base hit rate is high, so the lever is small. FY17 figures are 111 approved vs 114 rejected, about 49%. The casting and forging program is about 91% (40 vs 4), per the finalist's own cited source. That caps the lever at roughly 1.1-2x. Rejections are often 'can't validate part (no government data to compare)', which is a data-availability problem, not a targeting problem ML can fix.

4) Proving takes about six months of ordinary process time before any manufacturing. The briefing timeline is VE in 5 days, analyst review in 15, missing data in 30, the ESA's 90-day review, concurrence in 15, more data in 30 and the letter in 5, about 190 days in total. Then comes first-article hardware made in a qualified shop. The physical and procedural work dominates, much like the bespoke geothermal plant counter-example.

5) Sellers are not illiterate. The Schweizer 269 type certificate, Part 145 certificate, tooling and IP were sold through a multi-phase process run by an exclusive broker (Starman, qualified buyers, 60-day offer phase). Extant paid about $27M for the Astronautics line (BizTimes/AIN). Valuable lines go to specialist buyers at full price.

6) Legal title is doubtful (my own knowledge, not checked this run). Drawings held by machine shops are usually build-to-print data owned by the OEM or prime under NDA, so a retiring shop or bankrupt estate often cannot legally transfer them. ITAR also limits who can receive the data.

7) There is no hard exclusion: it is not drilling, and you own the asset rather than selling a service. But the core claims (a buyable exclusive right, a trivial proving step, an illegible outcome) do not hold. AMSC/AMC codes already state the outcome. The ladder from approved source to manufacturer to roll-up to sustainment prime is real (TransDigm, Ontic).
verifiers.killer: The 'right' does not exist as an exclusive, buyable asset. DLA SARs can be filed by reverse-engineering the OEM part, with no data purchase. Approval only adds your CAGE as an extra approved source on an AMSC B/C item, explicitly for 'sole source breakout' and multi-source awards. After that comes about 190 days of procedure, then first-article manufacturing. So the purchase gives no exclusivity, the proving step is physical and procedural rather than discovery, and success erodes the sole-source margin the exit depends on.

deep.name: LoadStudy Land (greenfield large-load study options, ERCOT/SPP)
deep.memo:
## LoadStudy Land: feasibility memo (ERCOT/SPP greenfield large-load sites)

*Research limit: WebSearch was refused because the shared per-turn search budget (200 calls) was already used up. I fetched primary pages directly instead. Every price and hit-rate figure below is marked as an estimate or as the candidate's own figure unless a URL is given.*

### Frame of reference
The rung is a land option plus a completed large-load interconnection result for one parcel, sold as a "power-ready" site. The market for this exists. But discovery (finding where the grid has room) is maybe 50-60% of the work (estimate), not the 80%+ the rubric needs. Since 2025-26 the proving step itself has become heavy:
- **Texas SB6** requires for any load over 75 MW: a study fee of at least $100k, proof of site control "through an ownership interest, lease, or another legal interest acceptable to the commission", per-MW financial security or a contribution in aid of construction (CIAC), and disclosure of similar requests ([SB6 enrolled](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm)).
- **ERCOT Batch Zero (PGRR145)** studies large loads system-wide, but only those meeting "study maturity and commitment criteria". The PUCT approved it 06/18/2026 and it took effect 07/11/2026 ([PGRR145](https://www.ercot.com/mktrules/issues/PGRR145)). Every request needs notarized Form W (controllable load) and Form X attestations, and ERCOT sets the calendar ([ERCOT LLI](https://www.ercot.com/services/rq/large-load-integration)).

This looks more like the geothermal counter-example than like Terranox: the regulatory and capital step dominates the rung.

### Step-up ratio
- **Unproven price:** ag land near 345 kV lines at ~$3-10k/acre, options ~$50-200/acre. These are the candidate's figures and unverified. The [Texas A&M Real Estate Center](https://trerc.tamu.edu/data/rural-land/) publishes regional rural prices, but the page renders them interactively and I could not extract them.
- **Proven price:** the candidate cites ~$800k/acre (Claros), unverified. My estimate for a Texas/SPP site with a study result but energization 3-5 years out is ~$25-150k/acre. Northern Virginia near-term powered land is ~$1-4M/acre (estimate).
- **Step-up:** ~5-30x on land value (estimate). It reaches ~100x only with near-term energized MW, which the utility controls. Buyers favour "power access within 18 to 36 months" and sites over 200 MW ([CBRE H1 2025](https://www.cbre.com/insights/reports/north-america-data-center-trends-h1-2025)).
- **Transactions/yr:** tens to low hundreds across ERCOT/SPP (estimate, not quantified).

### Hit rate and proving capex today and with ML
- **Capex per shot today:** the $100k+ SB6 fee ([SB6](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm)), plus per-MW security that scales with request size, plus option premium, engineering and legal. My estimate is ~$0.3-1M+ per 200-500 MW site. The security is refundable as milestones are met or on withdrawal, but it ties up capital.
- **Base hit rate:** ~15-35% of requests return usable MW at an acceptable cost and date (estimate). Most of the queue is speculative. ERCOT only says there has been a "rapid increase in Large Load interconnection requests" ([LLWG](https://www.ercot.com/committees/tac/llwg)). The 200+ GW figure is from memory and unverified.
- **With ML:** the lever is capped at 1/base rate, about 3-6x. It is weaker still because Batch Zero shares the capacity among all entrants against one base case. Headroom is not discovered privately; it is allocated.

### Data source
Named sources: ERCOT RPG submissions, ERCOT planning reports such as the [2025 Constraints and Needs report](https://www.ercot.com/gridinfo/planning), SPP ITP, FERC Form 715 (behind CEII clearance), utility IRPs, EIA-860 retirements, and county parcel rolls.
- **Why it seems illegible:** scattered PDFs and power-flow base cases.
- **Why it is in fact legible:** any developer can get CEII access, and standard PSS/E contingency analysis computes headroom directly. The outcome (MW at a substation plus a date) comes out of Batch Zero and TSP studies. This is the same failure as the killed "queue positions: lookup table matches ML" idea.

### How the right is bought
- **From whom:** private farmland owners, through 2-3 year purchase options. This part works: rights are bought, not first-come.
- **Price:** the candidate's ~$50-200/acre premiums (unverified).
- **Legal mechanics:** SB6 site control may not accept a bare option; that is left to the PUCT ("another legal interest acceptable to the commission"). Transfer to a buyer looks workable, since "a successor in interest" is covered in the large-load customer definition. Capacity under a financial commitment can be reallocated under PUCT rules ([SB6](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm)). Sellers near 345 kV substations are increasingly aware of their land's value (estimate).

### Capitalised buyer
Real and deep: hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI/Oracle at Abilene), developers and REITs (Stack, QTS, Aligned, Vantage), and infrastructure funds (Blackstone, KKR, DigitalBridge). They pay for MW plus an energization date, mostly when an energy service agreement (ESA) or energization is certain, not when a study comes back.

### Integration ladder above
Option plus study, then a permitted powered shell, then on-site or behind-the-meter generation, then a campus, then owner-operator, then power producer. The trillion-dollar path would be an "AI-compute utility". But every rung above the first is construction and power procurement, where ML gives no edge, and incumbents already hold those rungs.

### Who else does this
- **Lancium:** Abilene, Childress and Hall County "Clean Campuses", each 1 GW and up, "fully ERCOT-approved" ([lancium.com](https://www.lancium.com/)).
- **Tract** (site not readable), Crusoe, Prometheus Hyperscale, Skybox (from memory).
- **Data vendors selling substation-capacity scores:** LandGate, Paces (from memory, unverified).
- **Power-flow consultants and hyperscaler in-house energy teams.**

### Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
Take ERCOT's next published large-load status or Batch Zero results and the 2025 Constraints and Needs report. Back-test whether an ML ranking of 345 kV substations, built only from public PDFs, beats a plain power-flow and lookup baseline (substation rating minus existing and queued load) at predicting which sites received allocations. In parallel, get 5 broker quotes for studied-but-unenergized Texas sites, which settles the proven price.
- **Kill if:** ML lift over the baseline is under ~0.05 AUC, or the studied-site price is under ~30x farmland.

### Verdict
**Not feasible as a Terranox-shaped company.**
- **C1 frame:** 2. SB6 and Batch Zero turned proving into a capital and regulatory commitment run on ERCOT's schedule.
- **C2 step-up:** 2-3. About 5-30x realistically.
- **C3 hit-rate lever:** 1-2. Capped at 3-6x and shared across the batch.
- **C4 data and right:** 1. The outcome becomes legible through a standardised batch study, and the headroom is computable by engineers.
- **C5 ladder:** 3. The ladder is real but crowded and capital-heavy.

**Total ≈ 10/25.** This is a greenfield rerun of powered brownfields and queue positions. Recommend dropping it.

deep.name: Entitled Acre (data center rezoning arbitrage)
deep.memo:
## Entitled Acre: feasibility memo (data center rezoning arbitrage)

**Search limit:** The workflow's shared WebSearch budget was already used up, so no searches ran. I fetched pages directly instead. Figures with a URL come from those fetches. Anything marked *(est.)* is from memory or my own estimate and has not been verified.

### Frame of reference
The rung is: option a farm parcel, win a rezoning or special-use permit, and sell the entitled parcel. That is a discrete, sellable product. But picking the parcel is perhaps 30-50% of the work *(est.)*. The rest is 12-24 months of hearings, studies, buffer negotiations, litigation, and above all getting power. CBRE says power availability and delivery timelines are "the most decisive factors shaping site selection, leasing activity and pricing" (https://www.cbre.com/insights/reports/north-america-data-center-trends-h1-2025). JLL puts the average grid-connection wait in primary markets at over four years (https://www.jll.com/en-us/insights/market-outlook/data-center-outlook). The physical and political step is heavy and bespoke, which makes this closer to the geothermal counter-example than to drilling. **C1 = 2.**

### Step-up ratio
- **Unproven price:** Average farm real estate value in 2025 was $6,100/ac in Virginia, $9,350 in Ohio, $8,850 in Indiana, $4,720 in Georgia and $2,970 in Texas (USDA NASS Land Values 2025, https://www.nass.usda.gov/Publications/Todays_Reports/reports/land0825.pdf). Rural land in Northern Virginia near transmission lines is more like $20-60k/ac *(est.)*. Since 2023, owners there sign contracts contingent on rezoning, at prices that already assume the rezoning *(est.; the Prince William Digital Gateway consortium is the example)*.
- **Proven price:** Entitled data center land in Northern Virginia is about $1-2.5M/ac. The brief's Avison Young figure is about $4M/ac *(not re-verified)*. Entitled land in the Columbus and Atlanta exurbs is about $100-300k/ac *(est.)*.
- **Ratio:** Gross multiples are about 10-50x *(est.)*, but most of that premium is power. Cushman & Wakefield says "land values are diverging sharply between powered and non-powered sites" (https://www.cushmanwakefield.com/en/united-states/insights/data-center-development-cost-guide). The part that zoning alone creates and an option holder can capture is probably 3-20x *(est.)*.
- **Transactions per year:** A few hundred US data center land deals a year *(est.)*.

**C2 = 2-3.**

### Hit rate and proving capex today and with ML
- **Opposition is rising fast:**
  - May 2024-Mar 2025: 16 projects worth $64B were blocked (6) or delayed (10) (https://www.datacenterwatch.org/report).
  - Q2 2025: 30 projects were targeted by opposition and 20 of them (66%) were blocked or delayed, worth $98B (https://datacenterwatch.org/q22025).
  - 2025 as a whole: at least $156B was blocked or delayed (https://datacenterwatch.org/q3-q4-2025).
  - Q2 2026 alone: at least 45 projects worth about $68B (https://datacenterwatch.org/q2-2026).
- **The tracker has no approval rate.** Against an estimated 400-800 rezonings or permits filed a year *(est.)*, about 180 blocked or delayed a year implies 20-40% "blocked or delayed". Outright denial is about 10-15% *(est.)*, so the base approval rate is about 70-85% *(est.)*.
- **The lever is small.** The ceiling is 1/0.75, about 1.3x, or about 2x if a delay counts as a miss. Some denials get reversed anyway: Fort Worth's council approved after the Zoning Commission rejected, and Powhatan approved 3-2 (datacenterwatch.org/report).
- **Cost per attempt:** About $50-300k in filing, legal and studies, plus option premiums and 1-2 years of carry *(est.)*.

ML mostly helps avoid the minority of losing fights. It does not cut capex by 10x. **C3 = 1.**

### Data source
- **Named datasets:** County planning commission and board minutes, plus video, through Legistar/Granicus portals; comprehensive plans; zoning GIS; state utility commission dockets (the Virginia SCC); local news. Access is public and free.
- **Why it is illegible:** About 3,000 counties publish unstructured PDFs and video.
- **The outcome is already summarised:**
  - Votes are recorded: Culpeper's planning commission denied unanimously; Manassas voted 6-1 against.
  - Comprehensive-plan technology overlays and moratoria (Oldham County, Apex) flag the likely answer.
  - Data Center Watch already runs a structured tracker of opposition (https://www.datacenterwatch.org/).

A lookup table on overlays and moratoria likely matches ML. This is the same failure as the interconnection-queue idea. **C4 = 1-2.**

### How the right is bought
Through purchase options or contracts contingent on rezoning, signed with farm owners. These are ordinary private contracts, not first-come claims. Typical terms are a 1-5% option fee, 18-36 months, and closing on a final non-appealable rezoning *(est.)*. But the premium is now public knowledge: owners near power and fibre price it in or form selling consortiums *(est.)*. The information gap is weak.

### Capitalised buyer
Strong:
- **Hyperscalers:** Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta.
- **Colocation developers:** QTS (Blackstone), Compass, Vantage, Stack, Aligned.
- **Funds:** Starwood and GI Partners appear in the Data Center Watch report.

Spending is huge. JLL sees about $3T of data center spending through 2030 and $10.7M/MW shell-and-core cost in 2025 (JLL URL above). Buyers pay at closing, often only once power is confirmed and appeals are resolved *(est.)*.

### Integration ladder above
The rungs run: entitled land, then powered land (utility agreement or on-site generation), then powered shell, then a leased campus, then a data center REIT or operator. The market is very large, but every rung already has deep-pocketed incumbents. The trillion-dollar end of the ladder is an existing category (Equinix or Digital Realty scale), not a new one. **C5 = 3.**

### Who else does this
- **Tract:** It does exactly this rung. It developed the $14B Buckeye, Arizona project that was withdrawn and then re-sited (datacenterwatch.org/report).
- **Other site assemblers:** Headwaters Site Development, Province Group, Provident, Diode Ventures, Culpeper Acquisitions (same source).
- **Brokers and in-house teams:** JLL, CBRE and Cushman land teams, and hyperscaler site-selection teams.

### Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
In five Virginia counties (Loudoun, Prince William, Culpeper, Fauquier, King George), pull every data center rezoning or special-use filing from 2022-2026 out of the Legistar and agenda archives. Record each outcome. Then match about 20 parcels in the public land records to their pre-filing sale or option price and their exit sale price.

The test has three kill criteria:
1. The base final approval rate is 70% or more.
2. The median ratio of exit price to pre-filing price, after removing the power premium (powered versus unpowered comps), is under 10x.
3. A simple logistic model on comprehensive-plan overlay plus distance to substation matches an LLM-over-minutes model within 0.03 AUC.

Any one of these kills the idea.

### Verdict
**Does not pass. Score about 10/25 (C1 2, C2 2.5, C3 1, C4 1.5, C5 3). Not excluded.**

The buyer and the market are real. Opposition is rising, from 16 blocked or delayed projects over two years to 45 in one quarter, which helps the case somewhat. But approval is still the base case, so the ML lever is under 2x. The step-up comes mainly from power, which planning records cannot prove. Landowners already know about the premium, and Tract plus site assemblers already run this playbook. It does not fit the Terranox shape and should not go in the YC memo as a lead idea.

Sources: [Data Center Watch report](https://www.datacenterwatch.org/report), [Data Center Watch Q2 2025](https://datacenterwatch.org/q22025), [Data Center Watch Q3-Q4 2025](https://datacenterwatch.org/q3-q4-2025), [Data Center Watch Q2 2026](https://datacenterwatch.org/q2-2026), [Data Center Watch home](https://www.datacenterwatch.org/), [USDA NASS Land Values 2025](https://www.nass.usda.gov/Publications/Todays_Reports/reports/land0825.pdf), [CBRE H1 2025](https://www.cbre.com/insights/reports/north-america-data-center-trends-h1-2025), [JLL Data Center Outlook](https://www.jll.com/en-us/insights/market-outlook/data-center-outlook), [Cushman & Wakefield cost guide](https://www.cushmanwakefield.com/en/united-states/insights/data-center-development-cost-guide).

deep.name: Old Master Sleeper Attribution (Sleeper / Sleeper Atelier / Sleeper Masters / Provenance Capital)
deep.memo:
## Frame of reference
The rung is: buy a painting catalogued as "circle of", "follower of", "after" or unattributed; get it accepted as autograph; then consign it or sell it privately. Most of the work is spotting the picture and building the case for it. Cleaning, infrared reflectography (IRR) and pigment tests are cheap and can be outsourced. The weak point is the proving gate. Value depends on whether one named authority accepts the work, and that person or committee can refuse, delay or later reverse. Christie's own specialist turned down the Salvator Mundi before it was proven ([TAN](https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2024/03/14/its-time-to-end-the-predatory-practices-of-sleeper-hunters)). Works sold through Sotheby's and later called forgeries led to a $5.3M award over a "Frans Hals" and a $1.2M repayment over a "Parmigianino" ([Wikipedia: Ruffini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuliano_Ruffini)). So the frame exists, but proving is a social process, not a measurement like a drill core.

## Step-up ratio
- **Salvator Mundi:** bought for $1,175 at St. Charles Gallery, New Orleans, in 2005. National Gallery show in 2011. Sold for $80M in 2013, then $450.3M in 2017 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvator_Mundi_(Leonardo))). That is about 68,000x, but it took 8 years, happened before online bidding was common, and the attribution is still disputed.
- **Artemisia Gentileschi:** bought for £30k at a Danish auction in 2022 and sold at Christie's for £1.9M within a year, about 63x ([TAN](https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2024/03/14/its-time-to-end-the-predatory-practices-of-sleeper-hunters)).
- **Pierozzi miniature:** bought for €7,800 at Millon, then sold by Colnaghi for "six figures", about 13-60x (same source).
- **Cimabue:** estimate €4-6M, sold for €24M at Actéon. The expert Turquin attributed it before the sale, so the consignor kept the gain ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Mocked_(Cimabue))).
- **Caravaggio Ecce Homo:** listed at €1,500 as circle of Ribera. The state halted the sale within days ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecce_Homo_(Caravaggio,_Madrid))).
- **Early Rembrandt:** offered in New Jersey at "a few hundred dollars" and spotted by the dealer Talabardon ([ArtsJournal](https://www.artsjournal.org/?p=132676)). From memory, not re-verified: the hammer was about $870k, so the bidding war captured the step-up.
- **Thomaston "After Rembrandt":** $1.175M against a $10-15k estimate (finalist notes, not re-verified).

Realised multiple for a buyer who pays a contested hammer: about 3-60x (estimate). Lots above 10^3x are rare outliers.

Transactions per year: no published count. My estimate is single digits to low tens of seven-figure re-attributions a year worldwide.

## Hit rate and proving capex, today and with ML
- No base rate is published. My estimate is that under 10% of lots a specialist would bid on get upgraded.
- Cost per shot today (estimate): hammer of $0.5-50k, often bid far above estimate on promising lots, plus technical analysis of $2-30k, restoration of $5-50k and 1-8 years of carry.
- ML only improves which lots to bid on. It does not lower the cost of the authority's consent. Purchase price is the largest cost, and it rises exactly when a lot looks promising, because human bidders see the same signal.
- AI attribution has a poor public record. Art Recognition (founded 2019) called the National Gallery's Rubens "Samson and Delilah" 91% likely fake, and the gallery dismissed the claim. Two AI systems disagreed on the de Brécy Tondo. The only work sold on AI authentication alone made CHF 15k ([Art Law & More](https://artlawandmore.com/2024/12/19/first-artwork-authenticated-solely-by-ai-sold-at-auction/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Recognition)).
- Realistic capex lever with ML: 1.5-3x (estimate), not 10x.

## Data source
- Regional lot images on Invaluable, LiveAuctioneers, Drouot and Lempertz: public, multilingual, not structured.
- Getty Provenance Index: open CSVs on GitHub covering sales catalogs, Knoedler and Goupil ([GitHub](https://github.com/thegetty/provenance-index-csv)).
- RKD: RKDimages database and about 150k auction catalogues ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RKD)).
- Also: Witt and Frick photoarchives, and digitised sale catalogues on Heidelberg and Gallica.

Is the outcome summarised in a legible field? No. The "circle of" label is the mispricing itself, which is good for the thesis. Two things weaken that:
1. Hundreds of sleeper-hunting dealers already read these catalogues by eye ([TAN](https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2024/03/14/its-time-to-end-the-predatory-practices-of-sleeper-hunters)).
2. French regional houses hire experts such as Turquin before the sale, who write the answer into the catalogue (the Cimabue case).

## How the right is bought
- **From whom:** regional auction houses and estates.
- **Legal mechanics:** outright title under caveat emptor.
- **Price:** set at an open online auction where specialist dealers compete. Only lots that every human misses stay cheap.
- **Private estate buys** avoid the competition but do not scale.
- **Regulatory risk:**
  - TAN proposes "Sleeper Resale Rights": a 0.25-4% levy on the gain, payable for up to 100 years, aimed squarely at this model.
  - National heritage blocks: Spain halted the Ecce Homo sale.

## Capitalised buyer
Christie's and Sotheby's Old Master sales (with guarantees and private sales), dealers such as Colnaghi, Weiss and Moretti, the Leiden Collection, and museums. They are real and well capitalised, but they pay only after scholarly acceptance, not on a hit. The segment is small: Old Masters are roughly $0.5-1B a year at auction (estimate; I could not verify this against the Art Basel/UBS report).

## Integration ladder above
The rungs above are dealer gallery, conservation studio, attribution authority, art-backed lending and an art fund. The ceiling is the whole art market, about $60B a year (from memory, not re-verified). There is no trillion-dollar path, and the lending and fund rungs are already crowded (Sotheby's Financial, Athena).

## Who else does this
- Sleeper-hunting dealers: Talabardon & Gautier, Colnaghi, Moretti, and Simon and Parish (the Salvator Mundi buyers).
- Pre-sale experts: Cabinet Turquin.
- Specialists at the big auction houses.
- AI attribution: Art Recognition.
- Public sleeper hunting such as Bendor Grosvenor's BBC series (from memory).

## Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
1. **Upgrade set:** scrape about 20k "circle of", "follower of" and "after" Old Master lots sold at regional houses from 2018 to 2023. Match them by image (perceptual hash plus CLIP embeddings) against Christie's, Sotheby's and TEFAF lots up to 2026 to find works that came back with an upgraded attribution.
2. **Base rate:** count the upgrades as a share of all lots.
3. **Capture ratio:** for each upgraded lot, divide the regional hammer by the later proven price.
4. **Model test:** train a pre-sale model using only pre-sale fields. Measure what share of the cheap upgrades it ranks in its top 1%.

Kill criteria:
- Fewer than 5 cheap upgrades a year, where cheap means hammer below 5% of the proven price; or
- The model ranks fewer than half of them in its top 1%.

If either holds, humans already capture the step-up and there is no business.

## Verdict
Do not pursue. The scorers' and verifiers' 10/25 holds up:

| Criterion | Score |
|---|---|
| C1 Frame | 2 |
| C2 Step-up | 2.5 |
| C3 Hit-rate lever | 1.5 |
| C4 Data and right | 1.5 |
| C5 Ladder | 2 |

The rights are bought at contested public auctions where human sleeper hunters already set the price. Proof depends on a subjective, reversible gatekeeper. The market is capped in the low billions. The backtest above is the one cheap way to overturn this verdict.
